title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
authors: Chenzhi Liu,Yue Zhang,Jiehong Lin,Jianan Wang,Bo Wang,Zhongrui Wang,Xiaojuan Qi
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable atomic skills. It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference.
Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations.
Evaluations on RoboCasa, BEHAVIOR-1K, and real-world tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MobiAgent. It outperforms π0.5\pi_{0.5}-TA by 22.5 percentage points on BEHAVIOR-1K and enables robust recovery from execution failures. Through autonomous data recycling, success improves from 7.50% to 27.50% on RoboCasa and from 32.5% to 57.5% on Astribot S1.
introduction:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires executing complex, multi-stage tasks to achieve global goals, necessitating the seamless interleaving of distinct behavioral modes including global navigation and precise prehension. This domain poses significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and the capacity interference inherent in jointly modeling disparate sensorimotor mappings for locomotion and arm control.

Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, notably OpenVLA [14], π0\pi_{0} [37], and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [36], have demonstrated exceptional proficiency in tabletop environments by directly mapping multimodal observations to continuous actions. Building on this foundation, systems like Mobi-π\pi [45] and N2M [2] extend VLAs to mobile platforms, primarily optimizing the navigation-manipulation hand-off. Nevertheless, these monolithic architectures function predominantly as reactive policies tailored for short-horizon objectives. In long-horizon scenarios, they lack the hierarchical reasoning necessary for semantic task decomposition and struggle to maintain the long-term context required for closed-loop replanning, fundamentally limiting their autonomy and reliability.

To transcend short-horizon reactive policies, recent research explores hierarchical agentic frameworks that layer Large Language Models (LLMs) or Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over low-level controllers [47, 24, 12, 22, 10, 39, 50, 21], typically adopting a plan-execute-verify paradigm. Beyond their confinement to stationary manipulation, these architectures exhibit three critical bottlenecks:
1) Constrained Planning via Sub-task Mapping: They typically assign an individual, isolated policy to each decomposed sub-task. High-level planning is then reduced to discrete selection from a predefined list rather than open-ended generation, inherently limiting scalability and increasing system overhead as the required sub-task repertoire expands.
2) Inflexible Verification and Replanning: Stemming directly from this rigid policy mapping, dynamically replanning after a verification failure becomes highly cumbersome. This inflexibility is particularly fatal in mobile manipulation, where reflection and error recovery demand complex, continuous spatial reasoning (e.g., dynamic navigation, distance and viewpoint adjustments) prior to interaction.
3) Absence of Data Curation and Policy Self-Improvement: The vast majority of these frameworks operate open-loop regarding lifelong learning. While rare exceptions like RoboClaw [21] introduce automated data collection, the field still lacks a comprehensive pipeline for unconstrained data curation and recursive self-improvement.

To bridge the gap between robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement, we propose MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic system tailored for long-horizon mobile manipulation, as shown in Fig. 1. MobiAgent decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control based on atomic skills, partitioning the system into a deployment-time Inner Loop and an offline-training Outer Loop.

To overcome the bottlenecks of constrained planning and inflexible replanning, the Inner Loop shifts the execution paradigm from rigid sub-task policies to highly composable atomic skills within a receding-horizon control flow. First, a Task Planner dynamically composes these skills on the fly. By replanning after completing each plan, it swiftly adapts to environmental changes and enables open-ended plan generation, bypassing the scalability limits of predefined sub-task lists. Next, by breaking down traditional sub-tasks into finer-grained actions, the Skill Executor employs skill-specific flow-matching experts built upon a shared VLM backbone. This semantic partitioning allows diverse sub-tasks sharing the same underlying action to reuse a single action expert, maximizing reusability while avoiding capacity interference. Finally, a Reflection Critic provides continuous visual verification to trigger flexible replanning. Operating at this granular level allows the Critic to explicitly manage the complex spatial reasoning essential for robust error recovery.

The Outer Loop drives the automated data curation and evolution of the skill library, eliminating the need for manual data curation. First, a VLM-powered Data Curator processes startup demonstrations and deployment rollouts to autonomously segment and verify trajectory clips with instruction captions. Next, an Skill Generator clusters these instructions to establish a discrete vocabulary of atomic skills, seamlessly standardizing new rollout data into this inventory. Finally, a Skill Trainer uses this curated data to instantiate and continuously fine-tune the skill policies.

To evaluate MobiAgent on long-horizon mobile manipulation, we conduct experiments across the simulated RoboCasa [31, 32] and BEHAVIOR-1K [19] benchmarks, as well as four real-world tasks on Astribot S1. On BEHAVIOR-1K, MobiAgent achieves a 65.0% mean success rate, outperforming the task-specific π0.5\pi_{0.5}-TA baseline [16] by 22.5 percentage points, while component ablations demonstrate the importance of dynamic planning, skill-specific experts, and visual verification. Its critic-driven global replanning further enables recovery from failures such as object drops and pose misalignments. Finally, deployment-to-training updates improve success from 7.50% to 27.50% on RoboCasa and from 32.5% to 57.5% on Astribot S1, validating the Outer Loop’s ability to drive continuous, annotation-free policy improvement through autonomous data recycling.

title: I2CD: Direct Image-to-Convex Decomposition for Simulation-Ready Collision Geometry
authors: Qian Wang,Liam Merz Hoffmeister,Brian Scassellati,Daniel Rakita
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Physics simulators and motion planners require convex collision geometry, yet image-to-3D generative models output dense, frequently non-manifold visual meshes. Bridging the two today takes a slow, brittle reconstruct-then-decompose pipeline of repair, decimation, and approximate convex decomposition. We present I2CD, which predicts a convex decomposition directly from a single RGB image. Rather than train a new image-to-3D model, I2CD freezes the pretrained Hunyuan3D-2 image-conditioned diffusion transformer and shape decoder and trains only a lightweight cross-attention head (38 M parameters, under ten GPU-hours) whose learned “convex-slot” tokens emit the halfplane parameters of KK convex polytopes. The output is compact, convex by construction, and loads into physics engines without any post-processing, in ∼0.5{\sim}0.5 s per image. On 227227 held-out OmniObject3D and Google Scanned Objects instances, I2CD attains the highest volumetric IoU among eight reconstruct-then-decompose pipelines while running 66–37×37\times faster end-to-end. In a cross-simulator study in MuJoCo, PyBullet, Genesis, and Isaac Sim, every engine uses I2CD geometry as delivered, whereas raw generated meshes “load” everywhere but are silently replaced by a different collision shape in most cases or need seconds to minutes of per-object preprocessing. On a physical xArm7, I2CD produces planner-ready geometry for a 2020-object cluttered scene in 1111 s versus 328328 s for the strongest baseline, at comparable pick-and-place execution success (8585 vs. 9090 of 100100 trials).

title: KungfuAthleteBot: learning high-dynamic humanoid motion from video with unified robust recovery
authors: Zhongxiang Lei,Lulu Cao,Xuyang Wang,Tianyi Qian,Jinyan Liu,Xuesong Li
abstract: Video is an abundant, inexpensive source of human motion data that is rich in extreme athletic behaviours. Making it usable for humanoid robots, however, is not a matter of simply retargeting a reconstructed trajectory: video-derived motion is physically inconsistent, devoid of actuation information, and says nothing about failure or recovery. We present KungfuAthleteBot (KAB), a framework that treats “learning high-dynamic motion from video” as the central problem and resolves each of these three failure modes in turn. (C1) We build the KungfuAthlete dataset from videos of national-level martial artists and introduce a physics-guided parabolic trajectory correction that removes height floating, ground penetration, and high-frequency jitter from reconstructed aerial and landing phases. (C2) Because video carries no force information, strict tracking of a reconstructed trajectory is dynamically infeasible, and error-driven initialisation keeps re-launching the policy from infeasible aerial poses. We introduce physics-driven pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling, our central mechanism for making such references learnable: it biases initialisation towards dynamically feasible states, letting the policy discover feasible actuation patterns instead of imitating infeasible ones. (C3) Finally, we introduce a direct training paradigm in which disturbance rejection and fall recovery are learned inside the same policy that tracks the video motion, requiring no recovery reference data and no manual mode switching. On a real humanoid robot, KAB learns highly dynamic skills from video and recovers from arbitrary falls in ≈0.7\approx 0.7 s, to our knowledge the fastest reported recovery for a unified policy. Ablations on the unified policy confirm the necessity of its components, supporting the view that repairing and compensating video data – rather than only collecting more of it – is what unlocks high-dynamic humanoid skills. Code and data: https://kungfuathletebot.github.io/.
introduction:
Humanoid robots that can execute highly dynamic, athletic skills – aerial spins, flips, and explosive strikes – are a long-standing goal of the field (Fig. 1). The dominant bottleneck is no longer the control algorithm but the data that drives it Liao et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2026); Sun et al. (2025). Motion-capture pipelines require instrumented studios, wearable hardware, and bespoke collection procedures: they are expensive, slow to scale, and restricted to controlled environments. This paper starts from a different premise: compared with motion capture and wearable systems, video is abundant, inexpensive, and able to capture elite athleticism outside the laboratory.

Learning high-dynamic motion from video, however, is harder than learning from curated motion-capture data, and this is the problem we address. Retargeting a reconstructed human trajectory to a humanoid and running reinforcement learning on it does not work out of the box, for reasons that are specific and diagnosable:

(C1) Video reconstructions are physically inconsistent. Monocular reconstruction methods such as GVHMR Shen et al. (2024) and generative models such as GENMO Li et al. (2025a) produce motion that is globally smooth but locally unphysical: during flight the root height “floats” instead of following a ballistic arc, the feet penetrate the ground on landing, and frame-wise noise appears as joint jitter. This is not a cosmetic issue – a floating root makes the aerial phase dynamically impossible for any robot.

(2025a) produce motion that is globally smooth but locally unphysical: during flight the root height “floats” instead of following a ballistic arc, the feet penetrate the ground on landing, and frame-wise noise appears as joint jitter. This is not a cosmetic issue – a floating root makes the aerial phase dynamically impossible for any robot.

(C2) Video contains no actuation information. A trajectory reconstructed from pixels describes where the body goes, not how the joints are driven to get there. In explosive motions such as a backflip, the human and the robot realise the same joint trajectory with radically different torque profiles (e.g. at the knee); demanding strict tracking therefore asks the robot to reproduce a physically infeasible joint trajectory, and learning stalls.

(C3) Video says nothing about failure. A video ends when the motion ends; it provides no model of disturbance, loss of balance, or recovery. A policy that faithfully tracks video motion is therefore also a policy that has no idea what to do once the real world pushes it off the reference trajectory.

Our central claim is that these three failure modes are not incidental implementation details but the actual obstacles to learning high-dynamic motion from video, and that they can only be overcome jointly. Accordingly, the paper is organised as a single pipeline, where each technical contribution is precisely the remedy for one failure mode, and where an ablation shows that removing any one of them breaks the pipeline.

The video-to-robot pathway. Videos are segmented into clips, reconstructed to a kinematic sequence 𝐪hum1:T\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{hum}}_{1:T}, retargeted Araujo et al. (2025) to the robot to give a reference 𝐪ref1:T\mathbf{q}^{\mathrm{ref}}_{1:T}, and tracked by a policy π\pi. The last three steps are where the pathway breaks, and they require two sub-systems: a repair stage that restores physical validity, and a compensation stage that supplies, through learning, the dynamics and the failure model that video never contained. These are not independently swappable: without the compensation, strict single-stage tracking of an infeasible reference collapses (Fig. 4a), and without the unified recovery the robot cannot return to the motion once disturbed (Sec. 6.5).

Contributions.

A video-derived professional high-dynamic dataset (addresses C1). In collaboration with national-level martial artists, we construct KungfuAthlete from 197 training videos, segmented into 1,726 sub-clips, reconstructed and retargeted to a Unitree G1. It covers both sustained ground skills and highly non-stationary aerial skills, with higher body linear and angular velocities than the corpora compared in Table 1. Dataset, licence and released artefacts are detailed in Sec. 3.1.

A physics-aware repair of video artifacts (addresses C1). We replace the floating root trajectory with a physically consistent one: ground alignment from the lowest body point, event-aware propagation with contact detection, ballistic (constant-acceleration) interpolation of flight phases, penetration removal, and Savitzky–Golay smoothing. Unlike prior work that simply discards jump segments as unusable, our correction recovers them, preventing a large-scale waste of the most valuable video data.

We introduce pseudo-low-kinetic-energy (LKE) sampling, our central mechanism for making unreliable video references learnable: rather than initialising wherever the current tracking error is largest, it derives the initial-state distribution from a kinetic-energy proxy of the reference and therefore never concentrates capacity on dynamically infeasible aerial poses. A standard progressive-tolerance curriculum complements it (Sec. 4.3); Sec. 4.4 contrasts our setting – unreliable video-derived references – with prior high-dynamic tracking work that assumes faithful references.

A unified robust policy over video data (addresses C3). We propose a direct formulation in which one policy tracks the video motion, rejects disturbances, and recovers from arbitrary gravity-induced falls, with no recovery-specific reference data and no manual switching. It attains ≈0.7\approx 0.7 s recovery – to our knowledge the fastest reported for a unified policy – validated on real hardware.

Sec. 2 positions this work against prior art. title: Equivariant Visual-Tactile Diffusion Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Lik Hang Kenny Wong,Yiyao Ma,Xiu-Shen Wei,Zelong Tan,Zhuheng Song,Dongsheng Xie,Kai Chen,Qi Dou
comment: . Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
abstract: Imitation learning for contact-rich manipulation requires high-quality expert data that is expensive to obtain. This makes learning a sample-efficient policy a key issue. To address this, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy for data-efficient contact-rich imitation learning. VISTA projects visual and tactile observations into spherical tokens, injects tactile contact cues into visual spherical directions through permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, and rotates the fused harmonic representation using the end-effector orientation. The resulting representation conditions an equivariant diffusion policy to predict spatially consistent actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world robotic settings show that VISTA substantially improves data efficiency over strong visuotactile imitation learning baselines. Project website: https://vista-paper.github.io/
introduction:
Many daily contact-rich tasks, such as inserting a USB drive or wiping a table, require tactile sensing in addition to vision. For robots, however, using both modalities effectively remains challenging. Recent robotics research has increasingly adopted imitation learning with visual and tactile feedback for contact-rich manipulation [41, 8, 37], but expert demonstrations are expensive to collect and often cover only a limited range of object poses, gripper poses, and contact configurations [29]. Moreover, for tasks such as insertion, success depends heavily on the policy’s robustness to small deviations in observed object and robot poses [16]. Therefore, how can we learn robust visuotactile policies with fewer demonstrations?

Equivariance provides a principled way to reduce the spatial coverage required from data for a policy to achieve spatial robustness [36, 4, 26, 6, 15]. In an equivariant policy, if the observation is transformed by a spatial transformation from a symmetry group, the predicted action should transform in the corresponding way.
By building this symmetry into the architecture, the model can improve spatial generalizability across object poses, gripper poses, and scene configurations with fewer demonstrations than non-equivariant policies [35, 33]. This is especially appealing for contact-rich manipulation, where demonstrations are costly, and task success is sensitive to small spatial deviations. However, existing equivariant manipulation policies are still largely vision-centric. They are typically designed around RGB images, point clouds, or other global geometric observations [20], limiting their ability to handle contact-rich settings where local tactile feedback is critical.

In this paper, we propose VISTA, a workspace-level equivariant visuotactile diffusion policy. Our method is inspired by the observation that both egocentric camera and tactile sensors are often mounted on the end effector of a robot for manipulation tasks; therefore, global workspace rotations change the sensor-to-world transform while preserving the local contact measurement. Concretely, our method first maps egocentric vision and tactile observations into local spherical representations. It then performs permutation-equivariant spherical fusion, allowing tactile contact cues to modulate visual directions while preserving the spherical structure of the representation. The fused spherical representation is then transformed by the end-effector pose rotation and processed with an equivariant diffusion policy to achieve workspace-level equivariance. As a result, VISTA improves data efficiency and generalization under limited demonstrations. We evaluate VISTA on both contact-rich simulation tasks and real-robot experiments and show that the proposed framework enables more data-efficient contact-rich manipulation learning.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce VISTA, extending the workspace-level equivariant backbone from Image-to-Sphere Policy (ISP) [12] to the visuotactile setting for contact-rich tasks, enabling more data-efficient learning by incorporating local tactile feedback into an equivariant policy.

We design a spherical cross-modal fusion module that integrates tactile cues into the structured visual representation, allowing the downstream equivariant diffusion policy to leverage the fused representation effectively. Across eight simulated tasks, this design improves mean success by 6.8 percentage points over direct visual-tactile feature concatenation on the sphere.

We demonstrate data-efficient contact-rich manipulation across eight simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks: VISTA achieves 80.9% mean success, outperforming EquiDiff+Tac by 15.9 percentage points, and 73.3% average success on real robots.

1. We introduce VISTA, extending the workspace-level equivariant backbone from Image-to-Sphere Policy (ISP) [12] to the visuotactile setting for contact-rich tasks, enabling more data-efficient learning by incorporating local tactile feedback into an equivariant policy.

2. We design a spherical cross-modal fusion module that integrates tactile cues into the structured visual representation, allowing the downstream equivariant diffusion policy to leverage the fused representation effectively. Across eight simulated tasks, this design improves mean success by 6.8 percentage points over direct visual-tactile feature concatenation on the sphere.

3. We demonstrate data-efficient contact-rich manipulation across eight simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks: VISTA achieves 80.9% mean success, outperforming EquiDiff+Tac by 15.9 percentage points, and 73.3% average success on real robots.

title: HexVIO: Towards All-Day Stereo-Inertial Tracking Through Commodity DSPs
authors: Patrick Wolf,Mateo de Mayo,Daniel Cremers
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
The ability of a device to localize itself within its surroundings is a fundamental prerequisite for spatial computing. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) has proven to be a cost-effective and accurate solution for this task.
Robots, wearables, XR devices, and drones can benefit significantly from efficient implementations of VIO since they allow for cooler, lighter, and cheaper devices with longer battery life and a better user experience. In this work, we propose to enhance the efficiency of a VIO system by leveraging the Hexagon DSP, a commodity co-processor present in many modern smartphones and XR devices. Our approach offloads the visual frontend of a stereo-inertial odometry system to the DSP while keeping the backend on the main CPU. By optimizing the implementation for the DSP architecture, we achieve significant reductions in power consumption and latency compared to CPU-only execution. Our system, HexVIO, demonstrates a 67% reduction in power consumption or an 86% increase in throughput on a commodity smartphone, with the ability to sustain long-term real-time 30 fps tracking for 0.83 W, corresponding to ∼\sim18 hours of tracking on the testing device. These results highlight the potential of commodity DSPs for enabling all-day visual-inertial tracking in robotics and mobile devices.
introduction:
Recent advancements in robotics [1, 2], computer vision [3, 4, 5, 6], and foundation models capable of complex reasoning [7, 8, 9] have started to show the possibilities of perception engineering [10] as a new discipline and of spatial computing [11] as the ever more common class of problems that require a computing device to understand its surroundings. Different instances of this problem arise in important applications like autonomous vehicles, drones, humanoid robotics, wearables like smartglasses, and VR headsets. A fundamental capability that allows much of this reasoning comes from the ability of the device to localize itself and its movements in space. Utilizing cameras and inertial measurement units (IMU) for visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and visual-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (VI-SLAM) has shown to be a particularly good combination thanks to the low cost of these sensors, their reduced power consumption, and proven accuracy [12, 13].

The field of VIO and VI-SLAM has made rapid progress in the previous decade enabling this technology to be deployed in commercial devices like VR headsets and smartphones. However, existing limitations in terms of accuracy per watt remain in the literature [14], driving research into highly specialized hardware accelerators [15, 16]. These accelerators reach their efficiency through custom silicon, so they only ship in devices designed around them. We instead use a co-processor that existing devices already carry. It is nowadays common to find systems, even low-end ones, that have a GPU alongside the CPU. DSPs have developed from fixed-function audio and modem processors into increasingly general-purpose compute units that run at a fraction of the energy cost of a CPU [17]. The Hexagon DSP is now present in a multitude of devices spanning smartphones, VR, AR, and robotics (e.g., Snapdragon 8, XR2, AR1, and RB5 respectively). The DSP provides very long instruction words with wide vector lanes coupled with fast local memory. When properly utilized, this results in significantly reduced power usage for certain tasks compared to using the CPU or GPU. This kind of co-processor allows robots, XR devices, and smartphones to do long-haul vision tasks thanks to the low power required to perform them on these accelerators. The low power not only extends operation, but can also directly improve the target application: smaller batteries for lighter and cheaper drones, lighter headworn devices for reduced neck strain, and cooler smartglasses for improved comfort. The goal we work towards is tracking that runs for a full day on a device’s own battery. Even with all these benefits, very few works in the literature exploit it for the fundamental task of visual-inertial tracking and, to the best of our knowledge, none of them for the stereo-inertial sensor modality.

In this work, we offload the frontend of a visual-inertial odometry system based on Basalt [18] to the Hexagon DSP of a Samsung Galaxy S23 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, Hexagon V73). A direct port does not beat the CPU. Sparse tracking branches per feature and reads scattered pixels, the vector unit runs all lanes together and its gather reads only on-chip memory, and each DSP call costs hundreds of microseconds, so calling the DSP once per stage spends much of the gain on round trips. Most of the work is restructuring the frontend around these three constraints. The contributions of this work are:

The first stereo-inertial odometry system in the literature leveraging the Hexagon DSP co-processor.

title: DexJoCo-X: Benchmarking Action Representations for Multi-Hand Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Xiangwei Jiang,Yao Mu,Lixin Duan,Wen Li
abstract: As dexterous hands proliferate, collecting data and training policies separately for every morphology becomes increasingly impractical. Scalable cross-embodiment learning therefore requires a unified representation that captures shared manipulation structure while preserving morphology-specific control. Differences in hands, tasks, datasets, and control interfaces prevent existing studies from isolating the effects of representation, pretraining, and architecture. We introduce DexJoCo-X, a benchmark and toolkit for controlled comparison across seven representative dexterous hands, six single-arm and bimanual tasks, and 2,100 balanced demonstrations. DexJoCo-X provides a matched multi-hand, multi-task protocol with common scenes, success criteria, and execution interfaces, redesigned glove-to-hand mappings, and an automated pipeline that expands reviewed demonstrations across randomized scenes. Using π0.5\pi_{0.5}, Ego-Pi, and Being-H0.5, we examine whether a shared action interface is sufficient for multi-hand learning. Expanding π0.5\pi_{0.5} to an 80-dimensional bimanual output yields near-zero success. Ego-Pi preserves the pretrained action head through interleaved prediction and supports per-hand multi-task learning, but remains ineffective for seven-hand joint training. By contrast, Being-H0.5 combines cross-embodiment pretraining, a unified action space, and embodiment-aware experts, enabling one policy to control all seven hands. Within this architecture, function-aligned action slots achieve 47.7% mean success, compared with 47.0% for native coordinates and 33.1% for DexLatent. These results show that cross-embodiment representation depends on the entire learning system: action coordinates, pretraining, and architecture must jointly separate shared manipulation structure from embodiment-specific control.
introduction:
Learning manipulation skills that can be shared across dexterous hands is essential for deploying general-purpose robots on diverse hardware. Diverse hand kinematics and actuation fragment demonstrations and policies, making separate training costly and limiting experience reuse. Multi-embodiment datasets and generalist policies, including Open X-Embodiment/RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, HPT, and the π\pi series [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], establish a foundation for sharing robot experience. RT-2 [7] transfers vision–language knowledge to control. RDT-1B [8] uses unified action coordinates, and X-VLA [9] addresses embodiment heterogeneity through soft prompts, while Being-H0.5 [10] and Ego-Pi [11] connect human demonstrations with robot learning. Complementary approaches include diffusion policies with shared action latents [12, 13] and cross-hand reinforcement learning [14]. These efforts motivate action representations that link shared skills to embodiment-specific execution. Recent dexterous foundation-model frameworks, including UniDex [15] and XL-VLA [16], report promising multi-hand learning capabilities through different representations. Yet results obtained with different hands, datasets, and task protocols do not establish which approach best supports cross-hand manipulation under a common evaluation standard.

Existing benchmarks provide complementary capabilities: DexArt [17] studies articulated objects, Bi-DexHands [18] emphasizes bimanual control, DexJoCo [19] supplies functional tasks and demonstration tools, and DexVerse [20] broadens task and embodiment coverage. These benchmarks expand task coverage, but leave open which action representations best support cross-hand learning under matched conditions. A fair comparison requires the same hands, tasks, demonstrations, policy backbone, and success criteria. A shared control interface is also needed to evaluate new representations without rebuilding the hand-control pipeline. These needs motivate a dedicated benchmark for fair and accessible cross-hand evaluation.

To address these needs, we introduce DexJoCo-X, a unified benchmark and toolkit designed for fair comparison and straightforward integration of cross-hand policies (Fig. ). Built on DexJoCo, it combines seven hand interfaces, six tasks, and 2,100 demonstrations with a reusable collection pipeline. We fine-tune π0.5\pi_{0.5} [6] with the Ego-Pi protocol [11] as a per-hand multi-task reference, training one Native-action policy for each hand. Our central cross-hand comparison instead trains one Being-H0.5 policy [10] jointly on all seven hands under Native, FAAS, or DexLatent, and evaluates every hand on independent scenes. Our contributions are:

A unified cross-hand benchmark. Seven hands and six tasks share evaluation scenes, success criteria, and control interfaces for fair comparison of action representations under matched training conditions.

A reusable demonstration collection toolkit. Redesigned glove-to-hand mappings for all seven hands support human teleoperation, while automated scene expansion and trajectory verification scale demonstration collection.

A balanced multi-hand demonstration dataset. We collect 2,100 demonstrations spanning six single-arm and bimanual tasks, with 50 trajectories for each of the 42 hand–task pairs.

title: Beyond Reward Hacking: Proxy Divergence Across Four Layers of a Staged Humanoid Learning Pipeline
authors: Arunabh Bora
abstract:
A reinforcement-learning (RL) pipeline for a legged robot is assembled from proxies. A
reward stands in for intended behaviour, a curriculum gate stands in for competence, an
evaluation statistic stands in for robustness, and a reference motion stands in for an
achievable skill. The traditional view treats only the first of these as optimised
against, and so locates specification failure (reward hacking) in the reward alone. I
argue that all four are proxies in the same formal sense, that each has a characteristic
divergence mechanism, and that each admits a reformulation that closes it. For every
layer I state the traditional formulation, derive the condition under which it diverges
from its target, and give the alternative: first-order (L1) costs where quadratic
kernels are flat, peak and outcome statistics where curriculum gates average, gate
reachability and information checks, deterministic and phase-desynchronised evaluation,
curriculum state treated as part of the model, feasibility-first reference design with
residual feed-forward, and function-preserving input widening that lets one policy grow
instead of being retrained. The arguments are illustrated by measurements from one
continuous lineage of a PPO policy for a simulated 1.91 m humanoid, grown over four
stages and 13,500 iterations on a single laptop GPU. Among them, a curriculum gate built
on averaged error advanced at its rate limit on every check while the skill it gated was
absent, and a batched push test whose synchronised resets aliased the gait phase ranked a
0.5 m/s push as more dangerous than a 2.0 m/s one.
introduction:
GPU-parallel simulation has made it routine to train a locomotion policy
in hours on one machine [1, 2]. The resulting pipeline has a
standard shape: a weighted sum of shaped reward terms, a performance-gated curriculum over
terrain and commands, batched evaluation in the simulator, and, for skills beyond
locomotion, a tracking reward towards a reference motion [3]. Each of these
components replaces something physical with something computable.

The literature on specification gaming [4, 5, 6, 7] studies
the gap between a proxy and its target, but in robot learning it is applied almost
exclusively to the reward. The other components are treated as plumbing: a curriculum
threshold is a tuning constant, an evaluation script is assumed to measure what it
reports, and a reference motion is assumed to be achievable. My thesis is that this
traditional view is incomplete. A curriculum gate is optimised against just as a reward
is, because the policy that passes it is the one the gate selects. An evaluation
statistic is a proxy whose bias can be created by the harness itself, with no
optimisation at all. A reference motion is a proxy for a skill, and it can be wrong in a
way that no reward design can repair.

A four-layer formulation of proxy divergence (reward, curriculum,
measurement, reference), with, for each layer, the traditional formulation, the
condition under which it diverges, and a reformulation (Sections
IV–VII, summarised in Table III).

A four-layer formulation of proxy divergence (reward, curriculum,
measurement, reference), with, for each layer, the traditional formulation, the
condition under which it diverges, and a reformulation (Sections
IV–VII, summarised in Table III).

Curriculum gates as estimators: a dilution bound showing that gates on
error averaged over joints and time cannot reject large localised failures, a
reachability condition, an information argument for counting gate refusals, and the
observation that curriculum state belongs to the model, not the environment
(Section V).

Two systematic evaluation biases that do not shrink with sample size:
outcomes manufactured by exploration noise, and phase aliasing from synchronised
resets, with corrected estimators (Section VI).

Feasibility-first reference design: why tracking an infeasible reference
converges to a qualitatively different behaviour regardless of reward shaping, and
a static test, a correction and a residual action that avoid it
(Section VII).

Function-preserving policy growth through input widening and split
authority, as an alternative to retraining from scratch whenever the observation
changes (Section VIII).

title: Safe Streaming Flow Planning by Aligning Sampling Dynamics with Execution Dynamics
authors: Seunghwan Jang,Jeongyong Yang,Siddharth Ancha,SooJean Han
comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). Project page:this https URL
abstract:
Generative planners based on diffusion//flow matching can learn to synthesize long-horizon trajectories from demonstrations. However, real-world deployment requires (i) enforcing safety constraints during execution and (ii) tight online replanning at fast execution rates.
Prior safe diffusion//flow planners generate the agent’s full trajectory at once, while repeatedly perturbing intermediate states to satisfy safety constraints. This approach is not only computationally intensive, but also introduces distribution shift since the learned sampling dynamics is distinct from the system’s execution dynamics.
We propose SafeStreamingFlow, a goal-conditioned planner that aligns flow sampling dynamics with execution dynamics by sequentially integrating a learned state vector field with hierarchical state prediction.
Importantly, we need to enforce safety constraints only for the executed step via high order control barrier functions.
Across navigation, racing, and locomotion benchmarks, SafeStreamingFlow reduces planning latency and improves safety compared to existing methods, while maintaining competitive goal-reaching success.
Code is available on our project page: https://jang-seunghwan.github.io/SafeStreamingFlowPlanning/.
introduction:
Generative models [11, 20] that have driven rapid progress in image and language generation are increasingly being adapted to robotic tasks, particularly diffusion [14, 8, 15] and flow matching [30].
Deploying such models for robot planning, however, requires more than producing a plausible trajectory.
Most diffusion/flow planners typically generate an entire horizon as a single object in trajectory space and refine it through KK denoising/sampling steps, where each step updates all HH states in the trajectory [14].
In a closed-loop setting, this full-horizon procedure must be repeated at every control cycle to incorporate state feedback and new observations, generating H×KH\times K intermediate states per cycle [16, 13].

Another key challenge is enforcing safety constraints imposed at inference time, possibly never seen during training, in a manner that is both reliable and compatible with closed-loop execution. Many generative methods promote safety through guidance [7, 12], injecting heuristic costs, penalties, or constraint-related scores into the generation process to steer samples away from unsafe regions; such guidance either requires the constraint to be learned in advance or imposes it only softly, without formal guarantees [17, 21].
An especially promising approach to certified safety is to incorporate control barrier functions (CBFs) [2, 1] into the sampling procedure by solving quadratic programs (QPs) at inference time; the constraints then hold whenever each QP is feasible.
However, because intermediate sampling states are not physically executed, enforcing safety during sampling can disrupt dynamical consistency of the generated trajectories and induce local-traps, discontinuous trajectories that remain safe but infeasible to execute [30, 28].

In addition, safety enforcement further increases the computational burden because CBF-based corrections are applied across both the horizon length HH and sampling iterations KK, resulting in (H×K)(H\times K) QP solves to generate a single trajectory.
Streaming-based formulations [13, 16] have been introduced for real-time execution by aligning sampling time with execution time.
However, existing streaming approaches are developed primarily as policies for action imitation, leaving both the system’s execution dynamics and start–goal-conditioned planning unaddressed.

We propose SafeStreamingFlow, a safe streaming planner that aligns the generative process with execution (Figure 1).
Instead of sampling at the full trajectory level, SafeStreamingFlow integrates a learned state vector field in physical time and produces a one-step-ahead reference.
In this one-step prediction, however, the learned field tends to become a local inertial extrapolator rather than a goal-conditioned planner; we suppress this with a hierarchical state predictor that sequentially updates position then velocity.
The one-step-ahead reference is then tracked by a PD controller, and the resulting nominal control input is filtered through high order control barrier functions that minimally modify the executed input to satisfy safety constraints that were never seen during training.

Table 1 positions SafeStreamingFlow along four properties that classical and generative planners typically trade off: a cost-function-free formulation, multimodal trajectory generation, execution-time safety, and real-time streaming.
Classical planners (RRT*, A*) satisfy safety constraints by construction but require engineered costs and produce a single non-streaming plan; generative planners (Diffuser, SafeDiffuser) gain cost-function-free multimodality but offer only partial, non-streaming safety. SafeStreamingFlow is the only paradigm attaining all four.

title: Subject-Specific Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulations of Lower-Limb Exoskeleton Assistance: Metabolic and Biomechanical Effects of Joint Assistance Strategies
authors: Neethan Ratnakumar,Mariya Tohfafarosha,Xianlian Zhou
abstract: Lower-limb exoskeletons have made considerable progress in reducing energy expenditure during walking. However, designing optimal assistance strategies remains challenging, particularly given inter-individual variability in anthropometry and biomechanics. This study explores energy-optimal lower-limb joint-assistance strategies using predictive simulations with musculoskeletal models. Subject-specific models of six able-bodied subjects, with BMI-based muscle strength scaling, were used in predictive simulations to generate gait at self-selected walking speeds. Ideal actuators were incorporated to simulate various combinations of joint assistance at peak levels of 25​Nm25~\mathrm{Nm\par} and 50​Nm50~\mathrm{Nm\par} to examine the effects of assistance on gait and metabolic savings. The effects of each assistance configuration were assessed through cost of transport (\acsCOT), joint kinematics, muscle activations, assistive torques, and joint-level power metrics to characterize the biomechanical and energetic impacts of different assistance strategies. At 50​Nm50~\mathrm{Nm\par}, combined H+K+A (hip–knee–ankle) assistance resulted in the greatest mean COT reduction of 48.50 ±\pm 4.55%

title: On Representational Alignment among Embodied Agents
authors: Fulvio Mastrogiovanni
abstract:
Embodied agents interacting with the same physical process may maintain heterogeneous, asynchronous, and observer-relative representations.
Rather than assuming that such representations should always be globally aligned, we investigate which distinctions among them must actually be resolved for coherent interaction.
We formalize this question through relational sufficiency: an interaction-specific relational-evidence map defines the representational ambiguity left unresolved by comparison, and sufficiency holds when each residual ambiguity fiber lies within an interaction-equivalence class.
When this condition fails, additional sensorimotor anchors must separate precisely the ambiguities that can change the interaction-relevant outcome.
For smooth systems, we derive a local first-order lower bound on the number of independent scalar anchors required, given by the dimension of directions that are invisible to relational evidence but visible to the interaction-relevant map.
We instantiate the theory in two variants of an asynchronous hand-off scenario that share the same observer agents, representations, transports, and relational evidence.
Relative synchronization requires no additional anchor, whereas hand-off at an absolute time requires exactly one.
The analysis therefore provides a task-relative stopping condition for representational alignment: residual disagreement need not be eliminated when it is invariant with respect to the interaction.
introduction:
Embodied, cognitive agents do not observe and act in the world from a common viewpoint.
Their access to an environment is mediated by their body morphologies, sensors, action capabilities, interaction histories, and internal
representational processes.
Even when two agents cooperate by interacting with the same physical process, the representations available to them may differ in reference frame, time, content, abstraction level, or semantic form.
Partial and asynchronous observations further amplify these differences.
From the perspective of embodied cognitive systems, this raises a basic question: what kind of representational compatibility is actually required for coherent interaction between two or more embodied agents?

A common approach is to seek some form of representational alignment.
Different methods have been pursued toward this aim.
Distributed estimation methods aim at deriving mutually compatible estimates of a shared state;
multi-agent systems exchange information to coordinate private beliefs;
multimodal and cross-agent representation-learning methods construct mappings between heterogeneous latent spaces;
recent work has shown that local comparison spaces can support alignment even when a single global latent space is absent (Robinson, 2017; Moschella et al., 2023; Ghalkha et al., 2026; D’Acunto et al., 2026).
Similarly, recent embodied multi-agent architectures explicitly study the alignment of private world models through communication (Dongre and Hakkani-Tür, 2026).
These developments substantially weaken the requirement that different agents should maintain identical internal representations.
They nevertheless retain, in different forms, an objective of making the representations relevant to coordination mutually compatible.

This paper investigates a different possibility.
We ask whether some representational disagreements can remain unresolved because they are irrelevant to the interaction task.
More precisely, we consider embodied observer agents whose local representations may be heterogeneous and not directly comparable;
when required, observer-specific representations are transported into an interaction-dependent comparison context;
the resulting joint relational configuration may still be compatible with multiple underlying representational configurations.
We refer to this residual indeterminacy as relational ambiguity.
Our central hypothesis is that such ambiguity need not be eliminated in general.
It only needs to be resolved along those representational degrees of freedom that can change the task-relevant outcome.

This small shift changes the question from how two representations should be globally aligned to which relations between them must be determined.
The distinction is especially important in the case of embodied agents.
For such agents, representations are not detached descriptions, as they participate in a closed sensorimotor loop in which sensing produces observer-relative information, representations support action, actions modify subsequent interaction conditions, and new observations constrain what the agents can continue to represent.
Therefore, the environment may constrain local representations through the consequences of sensorimotor interaction without providing the agents with a
privileged, globally accessible representation of itself.

A minimal example illustrates the issue.
Let us consider two embodied observers coordinating around the future occurrence of an event, for example, to determine when such an event will occur.
The first observer represents the event through an estimated distance and velocity, while the second represents it directly through an estimated time-to-event.
Their native representations differ, but both can be transported into estimates of event time.
Let us suppose that the only relational evidence available after transport is the difference between the two estimates.
This evidence is invariant to a common temporal shift of both estimates.
If the interaction requires only relative synchronization, the common shift is therefore irrelevant, and every representation pair related by that shift supports the same task response.
If, instead, the interaction requires both agents to act relative to an external physical event, the same ambiguity becomes consequential.
Relative agreement is then insufficient, and some additional sensorimotor relation to the environment is required.
It is noteworthy that the observers, their representations, their transport mechanisms, and their relational evidence can remain unchanged across the two cases, since only the task determines whether the unresolved ambiguity matters.

We use this contrast to develop a theory of relational sufficiency among embodied observer agents.
Let a joint configuration of transported representations be denoted by qq, and let CI​(q)C_{I}(q) denote the relational evidence available for an interaction II.
The configurations that cannot be distinguished through this evidence form an ambiguity class ΩC​(q)\Omega_{C}(q).
Independently, the interaction induces an equivalence relation over representational configurations, such that two configurations are equivalent when they cannot be distinguished by the task-relevant response.
The resulting class is denoted by [q]Θ[q]_{\Theta}.
Therefore, the basic sufficiency condition studied in this paper is

It can be noted that this relation expresses a deliberately weaker requirement than representational identification or global alignment.
Relational evidence is sufficient whenever all configurations that remain epistemically indistinguishable are also indistinguishable to the
interaction.
The interacting agents do not have to determine which member of the equivalence class is the “correct” representation.

However, when this inclusion relation fails, relational evidence leaves unresolved a distinction that the interaction can detect.
We introduce sensorimotor anchors to characterize the additional information required in this case.
An anchor is not a global world representation or an oracle supplying ground truth.
On the contrary, it is an interaction-derived constraint that is available through the agents’ admissible sensorimotor coupling.
For example, it could be an environmental cue, a contact event, a landmark observation, or other locally obtainable consequence of interaction.
Anchors are sufficient when they separate those relational ambiguities that correspond to different task-relevant outcomes.
This leads to a principle that guides our model, that is, an embodied agent should resolve only those relational ambiguities that the interaction itself can distinguish.

In this paper, we develop this principle formally and examine its consequences in two analytically solvable variants of the same hand-off scenario.
The two variants share the same observer agents, local representations, representational transports, and relational evidence, but differ in their task invariances.
The first introduces an observer-relative synchronization task, in which the ambiguity preserved by relational evidence is entirely task-invariant and no additional anchor is required.
In the second, we discuss an absolute hand-off task, for which the same ambiguity is task-relevant and exactly one independent scalar
anchor is required.
The comparison therefore isolates task structure, rather than representational accuracy or sensing capability, as the factor that determines how much relational alignment is necessary.

The main contributions of the paper are as follows.

We formulate relational sufficiency for two embodied observer agents with heterogeneous local representations, and we explicitly distinguish relational epistemic evidence, task response, and interaction adequacy.

We establish a mismatch result showing that relational evidence is insufficient whenever it preserves ambiguities that the task can distinguish, and we characterize sufficient sensorimotor anchoring as the separation of such task-conflicting ambiguities.

We derive a local first-order lower bound on the number of independent scalar anchors required for relational sufficiency; the bound is given by the dimensional mismatch between directions that are invisible to relational evidence and directions that are invariant to the task.

We instantiate the theory in two asynchronous hand-off toy scenarios and show analytically that the same relational ambiguity requires no anchors for relative synchronization but one anchor for absolute interaction; we further show that adequacy can require less information than exact task-response reconstruction.

The remainder of the paper first positions the problem with respect to existing work on representation alignment, sufficient representations, decentralized information, and task-relevant observability, while introducing the hand-off scenarios that serve as a running example.
Then, we define the sensorimotor and representational model of embodied observer agents, develop the relational sufficiency and anchoring results, and instantiate them analytically in the two hand-off scenarios.
Finally, we discuss implications for representation alignment, learning for embodied agents, the degenerate single-observer case, and extensions to interactions involving more than two observer agents.

title: From Language Priors to Field Adaptation: Preference Learning for Traversability Estimation
authors: Simon Schwaiger,David Seyser,Alessandro Scherl,Zlatan Ajanović,Wilfried Wöber,Gerald Steinbauer-Wagner
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Image-based traversability estimation is inherently dependent on the robot platform, deployment domain, and mission preferences, which limits the applicability of purpose-trained models.
To facilitate domain adaptation, this work aims to reduce the number of required annotations in the target domain using sample-efficient preference learning.
Our method represents traversability through von Mises-Fisher mixture prototypes in a frozen vision-language feature space.
Relative natural-language rules provide a commonsense prior, while sparse relative image annotations adapt the prototype directions and utilities to a target domain through computationally and sample-efficient fine-tuning.
Experiments on WayFAST demonstrate accuracy competitive with end-to-end trained estimators while enabling sample-efficient image-based adaptation.
Qualitative experiments further demonstrate the language prior’s zero shot applicability and the fine-tuned estimator’s improved dense prediction on semantic maps.
Evaluation is complemented via semantic interpretation of learned prototypes by dissecting semantically close natural language prompts.
Code and trained estimators available at https://resireg.github.io.
introduction:
Image-based traversability estimation (TE) is important for autonomous outdoor navigation since it incorporates semantic differences between surfaces that might be geometrically similar but have different traversability properties.
However, TE is challenging due to the lack of platform- and domain-agnostic ground truth data.
Furthermore, the same terrain may have different traversability costs for different robots and application domains [1, 2, 3].
Existing methods have tackled TE by i) learning physical capability from robot-specific field experience [4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], ii) learning from absolute or relative human supervision [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15], and iii) using language and foundation models as broad priors [16, 17, 18, 2].
However, these methods either require i) physical robot experience, limiting zero-shot domain-adaptation, ii) platform-specific annotations, or iii) expensive computational power to provide semantically broad predictions, not suitable for targeted domain adaptation from experience.

We hypothesise that traversability does not need to be relearned from scratch as a dense visual prediction problem for each domain transfer.
We leverage terrain structure encoded in a frozen vision language model (VLM) [19].
The VLM feature space, aligned across frozen image and language encoders, is reused across application domains.
This allows our method to be used zero-shot on out-of-distribution domains using a generic language prior, while enabling subsequent fine-tuning on image-based field data.
Instead of training a prediction head on top of a frozen foundation model, our method models traversability using von Mises-Fisher (vMF) mixture [20] responsibilities over a set of prototypes with learned utility in vision-language feature space.
These prototypes are learned from relative annotations, both in language and vision, allowing a platform-agnostic language prior to bootstrap image-based fine-tuning.

Our method (see Fig. 1) is competitive in terms of prediction accuracy with end-to-end trained models [11], given the same amount of annotations, while offering language-based initialisation and sample-efficient learning from human annotations.
To this end, we combine the principle of visual prototypes in robotics [21] with recent VLM-based architectures [19], and extend this architecture with alternative mixture modes to extend the state of the art and outperform alternative approaches.
To our knowledge, this combination of language-based prior and sample-efficient adaptation has not previously been demonstrated for traversability estimation.
The sole reliance on relative labels also allows us to incorporate new information sources, such as human-in-the-loop, self-labelling, or large language model (LLM) and large vision language model (LVLM)-generated relative image labels [22].
Our experiments evaluate zero-shot and data-efficient adaptation, competitive fine-tuning accuracy, as well as downstream language-alignment of learned prototypes.

title: MixVLA: Adaptive Mixing of Non-Invariant Information for Generalizable Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Pingrui Zhang,Yu Zhang,Pengyuan Wu,Bin Wang,Haoming Song,Xianqiang Gao,ZhaxiZhuoma,Zhigang Wang,Dong Wang,Bin Zhao,Xuelong Li
abstract:
This supplementary material expands upon our main paper by providing additional theoretical analysis, implementation details, experimental results, and discussions to further support the proposed method MixVLA. 
⊳\triangleright Sec. A: We provide theoretical analyses of MixVLA, including the information-compression effect of IB, the statistical properties of adaptive mixing, and an illustrative regression analysis that characterizes when regularizing complementary information can improve OOD robustness. 
⊳\triangleright Sec. B: We provide additional implementation details, including model architectures, optimization settings, and training configurations. 
⊳\triangleright Sec. C: We report additional experiments and qualitative results, including ablations on mixing strategies, more visualizations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world demonstration videos. 
⊳\triangleright Sec. D: We discuss the limitations of the current framework and outline several possible directions for future research.
introduction:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) (Achiam et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023) have advanced rapidly in recent years and are increasingly applied to robotic manipulation.
This trend has led to the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Kim et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2022) that map multimodal observations and language instructions into low-level control actions.
Benefiting from rich cross-modal representations learned by VLMs, these models achieve competitive task success rates across both simulated (Liu et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025) and real-world (Walke et al., 2023) manipulation benchmarks.

Despite strong performance on in-distribution benchmarks, VLA models still struggle to achieve robust zero-shot generalization under out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts (Li et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026).
Recent studies (Fei et al., 2025b) show that even mild variations in lighting, appearance, or camera viewpoint can cause substantial performance degradation.
Some prior works (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Team, 2025) attempt to improve robustness through large-scale and diverse data collection, but they incur substantial labor and financial costs.
Other approaches (Abouzeid et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025) enhance specific aspects of generalization by introducing model-specific modifications, which often limit their general applicability.
In this work, we instead focus on improving zero-shot generalization through a model-agnostic training strategy that does not rely on additional out-of-distribution data.
As illustrated in figure 1, our key idea is to explicitly regularize the variability of non-invariant signals in the latent representation space.

To better understand this intuition, we analyze the problem from a representation learning perspective.
Policies trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) (Vapnik, 1999) tend to capture both task-relevant invariant correlations and environment-specific non-invariant signals.
While invariant features provide stable cues for action prediction, non-invariant factors such as lighting, texture, and viewpoint often contain both nuisance variations and complementary predictive information.
Under ERM training, directly relying on raw non-invariant features can introduce spurious dependencies under distribution shifts.
Conversely, enforcing strict invariance may be overly conservative, as it can discard informative signals that remain useful for action prediction.
This observation motivates explicitly regularizing the variability of non-invariant signals rather than relying on invariant features alone.

Building on the above insights, we propose MixVLA, a model-agnostic training framework that improves zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models, without modifying model architectures or requiring additional data.
The core of MixVLA is Adaptive Mixing of Non-Invariant Information (AMI).
Specifically, we first disentangle invariant and non-invariant representations using an information-theoretic objective.
We then perform stochastic mixing within the non-invariant feature space to regularize environment-specific variability while preserving complementary predictive cues.
The resulting mixed non-invariant representation is subsequently fused with invariant features for final action prediction, enabling a more favorable balance between robustness and policy expressiveness.
We evaluate MixVLA across a range of challenging manipulation settings, including the LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks, the RoboTwin perturbation suite, and real-world robotic manipulation tasks.
The results show that MixVLA substantially improves the robustness of VLA policies under diverse observation shifts without requiring additional data collection.

Our key contributions are three-fold:

A model-agnostic framework for generalized VLA models.
We present MixVLA, a model-agnostic training framework that improves the zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models under out-of-distribution (OOD) data without additional data collection or architectural redesign.

Adaptive mixing of non-invariant information (AMI).
We propose AMI, which adaptively mixes non-invariant representations and fuses them with invariant features to improve robustness under distribution shifts.

Consistent zero-shot gains on challenging manipulation benchmarks.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MixVLA consistently improves zero-shot task success rates under diverse perturbations.

1. A model-agnostic framework for generalized VLA models.
We present MixVLA, a model-agnostic training framework that improves the zero-shot generalization of Vision-Language-Action models under out-of-distribution (OOD) data without additional data collection or architectural redesign.

2. Adaptive mixing of non-invariant information (AMI).
We propose AMI, which adaptively mixes non-invariant representations and fuses them with invariant features to improve robustness under distribution shifts.

3. Consistent zero-shot gains on challenging manipulation benchmarks.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that MixVLA consistently improves zero-shot task success rates under diverse perturbations.

title: SceneFactory-3D: Lifting 2D Traffic Scenes into 3D Physical Counterfactuals for Scalable Physically Grounded Safety Evaluation
authors: Yicheng Zhu,Linfeng Tian,Tianmu Zhao,Yang Chen,Fan Zuo,Tao Li,Zilin Bian
abstract: Scalable driving simulators typically execute vehicle commands using prescribed behavioral or kinematic rules, overlooking the physics of tire-road interfaces, thereby limiting their ability to capture how adverse road and environmental conditions alter vehicle execution and propagate through traffic. To address this limitation, we present SceneFactory-3D, a GPU-batched, physics-grounded multi-agent driving simulator. Vehicles execute acceleration and steering commands via suspension- and friction-limited forces evaluated at each wheel-contact point. Spatially varying friction, per-world 3D heightfields, gravity, and rigid contact consistently govern wheel motion and chassis collisions. Per-world terrain isolation and GPU batching enable SceneFactory-3D to run matched physical counterfactuals in parallel: traffic scenario setup and vehicle controllers remain fixed while only the road condition changes, enabling the resulting closed-loop effects to be evaluated across parallel worlds. To demonstrate the advantage of the SceneFactory-3D-enabled counterfactual evaluation, we conduct an empirical study on vehicle controllers’ sensitivity to road conditions. We study three learned-policy families on 1,024 matched 12-vehicle worlds per condition, and two classical planners on a shared 32-world subset, across 21 friction and grade conditions. When friction drops from 1.0 to 0.18, the share of vehicles that clear the work zone safely falls by 6 to 90 percentage points across learned policies (18–19 for classical planners), and near-collision situations become more frequent for every learned policy.
introduction:
Traffic simulation makes large interactive experiments tractable by skipping some physics-grounded modeling. For example, a car-following law or a prescribed kinematic rule scales thousands of
vehicle interactions at low cost (Lopez et al., 2018; Treiber et al., 2000; Gulino et al., 2023; Kazemkhani et al., 2025). However, such rules also
fix how vehicle control execution responds to the physical environment: once a vehicle has decided to brake or
merge, the motion it realizes follows exactly the prescribed rule, which is detached from the underlying physics when the adverse road conditions affect vehicle control execution, resulting in a widening sim2real gap.

To motivate the integration of vehicle-environment interacting physics with driving and traffic simulations, consider a temporary
lane closure planned for winter in a city such as Rochester. Although the proposed merge path may remain geometrically feasible on a low-friction road, vehicles’ ability to follow that path, e.g., to brake safely for one another, depends on the physical conditions at the tire–road interface. If one vehicle cannot complete the merge as intended, it may alter the behavior and trajectory of every vehicle behind it, potentially changing the traffic outcome. A credible evaluation, whether for self-driving testing or traffic management and planning, must therefore capture how the same scenario and controllers perform under different road conditions. Without this physical modeling, the simulation may substantially overestimate safety and traffic efficiency when adverse conditions affect vehicle dynamics.

While existing work accounts for physical friction in 2D planar driving simulations, comprehensive physics-grounded vehicle–environment interactions go beyond what these two-dimensional models can faithfully represent. Planar single-track models can enforce friction limits through tire-force constraints and friction-circle checks (Althoff et al., 2017; CommonRoad, n.d.), but they do not explicitly capture how three-dimensional road geometry and gravity affect wheel-level contact. Road grade, banking, and elevation change the normal force at each wheel and, consequently, the friction available to the vehicle. These effects become especially important when friction varies across the wheels of a vehicle or between lanes across diverse terrains.

To support efficient and scalable simulation of many interacting vehicles across parallel 3D worlds with underlying physics, we present SceneFactory-3D, a GPU-batched simulator that extends SceneFactory (Zhu et al., 2026), a GPU-vectorized Isaac Lab platform
whose articulated vehicles drive on flat roads with only a planar friction mechanism. SceneFactory-3D replaces the default vehicle model with a custom tire-force model evaluated at each wheel–road contact. It supports spatially varying friction patches and a separate terrain heightfield for each parallel world. Wheel-contact queries, terrain preview, and chassis collisions all reference the same heightfield, ensuring a consistent representation of the physical environment. Finally, a canonical-route interface provides classical and learned controllers with the same geometric route reference.

As a physics-grounded and GPU-batched 3D platform, SceneFactory-3D makes matched physical environment counterfactuals practical at scale. From the same traffic scene, initial state, routes, and controller population, it instantiates parallel counterfactual worlds that differ only in their physical road conditions. This design makes three factors directly controllable: where a physical condition occurs relative to a planned maneuver, whether the controller observes that condition, and how its effect on one vehicle propagates through interacting traffic. We demonstrate this capability using route-conditioned policies trained with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). We compare a policy trained on nominal roads with two continued-training variants exposed to diverse terrain as well as two classical planners, across 21 physical conditions. Although terrain randomization and privileged physical context are established techniques (Peng et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2017), SceneFactory-3D enables their separation and evaluation via matched counterfactual worlds. Across 1,024 matched worlds per learned policy and condition, reduced friction degraded task completion for every controller, propagated to vehicles traveling in the unchanged lane, and was not anticipated by the preview-enabled policy. The magnitude of these effects varied more across training seeds than across training regimes, while the tested grades affected only a few policies.

In summary, our contributions are as follows. Section 2 highlights our unique contributions by comparing SceneFactory-3D with prior efforts on driving simulation, co-simulation frameworks, and learning-based driving and vehicle controls using simulations.

SceneFactory-3D: a GPU-batched physics-grounded multi-agent driving simulator where Per-wheel forces and rigid contact couple vehicle motion to spatially varying friction and 3D terrain. Per-world terrain ownership keeps wheel queries, observations, and collisions physically consistent.

A matched physical-counterfactual evaluation framework. SceneFactory-3D creates matched counterfactual worlds that differ only in road conditions and 2D-to-3D geometry differences, enabling controlled comparisons across classical and learned vehicle controllers in terms of physical behaviors and safety risks.

An empirical study of vehicle controller sensitivity to road physics. Across 21 friction and grade conditions, we evaluate two classical planners and three learned-policy families that separate terrain-diverse training from explicit terrain preview. When friction drops from 1.0 to 0.18, the share of vehicles that clear the work zone safely falls by 6 to 90 percentage points across learned policies (18–19 for classical planners), and near-collision situations become more frequent for every learned policy.

title: Permutation Robustness Is Not Enough: Action Collapse in Multi-Agent Transformer Policies
authors: Amit Thakur,Mukesh Singhal
abstract: Transformer policies are attractive for multi-agent robot learning because self-attention can model interactions among agents. However, multi-agent teams are unordered, while transformers typically process agents as ordered token sequences. We study how this mismatch affects cooperative navigation policies under agent-order permutations. Our results show that low permutation error alone can be misleading: policies may appear robust simply because all agents choose the same action. We therefore evaluate policies using both permutation-consistency metrics and action-collapse diagnostics, including action diversity, same-action fraction, and maximum action frequency. A PPO-ID baseline yields non-collapsed behavior but remains order-sensitive, while strong equivariance regularization can still induce homogeneous behavior. A weak equivariance penalty improves the robustness while preserving more diverse actions for teams with N=3N=3 agents, whereas teams with N=4N=4 agents require substantially smaller regularization weights. These findings suggest that multi-agent transformer policies should be evaluated not only by return and permutation robustness, but also by whether they maintain non-collapsed, differentiated multi-agent behavior.
introduction:
Multi-robot systems are naturally composed of exchangeable entities. A team of ground robots, drones, or manipulation agents should not fail because the observations of two robots are listed in a different order. Yet transformer policies, now common as interaction models, operate on ordered token sequences [18]. A typical multi-agent transformer forms tokens

Practical policies often add learned agent identity or sequence-position embeddings to the tokens. Such embeddings can improve nominal performance because agents may specialize, but they can also create an ordering shortcut: the policy attaches behavior to token slots rather than to physical context. This is problematic because robot ordering may change due to communication, batching, logging, dynamic team membership, or a deployment interface.

In this paper, we address the following question: do transformer-based multi-agent policies learn coordination or agent ordering? A natural test is to measure Eq. (2). However, our experiments reveal that low equivariance error can be misleading. A policy can satisfy permutation tests almost perfectly by outputting the same action for every agent. Such a policy can appear permutation-consistent for the wrong reason: not because it coordinates robustly, but because all agents behave nearly identically. We therefore evaluate task return, permutation consistency, and non-collapsed action behavior jointly.

Our contributions are as follows. (i) We formalize permutation sensitivity for transformer-based multi-agent policies with logit, policy-distribution, action, and return metrics. (ii) We introduce action-collapse diagnostics, including normalized action diversity, same-action fraction, and maximum action frequency. (iii) We show empirically that PPO-style training [13, 19] produces a strong non-collapsed baseline, but equivariance regularization still creates a measurable robustness-diversity tradeoff. (iv) We add a four-agent stress test showing that useful regularization strength is team-size dependent.

The practical message is deliberately conservative: a low permutation error should not be interpreted in isolation. A good multi-agent policy should satisfy three requirements simultaneously. It should solve the task, remain stable under benign relabelings of the same physical team, and avoid degenerate homogeneous behavior. The experiments below are organized around these three requirements.
