title: PointWAM: 3D World Action Modeling for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation
authors: Chunghyun Park,Beomjun Kim,Seungcheol Park,Heeseung Kwon,Yashu Shukla,Seunghoon Sim,Jinwoo Shin,Minsu Cho
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
World action models jointly learn to forecast world dynamics and predict robot actions, such that the learned internal world dynamics guide accurate actions.
Existing approaches typically represent the world as RGB frames or latent counterparts while predicting actions as end-effector poses or joint angles, but they often struggle to capture the 3D spatial structure and contact geometry central to dexterous manipulation.
We introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene (i.e., environment) and hands (i.e., actor), and jointly forecasts both as 3D point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame.
This explicit, disentangled representation enables effective pre-training on large-scale human demonstration videos without requiring any task-specific object or keypoint selection.
Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM predicts how the scene and hands co-evolve in 3D space over time, then retargets the forecast hand motion to robot actions.
Pre-training on human videos improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points, and scene-trajectory supervision adds 10.9 points over forecasting the hands alone.
With both, PointWAM surpasses the prior state of the art on ten DexJoCo tasks by 11.7 points and outperforms strong VLAs on a real robot.
introduction:
Dexterous robotic manipulation requires multiple fingers to precisely coordinate their 3D motion relative to object surfaces (Salisbury & Craig, 1982; Okamura et al., 2000), enabling robots to perform a wide range of tasks from grasping objects of varied shapes to tool use (Bicchi, 2000; An et al., 2026). Conventional Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) (Black et al., 2025; NVIDIA et al., 2025) map observations to motor commands without explicitly forecasting how the scene evolves. World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative by treating world and action modeling as deeply intertwined: they jointly learn to forecast how the world will change and what actions cause those changes (Li et al., 2025a).

Many existing WAMs build on video generation backbones and represent the world as RGB frames (Du et al., 2023) or their latent counterparts (Li et al., 2025a; Liao et al., 2026). These representations are limited in their ability to capture key aspects of physical interaction, including 3D spatial structure and causal relations between the actor and the environment. Point-based policies (Haldar & Pinto, 2025; Kim et al., 2026a) address the 3D action prediction problem by forecasting trajectories of 3D points, but do not model how the environment evolves. They also rely on humans or external perception models to select task-relevant objects for their scene inputs. Conversely, action-conditioned 3D world models forecast dense 3D scene trajectories, yet treat robot actions as inputs rather than quantities to be predicted (Huang et al., 2026).

In this work, we introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene (i.e., environment) and hands (i.e., actor), and represents both as three-dimensional point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame (Fig. 1). This explicit, disentangled world representation enables effective learning of cause-and-effect relations between the environment and the actor by modeling how their points co-evolve in 3D space over time. Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM forecasts trajectories for every observed scene point and hand keypoint in a common coordinate frame. Its action retargeter then converts the forecast hand trajectories into the corresponding robot actions.

The proposed approach offers three additional advantages. First, modeling both the scene and hands in a shared 3D space enables effective pre-training on human demonstration videos from EgoDex (Hoque et al., 2026) and VITRA (Li et al., 2026b). Second, no task-specific objects or scene keypoints need to be selected in advance, so scene forecasting is not restricted to a predefined set of target objects. Third, by decoupling hand-point trajectories from the scene, the forecast hand motion is amenable to effective retargeting onto robot hands for action prediction.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows.

We introduce PointWAM, which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in a shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling.

We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points.

We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, PointWAM surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on a real robot by up to 25 percentage points.

1. We introduce PointWAM, which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in a shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling.

2. We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points.

3. We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, PointWAM surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on a real robot by up to 25 percentage points.

title: FastOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Lightweight VLA Deployment
authors: Yoojin Oh,Jeongsol Kim,Yeonwoo Seo,Jangho Park,Seonghyun Jin,Sunwoo Park,Youngmin Kim,Youngjun Jun,Kyumin Choi,Jong Chul Ye
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging.
Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies.
In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation.
Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics.
Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model.
We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments.
On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of π0.5\pi_{0.5} with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.
introduction:
Recent progress in robot learning has moved toward large-scale foundation policies, ranging from Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Collaboration, 2024; Black et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2025a; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026a) to emerging World Action Models (WAMs) (Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). In particular, recent methods such as DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026) and Cosmos Policy (Kim et al., 2026) leverage pretrained video generation models to capture rich visual dynamics and achieve strong generalization and manipulation performance.
However, these powerful foundation priors also lead to increasingly large policy backbones and high computational cost, creating a tension between model capability and deployment efficiency on physical robots.
Lightweight VLA models such as SmolVLA (Shukor et al., 2025) address the efficiency side of this trade-off by directly designing smaller policies with less than 0.5B parameters.

A complementary direction is to transfer the capability of a powerful foundation policy into a compact student through knowledge distillation.
Knowledge Distillation (KD) (Hinton et al., 2015; Mansourian et al., 2025) has been widely studied for transferring the capability of a large teacher model into a smaller student. Specifically, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) (Agarwal et al., 2024) supervises the student using teacher predictions on its own generated trajectories, reducing distribution mismatch and compounding errors from offline distillation. OPD also provides dense supervision along the student trajectory, in contrast to the sparse rewards commonly used in reinforcement learning. While OPD has been actively explored in LLM post-training, recent works have extended it to diffusion and flow models (Li et al., 2026a; Fang et al., 2026b).
However, directly applying OPD to flow-based policies is computationally inefficient. It requires rolling out the student’s denoising trajectory and repeatedly evaluating the teacher at the visited timesteps, resulting in high training cost for large foundation teachers.

In this work, we revisit few-step flow-map models through the lens of
on-policy distillation (OPD) and introduce FastOPD, a
foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework for efficient policy distillation.
Our goal is to transfer the capabilities of a large-scale VLA into a
compact student while substantially reducing both training and inference
costs, without sacrificing policy performance
(see Fig. 1).
To reduce the training cost of conventional OPD, FastOPD combines
on-policy teacher supervision of the student’s velocity field with a
self-consistency objective (Frans et al., 2025).
Rather than querying teacher supervision throughout an entire
generation trajectory, the self-consistency objective propagates local
velocity supervision to finite-interval shortcut transitions, as
illustrated in Fig. 2.
This allows the student to approximate the teacher dynamics without
explicitly constructing or evaluating a teacher flow map over each
shortcut transition.
We further show theoretically that FastOPD implicitly recovers the
distribution induced by the teacher’s ideal shortcut model, providing a
distributional justification for few-step distillation.

Importantly, the same self-consistency formulation naturally induces an
any-step flow map (Boffi et al., 2024; Song et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025; Sabour et al., 2025),
allowing the distilled student to operate with substantially fewer
sampling steps at inference.
FastOPD therefore compresses the foundation VLA along two complementary
dimensions: model capacity and sampling complexity, enabling deployment
on resource-constrained, consumer-grade hardware.
The proposed formulation also enables stable training in the challenging
few-step regime without adversarial objectives or costly higher-order
derivative computations.
A concurrent work, VLA-OPD (Zhong et al., 2026), also studies on-policy
distillation for VLA models, but primarily uses expert supervision to
improve policy performance.
In contrast, FastOPD focuses on transferring a foundation policy into a
lightweight few-step student.

We evaluate FastOPD on two simulation benchmarks and one real-world
manipulation task, using diverse foundation teachers with 3B–6B
parameters (Black et al., 2025a; Yuan et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026a).
To maximize both architectural and inference efficiency, we adopt
SmolVLA as the lightweight student policy.
We compare against representative few-step distillation methods,
including CTM, DMD, and iMF.
Across these settings, FastOPD enables the compact student to recover up
to 84% of the performance of teacher models that are more than
7.3×7.3\times larger, using only one or two sampling steps.
This substantially reduces inference cost while retaining a large
fraction of the foundation policy’s performance.
To the best of our knowledge, FastOPD is the first OPD framework for
VLAs that jointly reduces both model size and the number of sampling
steps while retaining the capabilities of a large-scale foundation
policy.

title: Register-Routed Delayed Fusion: Rewiring Shortcut-Prone Observation Fusion in Visuomotor Imitation
authors: Jieting Long,Weidong Cai,Weiming Zhi
abstract: Visuomotor imitation policies combine high-dimensional visual observations with compact signals such as proprioception, and their fusion topology determines when and through which tokens these streams interact. In dense token fusion, visual tokens may attend directly to compact tokens from the first encoder layer, allowing action-predictive compact cues to influence spatial visual representations early in their formation. We ask whether controlling this route improves visual responsiveness and policy behavior. We introduce Register-Routed Delayed Fusion (RRDF), which masks direct compact–visual attention and stages cross-modal interaction through a learned register workspace. Its isolate–collect–route schedule protects an early stream-separated prefix and later permits only register-mediated exchange, while compact conditioning remains available to the native action generator. Across five simulation tasks and three real-robot tasks, RRDF matches or improves dense ACT under nominal conditions. Appearance-shift evaluations on four simulation tasks and held-out-position evaluations on three real-robot tasks also favor RRDF. Phase-matched input probes show lower measured state-to-image sensitivity, while ablations indicate that adding registers alone does not reproduce the full performance gain. These results support controlling cross-modal propagation while retaining compact action conditioning.
introduction:
Visuomotor imitation policies predict future robot actions from heterogeneous observation histories, typically combining high-dimensional visual inputs with compact signals such as robot proprioception and policy-internal context. Recent work focused more on action generation, including action chunking  [1, 2], diffusion  [3, 4, 5, 6], and flow matching  [7, 8, 9]. We examine how layer-wise observation-fusion routes affect visual representations and closed-loop policy behavior.

We study this fusion stage through its layer-wise communication topology. Under dense token fusion, spatial visual and compact tokens participate in unrestricted self-attention from the first encoder layer, creating a direct compact-to-visual route, 𝒞→𝒱\mathcal{C}\!\rightarrow\!\mathcal{V}. Compact signals are often strongly correlated with task phase and future actions, so this one-hop route allows action-predictive compact cues to influence spatial visual representations from the beginning of encoder computation. More broadly, imitation policies are known to exploit nuisance signals correlated with expert actions, leading to causal confusion and brittle behavior under distribution shift [10, 11]. Recent work further shows that proprioceptive signals can dominate vision–proprioception policies and suppress visual utilization [12]. We hypothesize that unrestricted early compact-to-visual attention can encourage overreliance on action-correlated compact cues at the expense of task-relevant visual evidence. Consistent with this hypothesis, our intervention analysis later reveals greater sensitivity to state relative to image interventions under dense fusion, at both the representation and action-output levels.

Our focus is therefore not whether compact conditioning should be available, but when and through which routes it enters spatial visual representations. Proprioceptive feedback provides useful control information and remains directly accessible to the action generator. We ask whether controlling early compact-to-visual propagation can improve policy behavior without removing this conditioning. To address this issue, we introduce Register-Routed Delayed Fusion (RRDF, illustrated in Figure 2), which masks direct compact–visual attention throughout the fusion encoder and delays cross-modal influence on the primary streams through a learned register workspace. Its isolate–collect–route schedule protects an early stream-separated prefix, collects cross-modal context in registers, and later exposes it only through register-mediated paths. Compact conditioning remains directly available to the native action generator.

Across five simulation tasks, RRDF matches or improves the reported nominal performance of dense fusion. Appearance-shift tests and real-robot held-out-position evaluations also favor RRDF, with task-dependent gains. Figure 1 illustrates a representative difference in trajectory adaptation. We examine these results through phase-matched input-sensitivity probes and fusion-topology ablations.

Concretely, this paper makes the following contributions:

We introduce a source-partitioned isolate–collect–route schedule that blocks direct compact–visual attention, jointly collects information before primary-stream readback, and preserves compact action conditioning.

We evaluate nominal performance on five simulation and three real-robot tasks, appearance shifts on four simulation tasks, and held-out-position configurations on three real-robot tasks.

We characterize the permitted encoder dependencies, show that register capacity alone does not explain the gains, and reveal reduced state-to-image sensitivity through phase-matched probes.

1. We introduce a source-partitioned isolate–collect–route schedule that blocks direct compact–visual attention, jointly collects information before primary-stream readback, and preserves compact action conditioning.

2. We evaluate nominal performance on five simulation and three real-robot tasks, appearance shifts on four simulation tasks, and held-out-position configurations on three real-robot tasks.

3. We characterize the permitted encoder dependencies, show that register capacity alone does not explain the gains, and reveal reduced state-to-image sensitivity through phase-matched probes.

title: Learning Reflexive Behavior for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Quan Nguyen,Yunho Kim,Joonho Lee
abstract:
During contact-rich manipulation, interactions between a robot and its environment carry information about local geometry: a surface prevents penetration, a bore guides a peg. A controller that exploits these interactions can can comply with environmental constraints while preserving task intent.
Robot-learning systems commonly use position, hybrid force–position, or Cartesian impedance control. Their prescribed tracking objectives, stiffness, or force-control directions may not match local constraints and may degrade performance.
We learn a proprioceptive reflex policy in simulation on three simple interaction primitives: a spring, a plane, and a rail.
The policy maps task-space commands to joint-position targets using state history, without direct force or geometrical measurements.
Once trained, it serves as a frozen execution layer beneath higher-level controllers.
We evaluate it in dual-arm box lifting, peg insertion, and surface following.
In box lifting, the reflex kept the force below the threshold while the baseline failed. In rough-surface following it stayed below the 10 N reference, on par with tuned hybrid force-position control. In 0.02 mm peg insertion It reduced mean estimated contact force to less than half that of the baseline while increasing hardware success rates from at most 22 % to 36–58 %. By separating contact response from command generation, the reflex policy provides motion planners, learned policies, and teleoperators with robust contact-rich execution.
introduction:
In contact-rich manipulation, environmental geometry shapes how a robot or its tools can move and provides guidance for completing a task. A surface supports sliding while restricting penetration, and a groove guides motion along a path. By maintaining contact while yielding in constrained directions, a robot can exploit this geometry to guide execution despite errors in perception, grasping, or nominal motion.

High-level commands from a motion planner, a learned policy, or a human operator may specify the intended behavior without matching the exact geometry of the current task instance [1, 2, 3].
For example, a surface-search command is useful only if execution maintains contact while moving over the actual surface. Li and Brock [1] separate task structure from instance-specific geometry and recover the latter through interaction with environmental constraints. Compliant execution beneath high-level policies similarly supports adaptation to local contact [2]. These observations motivate an execution capability that makes environmental constraints useful to a broad range of command sources.

We present a method for training a proprioceptive reflex policy through  RL (RL) using three primitive interaction scenarios shown in Fig. 1 (bottom).
The proposed a control hierarchy is shown in Fig. 1C with high level controller supplies contact intent and nominal motion while the reflex policy adjusts joint-space targets using a history proprioceptive measurements, and a compliant joint controller executes them. A single training environment samples virtual spring, plane, and rail constraints alongside free-space motion. The objective encourages progress toward a compliant reference and command-derived interaction force while penalizing excessive loading. This formulation builds directly on three prior designs: the force-threshold penalty of  FORGE (FORGE) [4], through which an RL policy learns to respect a maximum allowable force; the force-compensated position reward of Zhi et al. [5]; and the interaction-mode command of Lee et al. [6], which tells a controller whether contact is permitted.

We evaluate our approach across the two robot embodiments shown in Fig. 1. We apply the learned reflex controller to improve performance on dual-arm box lifting (A) and high-precision peg insertion (B) tasks. The results show that the learned reflex supports stable lifting under imperfect motion commands, enables insertion under hole-position uncertainty, and follows rough surfaces while limiting contact loading. Our contribution is a reusable reflex-training paradigm that uses simple interaction primitives to train policies that adapt task-level motion commands to local contact.

title: SARI: Phase-Split Sim-Real Co-Training for Contact-Rich Manipulation
authors: Xingxin He,Yuxuan Jiang,Haonan Zhang,Chuhan Cui,Kaile Li,Zhongxing Zheng,Caihao Xu,Ziqi Wang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often require costly real-world demonstrations to adapt to contact-rich manipulation tasks, particularly when generalization across object placements is needed. We propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split sim-and-real co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them. Specifically, free-space approaches require spatial diversity but tolerate modest simulation gaps, making them ideal for synthetic generation; conversely, contact interactions demand accurate physics but vary little across object placements, allowing a few real demonstrations to generalize across the workspace. SARI generates diverse simulated approaches in a photorealistic digital twin while collecting real contact interactions at only a few placements. Post-trained on these phase-segmented demonstrations, a single policy seamlessly stitches simulated approaches with real contact interactions using visual appearance alignment and a shared camera-relative action representation—without explicit phase labels or hand-coded switches. Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3% and achieves 27.5% success at unseen placements, where all full-task sim-real baselines fail completely (0%).
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong and
increasingly general manipulation capabilities, but this progress
has been enabled by human-collected robot data at a formidable scale.
Recent VLAs, including π0.5\pi_{0.5} [1], GR00T N1.7 [2],
and GEN-1.5 [3], are trained on large and diverse
collections of robot, human, and synthetic data. Yet adapting these models
to a new, contact-rich task still commonly requires many task demonstrations,
and long-horizon tasks amplify this demand because errors and distribution
shifts accumulate over time.

An important cause is the limited spatial generalization of VLA policies.
Although visual encoders are pretrained on broad data, post-trained policies
can still overfit an action sequence to the specific object placements observed in
their demonstrations, rather than reliably extrapolating across the
workspace [4, 5]. Consequently, achieving workspace-wide coverage requires the redundant repetition of near-identical free-space approaches, rather than focusing effort on contact-rich supervision.

Simulation offers an effective route to alleviate this human collection burden.
Recent advances, including MimicGen [6],
DemoGen [4], Real2Render2Real [7], and
others [8, 9], synthesize additional demonstrations by transforming a small set of
source demonstrations, generating trajectories in reconstructed scenes or combining simulated
and real data for policy training.
These methods can efficiently expand workspace coverage, diversify trajectories, and
eliminate redundant teleoperation of identical free-space approaches.

However, existing synthetic-data pipelines commonly assume that simulation is reliable throughout an entire task or require accurate modeling of contact
dynamics [10, 4, 8, 9].
In contact-rich manipulation, unmodeled friction, compliance, object resistance,
and visual sim-to-real discrepancies can make synthetic contact data unreliable.
To bridge this gap, straightforward sim-and-real co-training mixes full-task simulated and real demonstrations; yet, this still wastes costly real-world effort on free-space approaches and allows the spatially narrow real-data distribution to override and dilute the broad spatial coverage provided by simulation.

To address these challenges, we propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them.
Simulation can cheaply provide broad spatial coverage for free-space approaches, while a few real demonstrations suffice to teach contact interactions that generalize across placements.
Specifically, the approach phase requires broad spatial diversity but tolerates modest simulation gaps, making it ideal for synthetic generation. Conversely, the interaction phase demands accurate contact dynamics but varies little across object placements, allowing a modest number of real demonstrations at a few placements to generalize across the workspace.
Figure  contrasts this phase-split allocation with full-task sim-real co-training.

We instantiate this phase-specific allocation using a Gaussian-Splatting [11]
digital twin that generates simulated approaches across all placements, while collecting real contact interactions near the pre-contact boundary at only a subset. To enable a single policy to learn seamlessly from both sources without phase labels or a hand-coded switch, we align visual appearances and express actions in a shared camera-relative representation.
Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3% and achieves 27.5% unseen task completion, whereas all baselines achieve 0%.

Our core contributions are:

We introduce SARI, a phase-split sim-and-real co-training
framework that decouples workspace-wide spatial reaching from contact interactions, allocating data collection to the domain best suited for each phase.

We present a sim-to-real alignment pipeline, enabling a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approaches with real contact interactions without explicit phase labels or switching heuristics.

We evaluate SARI on a Franka robot across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our camera-relative action representation serves as the key mechanism to unlock zero-shot spatial generalization to unseen placements while reducing real-world collection time.

1. We introduce SARI, a phase-split sim-and-real co-training
framework that decouples workspace-wide spatial reaching from contact interactions, allocating data collection to the domain best suited for each phase.

2. We present a sim-to-real alignment pipeline, enabling a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approaches with real contact interactions without explicit phase labels or switching heuristics.

3. We evaluate SARI on a Franka robot across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our camera-relative action representation serves as the key mechanism to unlock zero-shot spatial generalization to unseen placements while reducing real-world collection time.

title: LOCUS: Landmark-Oriented Container Discrimination Using Spatial Graphs
authors: Taylor Bergeron,Shibani Senthilbabu,Kevin Leahy
abstract: As robots are increasingly deployed in unstructured, real-world environments, the ability to reason about complex spatial and semantic relationships among objects remains a fundamental challenge in enabling robust and generalizable manipulation and navigation. For example, deciding where to search for an object that is not in plain sight depends on where it is physically plausible as well as semantically likely. Popular methods such as cosine similarity with CLIP struggle to disambiguate between spatially and semantically similar objects that could contain a target object. We propose Landmark-Oriented Container Discrimination Using Spatial Graphs (LOCUS). To jointly reason about spatial information and semantics, we train a GNN to update CLIP embeddings on a full environment scene graph by passing embedding information between nodes based on proximity. CLIP embeddings, augmented by semantic knowledge from a fusion of household ontologies provide a robust semantic signal. We evaluate in simulation on a noiseless scene graph from simulator metadata, making the approach detection-agnostic. Our approach outperforms random, CLIP, Tidybot, and an LLM planner in the majority of room classes and configurations in simulation. To show our approach is robust to scene graph node placement and label noise, we demonstrate a physical mobile manipulator running in an exploration pipeline start-to-finish including scene graph labels from Detic.
introduction:
To accomplish many complex tasks in the real world, robots must understand physical and semantic relationships between objects in their environment. For example, to find occluded objects in household or search-and-rescue tasks, a robot needs both general and domain-specific knowledge of object relationships to hypothesize where an object may be hidden, including inside other containers.
The robot may also be provided with a general floor plan which it can use to inform its search, but have no knowledge about the items within each room. In many cases, there are multiple instances of the same container object which could contain the target object, such as multiple drawers that could contain a fork, and the robot must find a way to discriminate between the containers to generate a container search order. We posit that the correct approach requires both the generality of Large Language Models (LLMs) or Vision Language Models (VLMs) and the structured knowledge of an ontology.

We introduce a novel approach, Landmark-Oriented Container discrimination Using Spatial Graphs (LOCUS), the first reasoning pipeline for concealed objects that makes instance-level decisions between containers of the same class. Locus is Latin for place — reflecting our hypothesis that where a container is matters as much as what it looks like. LOCUS combines domain specific formal ontologies and general semantic knowledge. It accounts for cases not explicitly covered in the ontologies with the spatial relationship between objects in the environment in order to find an occluded object and is generalizable sim-to-sim and sim-to-real. We pretrain a GNN over scene graphs and use ontologies to learn typical spatial relationships and augment each scene graph node’s CLIP  [1] embedding.

Our contributions include:

title: ManiPhysicsBench: Physics-Based Assessment of Object Preservation in VLA Manipulation
authors: Sangwu Park,Yeonjun In,Wonjoong Kim,Sungwon Kim,Sein Kim,Chanyoung Park
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform diverse manipulation tasks, but task success in existing rigid-body benchmarks does not indicate whether they preserve objects. We introduce ManiPhysicsZoo, which consolidates literature-supported material properties, 3D meshes, and supporting references into reusable object assets. Using these assets, a solver-based assessment computes grasp-specific damage thresholds from object geometry, material properties, and recorded grasp conditions and compares them with recorded contact forces to assess potential deformation and fracture. Building on these components, ManiPhysicsBench evaluates object preservation in LIBERO and SimplerEnv across three physics axes and three difficulty levels. Public VLA checkpoints show a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. Their gripper commands concentrate near full opening and closure, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects, consistent with binary gripper supervision. We examine how object-specific continuous gripper labels change model behavior by retraining a VLA model. The retrained model shows more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success, but lower task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions. Their recent performance and generality across tasks and embodiments have made them a major paradigm in robot learning (Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b; Bjorck et al., 2025). This capability has been evaluated through manipulation tasks in simulation and in the real world, which serve as a standard protocol for VLA evaluation (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b).

However, task completion alone does not establish whether a policy handles objects without damaging them. In real-world deployment, VLAs may need to grasp and move objects with diverse physical properties, such as fragile eggs and rigid wooden boxes. Humans take these properties into account by holding fragile objects firmly enough to prevent slipping but gently enough to avoid damage, while using a stronger grip when handling rigid objects. In this sense, physical properties determine which actions are appropriate, and a genuinely generalist policy should be able to complete a task while preserving the object. We therefore ask: Can current VLAs account for objects’ physical properties to complete manipulation tasks without causing damage?

The direct way to evaluate this ability is to conduct real-world experiments. However, fractured or permanently deformed objects cannot be reused under the same conditions, so repeated trials incur object replacement costs. Moreover, damaged objects and fragments may pose safety risks to the robot and its surroundings. Therefore, a simulation-based framework is needed to assess object preservation under repeatable conditions. Yet widely used simulation benchmarks do not account for object damage when evaluating task success (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024b). Because objects are modeled as rigid bodies, a policy can receive the same success score regardless of whether it handles the object carefully or uses gripping that would damage it in the real world. Adjacent lines of work, including physical understanding benchmarks, robot safety benchmarks, and tactile and force-aware VLAs, leave this gap open, as none of them judges a policy’s actions against a physically grounded criterion for object preservation (Chow et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2026; Balaji et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). These limitations highlight the need for a common evaluation protocol that assesses whether policies complete tasks while respecting each object’s physical constraints.

Developing such an evaluation protocol requires defining preservation criteria for each object and reliably assessing how policy-applied forces affect its state during a rollout. This entails two challenges. First, defining physically grounded preservation criteria requires object-specific material properties, geometric meshes, and supporting references, but these resources are not readily available in a unified, verifiable form. Second, evaluating object preservation requires translating the forces applied during a rollout into predictions of deformation or fracture, but the rigid-body simulators used in standard manipulation benchmarks do not model these outcomes.

To address the first challenge, we propose ManiPhysicsZoo, an object library that consolidates object-specific material properties, 3D meshes, supporting references, structural information, and validation status into reusable assets. These assets can be reused for evaluating new policies, robots, and objects across simulation environments. The supporting references justify the material properties and preservation criteria, making their physical basis traceable and verifiable.

To address the second challenge, we introduce an assessment method that uses physics solvers to determine whether contact forces recorded during a manipulation rollout could cause object deformation or fracture under the corresponding grasp conditions.
After each rollout is completed, the physics solver combines the recorded grasp information with the material properties and 3D mesh from ManiPhysicsZoo to compute a damage threshold for each grasp. We compare the recorded contact forces with the corresponding thresholds and judge an interaction to be potentially damaging if its force exceeds the threshold. We justify each threshold using material properties and damage criteria supported by the literature, and document the modeling assumptions to make the resulting evaluation traceable and verifiable.

Building on these two components, we construct ManiPhysicsBench, a physics-based benchmark for evaluating object preservation during manipulation. ManiPhysicsBench constructs manipulation tasks in LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) and SimplerEnv (Li et al., 2024b) using objects selected from our ManiPhysicsZoo.

Solver-based assessment enables object-preservation evaluation on these platforms, even though their simulators model objects as rigid bodies. The benchmark is organized into three physics axes: brittle fracture, soft object deformation, and thin-walled container deformation. Each axis includes high, medium, and low difficulty levels, with higher difficulty corresponding to a narrower range of gripping forces that allow the object to be lifted without damage.

We evaluate public VLA checkpoints (Kim et al., 2025; Li et al., 2024a; Black et al., 2025a; Fang et al., 2026) on ManiPhysicsBench and observe a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. To investigate this gap, we analyze the policies’ gripper commands to examine whether they adapt their gripping behavior to objects’ physical properties. We find that these commands concentrate near fully open and fully closed states, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects.

This pattern motivates examining the role of gripper supervision. Standard VLA pipelines often binarize gripper labels into open and close, which may limit the learning of object-dependent gripper control (Walke et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024). We therefore replace binary labels with continuous labels derived from object-specific physical constraints and evaluate how retraining with these labels affects gripper behavior and safe success. Retraining yields more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success. However, task success decreases, and the resulting object-preserving behavior shows limited generalization.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

ManiPhysicsZoo. An object library that consolidates object-specific meshes, properties, and supporting references into reusable assets for physically grounded preservation assessment.

Physics solver-based assessment. A solver-based pipeline that computes damage thresholds for each grasp from object geometry, material properties, and grasp conditions.

ManiPhysicsBench. A benchmark that evaluates across three physics axes and three difficulty levels whether VLA models manipulate objects while respecting their physical constraints.

Evaluation and behavioral analysis. An evaluation of public VLA checkpoints, reporting the gap between task success and safe success. We analyze gripper behavior and examine the effects of object-specific continuous gripper supervision, identifying improvements in safe success alongside reduced task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.

1. ManiPhysicsZoo. An object library that consolidates object-specific meshes, properties, and supporting references into reusable assets for physically grounded preservation assessment.

title: Skill2Real: Agentic Skill Learning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Manipulation
authors: Xincheng He,Siyu Ma,Chang Yu,Yunuo Chen,Yanjia Huang,Ying Nian Wu,Yin Yang,Chenfanfu Jiang
abstract:
Sim-to-real learning commonly adapts policies or representations to domain
variation, often directing the learning budget toward task-agnostic low-level
representations at the expense of task-level knowledge. Skill2Real builds on
cross-domain grounding from foundation vision-language models (VLMs) to
acquire validated, reusable skills in simulation through a shared
code-based policy interface. In its
asymmetric Proposer–Verifier–Governor (PVG) loop, the Proposer acts
from public observations and API returns, the Verifier diagnoses outcomes with
privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor admits updates supported by
validation rollouts. A Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills; a
Brain then composes the frozen library into long-horizon programs with planning
and recovery. At deployment, this hierarchy is grounded in real observations
through the same interface. On unseen LIBERO-Pro Long, frozen LIBERO-90
skills raise success from 2.0% to 56.3% with Astra and from 0.5% to 49.0%
with Opus 5. Robosuite success reaches 85.1–89.4% across seven tasks. On a
real UR5e, the same agent’s mean completion rises from 27.50% to 78.75% across
four tasks with Skill2Real, a controlled gain that, with cross-model
improvements, shows Skill2Real adds a capability orthogonal to the foundation
model by learning transferable task knowledge in simulation.
Project page: skill2real.github.io.
introduction:
Zero-shot sim-to-real robot manipulation aims to convert experience acquired
in simulation into behavior that can be executed by a physical robot without
real-world task training. Simulation provides a scalable environment for
learning such behavior, but discrepancies in appearance, dynamics, contact,
and embodiment can prevent policies learned in simulation from transferring
reliably to reality (Tobin et al., 2017; Chebotar et al., 2019). For long-horizon manipulation,
the challenge extends beyond transferring individual actions: a robot must
reliably execute local manipulation skills, compose them into task-level
behavior (Gupta et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2025b), and recover when
intermediate actions fail.

Existing methods leave a central bottleneck unresolved: learning reusable,
composable task knowledge from privileged simulation evidence without spending
the learning budget on task-agnostic low-level representations. Randomization
and asymmetric actor–critic methods improve transfer by adapting neural
policies or representations (Tobin et al., 2017; Pinto et al., 2018). Appearance-heavy
domain randomization can therefore spend much of the learning budget modeling
task-irrelevant variation in lighting and texture rather than acquiring
reusable manipulation knowledge. Code-generation
methods make behavior composable, but assemble supplied primitives rather than
acquire local skills and task strategies from experience (Liang et al., 2022).
Representative skill-library systems accumulate programs through human guidance
or real-world execution feedback (Tziafas & Kasaei, 2024; Lu et al., 2026).
Skill2Real instead relies on foundation VLMs for cross-domain grounding and
directs simulation learning toward validated, hierarchical executable
knowledge.

We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns executable
robot skills through a shared code-based policy interface. The key idea is to separate the
information used to supervise skill learning from the information required to
execute learned skills: simulator privilege can evaluate and improve behavior,
while persistent skill knowledge is expressed entirely through public
observations and API semantics. The shared interface defines the transfer boundary:
programs invoke operations with common semantics, while each backend provides
its own perception, calibration, and low-level execution. This separation lets
task knowledge be reused across simulation and reality without incorporating
simulator-only state into the deployed policy.

Skill2Real realizes this idea with an asymmetric
Proposer–Verifier–Governor (PVG) loop that learns a two-level skill
hierarchy. The Proposer executes programs from public observations and proposes
reusable updates; the Verifier turns privileged simulation outcomes into
publicly grounded diagnoses; and the Governor aggregates evidence across
validation rollouts to admit supported updates into memory. Stage I learns
Cerebellum skills for reusable local manipulation. Stage II freezes this
library and learns Brain skills that compose it into long-horizon task programs
with planning and recovery. At deployment, the Proposer grounds both frozen
memories in current observations through the real code-based policy
interface.

Our experiments test whether frozen hierarchical knowledge generalizes across
task suites, Proposers, and the real robot. As frozen LIBERO-90
libraries (Liu et al., 2023) progress from no memory through the
Cerebellum to the full hierarchy, success on unseen LIBERO-Pro Long
tasks (Zhou et al., 2025) rises from 2.0% to 35.3% to 56.3% with
Astra and from 0.5% to 29.3% to 49.0% with Opus 5, showing that both skill
levels transfer across Proposers beyond the source tasks. Across seven single-arm and bimanual
Robosuite tasks (Zhu et al., 2020), independently learned libraries raise
mean success from 16.6% to 85.1% with Sol and from 19.4% to 89.4% with
Opus 5, demonstrating consistent gains across Proposers. On the real UR5e, the
full Brain–Cerebellum hierarchy reaches 78.75% mean task completion versus
56.25% with local skills alone, confirming the value of task-level composition
for long-horizon behavior.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns
executable robot programs in simulation and transfers frozen skill
knowledge through a shared code-based policy interface using only public observations at
deployment, without real-world task-policy adaptation.

Proposer acts on public observations, the Verifier translates privileged
execution evidence into public feedback, and the Governor admits updates
supported by validation rollouts.

We develop a hierarchical policy learning strategy in which the
Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills and the Brain learns
long-horizon compositions conditioned on the frozen Cerebellum library,
enabling task-level planning and recovery.

Proposer acts on public observations, the Verifier translates privileged

title: SimpleTouch: Can Vision-Language-Action Models Master Contact-Rich Manipulation Without Tactile Policy Pretraining?
authors: Chen Yang,Linzhe Shi,Changjie Wu,Hang Zhang,Ronghan Chen,Lingjun Zhang,Xu Hu,Mu Xu,Jiansheng Fan,Chen Wang
abstract:
Tactile sensing provides essential contact information for robotic manipulation, yet incorporating it into pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging.
A common concern is that simply introducing touch during task-specific fine-tuning may fail to bridge the cross-modal gap, yielding limited gains or even reduced success.
Consequently, existing methods often rely on large-scale tactile policy pretraining or separate visuotactile alignment, adding data requirements and training stages.
We introduce \simpletouchfontSimpleTouch, a simple VLA extension that augments π0.5\pi_{0.5} with a tactile expert, to test whether these additional stages are necessary.
Leveraging all tokens from a frozen pretrained tactile encoder, the expert learns from action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents.
This single-stage training uses only task demonstrations, without additional tactile policy pretraining or separate alignment.
With 50 demonstrations per task, \simpletouchfontSimpleTouch achieves the highest success rate among evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC tasks.
Its average success rate reaches 77.5%, compared with 45.2% for FTP-π0.5\pi_{0.5} and 66.7% for FTP-1, corresponding to gains of 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively.
Across four real-world tasks, it averages 71.3%, exceeding FTP-1 by 8.8 percentage points.
These results demonstrate that, given pretrained VLA and tactile representations, additional tactile policy pretraining is not a prerequisite for strong performance on these tasks, offering a simpler route to contact-rich manipulation.
Project page: https://simpletouch-robot.github.io/
introduction:
Robot manipulation has made substantial progress through learned policies (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023) and pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models (Kim et al., 2025b; Black et al., 2024). Much of this progress has relied on visual perception as the primary interface for scene understanding. However, visual observations do not fully determine contact-rich interaction: two manipulation states can appear visually similar while requiring different actions because their contact geometry, deformation, or slip state differs (Li et al., 2014; Yuan et al., 2017). Tactile sensing supplies local feedback about these otherwise hidden contact states, motivating policies that learn from touch and use it during manipulation (Xue et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025; Lou et al., 2026).

However, adding touch to a pretrained policy does not automatically make it useful. Tactile observations lie outside the pretraining modalities of many VLA backbones, and directly incorporating them during fine-tuning can yield limited gains or even reduce success (Niu et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2026a). The central challenge is therefore not merely obtaining tactile features, but presenting them to a pretrained VLA in a form that preserves contact information while allowing the policy to learn their task-specific use from limited demonstrations. Representative responses include large-scale tactile policy pretraining, as in FTP-1 (Yuan et al., 2026a), and separate visuotactile representation alignment, as in VITaL (George et al., 2025). These routes provide useful priors but introduce additional data requirements and training stages. Meanwhile, pretrained tactile encoders already offer reusable contact representations (Zhao et al., 2025). This distinction between acquiring tactile representations and learning a tactile policy motivates our question: given a pretrained VLA and tactile encoder, can a policy learn strong contact-rich manipulation from task-specific tactile demonstrations without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage?

We introduce \simpletouchfontSimpleTouch, a simple recipe that augments π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025) with one tactile expert, without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage. Its design follows two principles. First, it preserves the pretrained tactile representation: we freeze the tactile encoder and retain all current tokens, including global and spatial features, as a stable source of contact information. Second, it learns the task-specific use of that representation through a tactile expert. The tactile expert processes current tactile features separately from the visual-language backbone, and the action expert reads them through layerwise attention. During joint training, the expert learns from both action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents through latent flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023). This task-trained pathway gives action generation direct access to high-fidelity tactile features. During task-level training, we jointly optimize the pretrained π0.5\pi_{0.5} policy, including its visual-language backbone and action expert, together with the tactile expert, while keeping the tactile encoder frozen.

With 50 demonstrations per task, \simpletouchfontSimpleTouch achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC (Chen et al., 2026a) tasks. Its mean success rate of 77.5% exceeds those of FTP-π0.5\pi_{0.5} and the pretrained FTP-1 policy by 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively. Across four real-world tasks, \simpletouchfontSimpleTouch averages 71.3%, surpassing FTP-1 by 8.8 points and showing improvements in real-world experiments as well. At deployment, the tactile expert processes the current observation once, and its layerwise cache is reused throughout action-flow integration; future tactile prediction is used only as training supervision. Together, these results show that, given strong pretrained VLA and tactile representations, a frozen tactile representation and task-trained tactile expert can achieve strong performance without additional tactile policy pretraining or explicit alignment.

title: Localized Conformal Safety Monitoring with Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
authors: Luís Marques,Rong Fang,Disha Kamale,Dmitry Berenson
comment: . Extended abstract. Disha Kamale and Dmitry Berenson are joint senior authors
abstract:
Monitoring planned driving trajectories requires accurately estimating the collision likelihood
with actors whose motion is itself impacted by the ego motion.
Existing classical approaches are often limited by the quality of their forecasting model.
Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise in reasoning about the consequences of high-level actions, yet their approximate
predictions are unsuitable for safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving.
Conformal prediction (CP) has emerged as a data-driven framework for quantifying the uncertainty of black-box model predictions.
We propose Split Label-Localized Conformal Prediction (SLLCP),
a post-hoc calibration layer over frozen VLMs that transforms their unreliable predictions into probabilistically calibrated safety prediction sets.
We consider how the ability to estimate safety can depend on the observed driving scene and introduce a localized procedure that upweights
relevant past experience when calculating uncertainty thresholds. We provide label-conditional finite-sample distribution-free coverage under exchangeability.
Evaluated over 15k CARLA trajectories from unseen scenarios, SLLCP correctly flags
89.6%89.6\% of collision-causing trajectories with a Qwen backbone and 88.4%88.4\% with a
Cosmos backbone, while the base VLMs only flagged 4.6%4.6\% and 39.1%39.1\% of the collision-causing trajectories,
respectively. These results indicate that local, label-conditional
calibration can reduce missed unsafe trajectories.
introduction:
Before self-driving cars execute planned trajectories, they must
assess whether the intended motion can be safely executed, considering the surrounding scene.
This is nontrivial: pedestrians and other vehicles move in response to the ego vehicle.
For example, a trajectory passing a pedestrian near the curb may be
collision-free if the pedestrian waits, but unsafe if they step into the
vehicle’s path.
Further, the information available at planning time might miss occluded actors and not provide sufficient signal to enable accurate forecasting of the scene’s evolution.
Even seemingly robust driving policies can demonstrate degraded performance when operating in unfamiliar
scenarios — Fail2Drive reports substantial drops in closed-loop success under
controlled scenario shifts [5].

We study the problem of designing a
safety monitor that examines each
candidate trajectory before execution, independently of the quality of the underlying planning module.
That monitor should flag trajectories that would collide within a fixed
time horizon, while avoiding unnecessary alarms hindering task progress.
In general, a safety monitor might need to reason about the candidate
motion and the scene jointly, while considering uncertainty in the true unknown
outcome.
While vision-language driving systems, such as SimLingo, incorporate scene
understanding with action-taking [17], we aim to construct a monitor that can be applied post-hoc over any base planner.
We seek a theoretically-informed way to probabilistically limit the number of missed unsafe trajectories.

Safety monitors. Driving pipelines often forecast the motion of nearby actors
before checking a planned trajectory for collision [16].
Model-based safety checks can account for uncertain actor motion and
dynamics [9], but their assurances
depend on assumed scene knowledge. When an actor is missed entirely or its response to the
ego vehicle is incorrectly predicted, using a collision check may fail.
We thus investigate the complementary problem of assessing candidate trajectories using
front-facing images, so that a vision-language model (VLM) can assess hard to model risks.
A VLM’s raw safe/unsafe prediction provides no
assurances of low-rate missed collisions, since VLM spatial reasoning can be
unreliable [18]. Hence, we aim to augment VLMs’ common-sense reasoning with a post-hoc calibration layer providing probabilistic
guarantees on their prediction performance.

Conformal prediction in robotics. Conformal prediction
(CP) transforms approximate predictions into prediction sets with finite-sample guarantees under
exchangeability [19, 1]. In
robotics, CP has calibrated: forecasts in dynamic scenes for social navigation
 [9, 3]; how dynamics uncertainty varies over a system’s
state–action space [11]; action uncertainty for Lie-algebraic systems [12]; and motion uncertainty across
contact modes [13].

In this extended abstract, we propose a monitor calibrating a base VLM safety prediction in a scene-adaptive manner.
Our key contributions are:

We develop Split Label-Localized Conformal Prediction (SLLCP), a post-hoc method over a planner-agnostic generated trajectory image and a frozen VLM backbone, that
provides probabilistic guarantees on a low probability of missing unsafe trajectories.

provides probabilistic guarantees on a low probability of missing unsafe trajectories.

We empirically validate the tradeoff between missed unsafe trajectories and
false alarms on edge-case CARLA scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in the calibration of two open-weight VLMs, using the same hyperparameter set.

provides probabilistic guarantees on a low probability of missing unsafe trajectories.

2. We empirically validate the tradeoff between missed unsafe trajectories and
false alarms on edge-case CARLA scenarios, demonstrating significant improvements in the calibration of two open-weight VLMs, using the same hyperparameter set.

title: Proprioceptive Sketches as Long-Horizon Intent for Generative Action Policies
authors: Fangyuan Wang,Songhao Huang,Haoxiang Sun,Shipeng Lyu,Chengyang He,Anqing Duan,Peng Zhou,David Navarro-Alarcon
abstract: Generative robot policies predict short action chunks but lack explicit long-horizon intent. Recent methods expose longer-horizon structure through language plans, subgoal images, or video forecasts, which are costly to generate and still need to be translated into robot motion. Predicting future robot motions avoids this translation, but a dense, time-indexed trajectory requires numerous parameters to cover the full remaining task, and over a short horizon it largely repeats the action chunk and adds little guidance for action generation. We propose Proprioceptive Action Models (PAM), which jointly generate a compact, timing-free sketch of the robot’s remaining joint-space path and a dense executable action chunk within a single transformer denoiser. The sketch parameterizes the path by arc length rather than time, capturing geometric intent invariant to execution timing. Block-causal attention and a staggered denoising schedule maintain directed sketch-to-action dependence, ensuring the action tokens condition on a progressively cleaner sketch throughout sampling. In simulation, PAM improves over its action-only counterparts on Push-T and LIBERO-Long; on four real-world bimanual tasks, it raises success from 47.5% to 75.0%. Project page: https://nicehiro.github.io/pam_dp/.
introduction:
Generative action policies have become a dominant paradigm for visuomotor robot control, producing temporally coherent commands through action chunking (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Black et al., 2025b; Reuss et al., 2025). Despite strong performance on short-horizon tasks, these policies remain less effective on long-horizon manipulation (Fan et al., 2025). One approach to this challenge is to guide action prediction with visual forecasts (Black et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2025), predictive scene latents (Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Zhu et al., 2025), or language-based plans and reasoning (Wen et al., 2025; Zawalski et al., 2025). These representations capture anticipated scene evolution or semantic task structure, but can be costly to generate or require additional learned mappings to continuous control. This motivates a compact representation of long-horizon intent closely tied to the robot’s own motion.

Future robot configurations provide a natural representation of the robot’s intended motion. Demonstrations contain synchronized proprioceptive measurements, providing supervision without additional annotation in a space directly related to robot control. Prior work has used robot-motion representations to guide action prediction, including image-plane trajectories (Gu et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2025) and predicted end-effector paths (Chen et al., 2026). However, a dense, time-indexed configuration trajectory over the full remaining task is long and varies in length across demonstrations, making it difficult to represent with a limited number of parameters. Restricting the prediction to a short horizon instead makes it largely redundant with the executable action chunk, so it provides little additional guidance for action generation. An effective intent representation should therefore cover the full remaining motion with a fixed number of parameters while providing information beyond the action chunk.

We introduce the proprioceptive sketch, a compact representation of the robot’s remaining configuration-space path to task completion. The sketch uses arc-length parameterization to remove execution timing and a small number of B-spline coefficients to limit geometric details. In the handoff task in Figure 1, the sketch describes the arm paths toward the transfer region and around the barrier without specifying motion speed or the duration of the exchange. It provides long-horizon geometric context for predicting a separate, short-horizon action chunk. Only the action chunk is executed, determining the immediate motion and gripper commands.

Proprioceptive Action Models (PAM) jointly generate the sketch and an action chunk within a single transformer denoiser. As illustrated in Figure 1, both outputs are initialized with Gaussian noise and refined through iterative denoising. A block-causal attention mask allows action tokens to attend to the sketch while preventing sketch tokens from reading the action stream. Following Diffusion Forcing (Chen et al., 2024), we train the denoiser with varying corruption levels across the two streams and use a staggered denoising schedule that denoises the sketch ahead of the actions, providing cleaner geometric context for action generation.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate the proprioceptive sketch, a compact, timing-free representation of the remaining configuration-space path that serves as an explicit intermediate variable for action generation and is, by construction, invariant to temporal reparameterization of the demonstrated path. Second, we develop a joint generator with directed attention and staggered denoising to guide action prediction with the sketch. Third, we apply PAM to a diffusion transformer trained from scratch (PAM-DP), and a pretrained vision-language-action model (PAM-VLA). We evaluate PAM-DP on Push-T and four real-world bimanual tasks, and PAM-VLA on LIBERO-Long.

title: CSIR: Contextually and Socially Informed Robots for Efficient Person Goal Navigation
authors: Tyler Chung,Nahl Farhan,Hao Zhang,Mingfeng Yuan,Jinjun Shan,Amy Wu,Yue Hu
abstract:
We address the Person Goal Navigation (PersonNav) problem, enabling robots to search for people under realistic constraints on information accessibility and language uncertainty. This tackles the current solutions revolving around rigid person finding systems requiring exact knowledge of the individual for item-delivery in indoor settings. While the focus in literature is on learned methods using unavailable public or sparse data due to human privacy. We propose a planning framework that combines distance and semantic information about the recipient (habits and intent) weighted by the trust of the user-provided information. A synthetic benchmark of scenarios is also developed including actors, items, and requests to evaluate performance before real-world deployment aiming to simulate natural language human-robot interactions.
Results show our informed search outperforms classical distance-based graph baselines, while semantics alone lead to ungrounded, sporadic search. Our method achieves strong gains over baselines, with an LLM-based variant performing comparably, and its explicit belief representation naturally supports future Bayesian filtering. Hardware tests demonstrate our method supports real-world embodiment able to leverage between semantic and distance information in a real setting. This work moves toward more intelligent mobile service agents capable of human-like, informed search in realistic environments to be leveraged in day-to-day use.

introduction:
About one in three physicians experience burnout interfering with not only their well being but ability to provide quality care for others [1]. As result of the working conditions, this has led to an increase in burnout, health issues, and errors in medical practice [2]. To alleviate staffing pressure, nursing robots are used to automate item-delivery tasks [3], with platforms such as MOXI or TUG use voice or graphical interfaces to schedule and design routes for transportation in hospitals [3]. One limitation is that current tools require fixed location scheduling to deliver items, but people are dynamic, not bounded to locations as they are goal driven. This realizes the problem that these solutions lack the capability to perform its tasked when the assumption that people are static fail. Moving away from fixed location settings and towards dynamic goal-driven people raises the question of “How can robots find people given partial observations of their behaviours and the environment”, we define this problem space as Person Goal Navigation (PersonNav). While this is motivated by the healthcare landscape, this problem expands to other tasks ranging from food delivery, office supply transportation, to nursing home monitoring.

This paper proposes the development of a travel efficient PersonNav framework for indoor item-delivery tasks under limited and uncertain information about the recipient (whom we want to deliver to). Our proposed task space for PersonNav is catered to real-world feasibility in indoor item-delivery scenarios, where a user requests the agent to deliver an item to a recipient (consented information to the robot). Current methods in literature require critical pieces of information from human-activity logs [4] or daily schedules [5], but are partially or fully unavailable in the real-world due to privacy reasons. The current gap is that existing methods leverage critical and sensitive information without consideration of realistic information availability. To address this problem, our work aimed to investigate methods to extrapolate a person’s location from natural language requests and handle information uncertainty (e.g. Low: “They might be at …” vs High: “They’re definitely at …”). We hypothesized that by using several weaker/indirect signals of the person’s whereabouts, we can improve search under uncertain information gains for efficient indoor item-delivery tasks while abiding by real-world constraints in human privacy. The contributions of this paper are:

Contextually and Socially Informed Robots (CSIR), that addresses the PersonNav problem aimed to perform efficiency item-delivery tasks under varying linguistic uncertainty.

title: Around the World: Unified Learned Locomotion on a 270 g Continuous-Rotation Quadruped
authors: Arturo Flores Alvarez,Nathan Lintu,Dennis Hong
comment: including appendices. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Closed-loop learned locomotion is established on commercial quadrupeds
but remains uncommon at the sub-kilogram scale. Continuous-rotation
legs give MiNI-Q, a 270 g270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} quadruped, access to supporting
configurations on either side of the body. We exploit this range with
a single posture-conditioned reinforcement-learning policy that runs
entirely onboard. A continuous joint-space reference on the torus
T8T^{8} and its gravity-conditioned transformation connect upright
walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery without state machines
or phase switching. Coordinated posture and release curricula train
this behavior family; identified actuation, cross-engine validation,
and embedded execution support hardware transfer. The same
sub-100k-parameter network tracks forward velocity with RMSE of
0.037 m s−10.037\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} upright and
0.050 m s−10.050\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} inverted, resumes walking in 24 of 30
release trials, and operates with four interchangeable foot geometries
across four indoor surfaces. Hardware experiments and simulation
ablations connect these capabilities to the representation,
conditioning, and training choices that exploit the platform’s motion
range. Demonstration videos and supplementary material are available
on the project website:
https://submissionreview.github.io/around-the-world/.
introduction:
Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion and diverse
behaviors on quadruped robots [13, 34, 27].
At the sub-kilogram scale, learned locomotion remains less
established [15, 1]. Small, low-cost
quadrupeds are widely available for educational and research use, but
closed-loop learned control with sim-to-real transfer at this mass is
comparatively rare. The closest sibling platforms in this class,
MiNI-Q [20] and Q8bot [41], have been
reported as hardware introductions or under open-loop control.
MiNI-Q is a 270 g270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} quadruped whose eight belt-driven joints
rotate without mechanical stops. This range permits supporting leg
configurations on either side of the body and continuous changes of
stance.

That topology has two consequences for control. First, each joint
lives on the circle S1S^{1} rather than a bounded interval, so the joint
space is the torus T8=(S1)8T^{8}=(S^{1})^{8}. One policy can therefore represent
inverted gaits, mid-flight repositioning, and interpolated postures
that joint limits would exclude. Second, the platform is modular
enough that reprinting lower links, swapping foot geometries, and
reflashing compute are part of ordinary laboratory iteration. These
properties also introduce specific challenges. Unbounded joints break
standard observation pipelines at ±π\pm\pi. The 270 g270\text{\,}\mathrm{g} mass
sits near simulator integration regimes where effort-mode and
position-mode actuation diverge, and the lower links weigh only
1 g1\text{\,}\mathrm{g} each. The belt drive introduces measurable backlash, the
onboard compute is a pair of microcontrollers linked over
I2C rather than a single processor, and printed foot
geometry varies with manufacturing tolerance and wear.

On this miniature platform, learning must turn the continuous-rotation
range into a controller that follows posture and velocity commands,
repositions its legs during a fall, and resumes walking after contact.
Periodic joint representations and training across postures and
release conditions connect these behaviors. Hardware deployment
further requires transfer to the dynamics of the geared servos,
lightweight links, and interchangeable feet within the robot’s onboard
sensing and compute budget.

The published MiNI-Q platform demonstrates inverted mobility using
precomputed trajectories [20]. We exploit its leg
symmetry to connect these behaviors in one closed-loop policy. To our
knowledge, this is the first demonstration on a sub-kilogram quadruped
of a single learned policy, executed entirely on onboard
microcontrollers, that unifies upright and inverted locomotion,
continuous posture conditioning, and landing recovery.
Our contributions are:

Unified locomotion and recovery across body orientations.
A gravity-conditioned reference exploits the leg symmetry to connect
upright walking, inverted walking, and landing recovery in one
policy, with periodic observations and a release curriculum. No
state machines or phase switching are used; a compact network runs
entirely onboard at 50 Hz50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}.

Continuous posture conditioning during locomotion.
A continuous joint-space command on T8T^{8} represents stance, body
attitude, and interpolated references, including their inverted
counterparts, while the same policy follows a velocity command. An
interpolation curriculum reaches intermediate postures that are
never presented as discrete training targets.

Onboard transfer across foot geometries.
Foot-shape randomization, identified actuation, and embedded execution
support the same trained policy across tested foot variants and
surfaces without retraining, connecting the formulation to a modular
miniature robot.

Each contribution is evaluated in Section VI and
ablated in Section VI-G. The supporting identification,
validation, and onboard inference pipeline is detailed in
Sections III–IV and
Appendix A.
