title: RoboBridge: A Self-Evolving Embodied Agent Framework for Sim-to-Real Transfer
authors: Chenxi Li,Zhangrui Zhao,Rui Li,Yuan Gao,Kehui Liu,Jiarui Li,Dong Wang,Tong Si,Minting Pan,Wanli Ouyang,Dongzhan Zhou
abstract: A key challenge in bringing embodied intelligence into the real world is transferring capabilities from simulation to reality and enabling agents to continually adapt after deployment. End-to-end vision-language-action policies provide strong manipulation capabilities, but their transfer to physical environments typically relies on calibrating simulated visual and dynamical conditions, collecting additional target-domain demonstrations, and optimizing the policy through further training. Tool-using embodied agents offer flexible task orchestration, yet existing systems primarily emphasize task execution and experience reuse within a given environment, with limited support for transferring procedural knowledge and continuously adapting it across simulation and reality. We propose RoboBridge, a framework that treats sim-to-real transfer as the continued adaptation of executable task skills. The agent represents task knowledge as procedures connecting task intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. Interaction feedback is used to generate candidate skill revisions, which are evaluated before being persisted or rejected. A pretrained vision-language-action policy is exposed as a reusable action tool and enhanced with inference-time guidance, enabling fine-grained execution without retraining the underlying policy. RoboBridge grounds transferable skills in task semantics and interaction interfaces shared across simulation and reality. This representation preserves reusable task structure while allowing environment-dependent operations to be selectively revised through real-world execution feedback. We evaluate the framework on LIBERO-PRO and corresponding physical tasks, studying both skill evolution and post-transfer adaptation. Our framework provides a route from one-shot policy deployment to continual procedural learning across environments.
introduction:
Reliable sim-to-real transfer requires robotic systems to preserve task performance across differences in visual observations and physical dynamics (Zhao et al., 2020).
End-to-end vision-language-action models provide fine-grained manipulation capabilities by mapping visual observations and language instructions to action sequences (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024). The policy-centered pathway illustrated in Figure 1 includes adapting simulation conditions using real-world experience (Chebotar et al., 2018). For pretrained VLA models, adaptation to new robotic settings commonly involves target-domain demonstrations and policy fine-tuning (Kim et al., 2025). In this formulation, task knowledge is largely embedded in model parameters and learned action distributions. This makes it difficult to isolate a reusable task procedure and selectively revise it when execution conditions change, tying procedural adaptation closely to policy optimization.

Tool-using embodied agents offer a way to make task procedures explicit (Singh et al., 2022; Rana et al., 2023). An agent harness provides the observation and tool interfaces through which the agent organizes subtasks, invokes operations, and verifies their outcomes (Liu et al., 2026a). Successful procedures can then be retained as skills for subsequent execution (Wang et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2026). Feedback-based memory updates and skill refinement extend this reuse across interactions (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026), and recent robotic systems further incorporate repair validation and validation-gated skill updates (Lu et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026). Sim-to-real deployment requires these mechanisms to govern which parts of a transferred procedure remain applicable and how the others should be refined using target-environment feedback. Meanwhile, task decomposition and tool selection still require an underlying capability to execute continuous, fine-grained manipulation (Yu et al., 2023). Recent harnesses address this execution requirement by exposing frozen VLA policies as reusable manipulation primitives (Zhang et al., 2026b). This perspective motivates a framework that combines revisable task knowledge with the manipulation capabilities of pretrained policies.

We propose RoboBridge, a self-evolving embodied agent framework for sim-to-real transfer of procedural skills. RoboBridge incorporates a pretrained VLA policy as a reusable action tool within an agent harness. The policy supplies short manipulation segments, while the agent determines how these operations are organized, when they should be invoked, and whether their outcomes satisfy the task. Task knowledge is stored as procedural skills connecting intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. This organization preserves pretrained execution capabilities while exposing task procedures for revision through interaction. As illustrated in Figure 1, skills evolved in simulation are reused in reality through aligned task semantics and interaction interfaces, with action tools instantiated for each environment. Real-world execution feedback then supports continued skill adaptation. Effective transfer requires both reliable revision of the transferred procedures and accurate execution of their local operations.

Reliable execution presents a complementary challenge: even a suitable task procedure can fail when a frozen policy produces actions that do not meet the current subtask requirements (Liu et al., 2026b). Prior work has explored adapting pretrained policy behavior during inference through external guidance or verification (Wang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026b). RoboBridge therefore augments the policy tool with inference-time guidance. The agent determines whether guidance is needed and configures a reward specification from the subtask objective, execution constraints, and observed feedback. This reward steers action generation toward the intended operation while keeping the policy parameters fixed. Skill evolution thus adjusts the procedure across episodes, while inference-time guidance adapts action generation within an invocation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A self-evolving framework for procedural sim-to-real transfer.
We integrate pretrained action capabilities with explicit task skills, enabling procedures evolved in simulation to be reused through aligned interaction interfaces and further adapted from real-world feedback.

Controlled skill evolution.
We develop a feedback-driven process for adding, revising, and deleting procedural knowledge, with validation governing which updates are persisted and which are rejected or rolled back.

Adaptive policy-tool orchestration.
We enable the agent to determine when to invoke the pretrained policy, when to activate inference-time guidance, and how to configure subtask rewards, supporting context-dependent execution with frozen policy parameters.

title: RoboChemGym: A Protocol-Driven Generative Simulation Framework for Long-Horizon Chemical Manipulation
authors: Chenxi Li,Haiyuan Wan,Rui Li,Jingyuan Li,Sha Zhang,Bohan Feng,Jianbao Cao,Zhangrui Zhao,Di Hu,Wangmeng Zuo,Shixiang Tang,Minting Pan,Dongzhan Zhou
abstract: Wet-lab experimentation serves as the gold standard for hypothesis verification in scientific discovery; yet it is inherently labor-intensive, costly, and safety-critical. Embodied agents hold the promise of automating these tedious workflows, but their development is hindered by the scarcity of real-world training data. While simulation offers a scalable alternative for producing demonstrations, current methods primarily target relatively short-horizon tasks with loosely structured interactions, failing to meet the strict procedural constraints and fine-grained manipulation demands of chemical experiments. To bridge this gap, we introduce RoboChemGym, a framework that autonomously generates high-fidelity manipulation demonstrations aligned with real-world experiment protocols, featuring a self-improving task synthesis mechanism to iteratively refine task execution and scene configurations, enabling the reliable generation of expert trajectories for complex, multi-object protocols exceeding 10 interaction steps. Furthermore, we introduce a hierarchical benchmark that systematically assesses performance across varying granularities, spanning from atomic operations to full-cycle experimental workflows. RoboChemGym sets a scalable paradigm for the automated data synthesis and capability evaluation of embodied agents in intricate chemical tasks, serving as a critical stepping stone toward fully intelligent laboratories.

title: AdaTempo: Learning Shared Relative Tempo from Demonstrations for Faster Robot Manipulation
authors: Jiale Cao,Yike Niu,Zhengrong Xue,Huazhe Xu
abstract:
Visuomotor policies trained via imitation learning
often inherit the unnecessarily slow timing of teleoperated
demonstrations. Yet uniform speedup is unreliable because
different phases of a manipulation task tolerate acceleration
differently. In this work, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method that accelerates visuomotor policies by exploiting shared relative-tempo structure in demonstrations. AdaTempo establishes phase correspondence, aggregates the aligned relative tempo into a consensus, and maps it to a continuous speedup profile used to resample demonstrations into accelerated training trajectories. Training
standard policies such as ACT or Diffusion Policy on these
resampled trajectories directly embeds the desired tempo in the
learned behavior, without runtime tempo selection or online
retiming. Extensive evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves
up to a 3.57×3.57\times speedup and yields a stronger success–speed trade-off than the original policies and representative acceleration baselines.
introduction:
Visuomotor imitation learning has become a practical paradigm for acquiring
complex manipulation skills from teleoperated
demonstrations [1, 2, 3]. Recent
large-scale policies have further improved generalization across tasks and
robot embodiments [4, 5, 6]. Yet standard imitation
objectives optimize what actions to reproduce, not how quickly they should be
executed. Since teleoperated demonstrations are often slow and cautious, the
resulting policies tend to inherit this conservative execution
timing [7, 8, 9, 10].

Removing this inefficiency is not as simple as downsampling the demonstrated
trajectories by a constant rate. Different phases of a manipulation task
tolerate acceleration differently. Uniform acceleration can skip important
intermediate states, alter the closed-loop state distribution, or request
motions that the controller cannot track over the shortened time
horizon [8, 10, 11]. Effective
speedup therefore requires determining both how much to accelerate a task and
how to distribute that acceleration over its progress.

Recent work has made substantial progress in accelerating learned manipulation
policies beyond demonstration
speed [7, 9, 8, 10, 11]. However, existing methods typically determine
how acceleration should vary using policy-derived proxies,
interaction-based optimization, or additional runtime mechanisms, requiring auxiliary machinery during training or deployment. This motivates a
central question: can demonstrations themselves provide a direct and
fine-grained supervisory signal for phase-dependent speedup?

As illustrated in Fig. , our key observation is that
demonstrations may differ in absolute speed yet
tend to exhibit similar relative-tempo patterns over task progress, consistent
with prior observations of approximate relative-timing invariance in skilled
movement [12]. Rather than absolute speed, we focus on
relative tempo: within each demonstration, which phases are executed relatively
faster or slower? When corresponding phases exhibit similar relative tempo
across demonstrations, this consistency suggests phase-specific task
characteristics. Phases consistently executed more cautiously, such as
grasping or insertion, may tolerate less temporal compression, while relatively
fast phases such as free-space transport offer greater acceleration potential.

Based on this insight, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method
for learning cross-demonstration relative tempo to accelerate visuomotor policies. AdaTempo aligns demonstrations with different durations, constructs
episode-relative tempo profiles at corresponding task phases, and aggregates
them into a cross-demonstration consensus while downweighting phases with high
disagreement. It maps this consensus to a continuous speedup profile used
for smooth virtual-time resampling of the original trajectories. A standard visuomotor policy, such as ACT or Diffusion Policy (DP), is then trained on the
accelerated trajectories. The desired tempo is thus embedded directly in the
learned behavior, requiring no runtime tempo-selection module, online retiming,
or changes to the control interface at deployment.

Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves
up to a 3.57×3.57\times speedup over demonstrations and yields a stronger
success–speed trade-off than the original policies and representative
acceleration baselines. Our contributions are:

We identify shared relative tempo across demonstrations as a self-supervised cue for phase-dependent speedup, revealing recurring phase-wise timing structure beyond demonstrator-specific absolute speed.

We develop AdaTempo, which phase-aligns demonstrations, converts their relative-tempo consensus into a continuous speedup profile for offline virtual-time resampling, without auxiliary models or additional mechanisms at deployment.

We validate AdaTempo across 11 simulated and real-world manipulation tasks with ACT or DP, achieving up to a 3.57×3.57\times speedup and a stronger success–speed trade-off than representative acceleration baselines.

1. We identify shared relative tempo across demonstrations as a self-supervised cue for phase-dependent speedup, revealing recurring phase-wise timing structure beyond demonstrator-specific absolute speed.

2. We develop AdaTempo, which phase-aligns demonstrations, converts their relative-tempo consensus into a continuous speedup profile for offline virtual-time resampling, without auxiliary models or additional mechanisms at deployment.

3. We validate AdaTempo across 11 simulated and real-world manipulation tasks with ACT or DP, achieving up to a 3.57×3.57\times speedup and a stronger success–speed trade-off than representative acceleration baselines.

title: GeoScaffold: Learning Compact Geometric Latents via Reconstruction for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Yixuan Jiang,Wentong Li,An Liu,Zihao Xin,Fulin Tang,Cong Leng,Yang Gao,Jian Cheng
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adopt streaming Video-LLM policies that map egocentric RGB observations and instructions directly to low-level actions. Yet these policies inherit weak 3D geometric priors from 2D pretraining. Existing geometry-aware extensions charge a persistent inference-time price: depth sensors, 3D encoders, or per-step perception tool calls. We propose GeoScaffold, a geometric supervision framework that pays this price once, at training time, by internalizing geometry into the policy itself. It first learns a compact depth tokenizer on depth maps from the training trajectories and freezes it. It then fine-tunes the policy with a handful of learnable geometry query tokens, training their hidden states to reconstruct navigation-critical geometry such as depth, connectivity, and traversability. This supervision turns the query states into compact geometric latents for action decoding, and through the shared weights also internalizes geometry into the backbone’s own representations. Like a scaffold, the tokenizer, target generators, and reconstruction heads are discarded after training, leaving the backbone and action interface unchanged. Extensive experiments show that GeoScaffold consistently outperforms leading vision-only navigators on continuous VLN benchmarks, offering a practical paradigm for lightweight edge deployment of spatially aware embodied navigation models.
introduction:
Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions while moving through a previously unseen environment (Anderson et al., 2018; Ku et al., 2020; Krantz et al., 2020). Recent progress has increasingly moved VLN toward an end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm, in which a Video-LLM policy maps egocentric RGB observations and the instruction to navigation actions step by step (Zhang et al., 2024b; Cheng et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a; Xin et al., 2026b). However, the backbones underlying these policies are pretrained almost entirely on internet-scale 2D data, which makes them strong at semantic recognition yet weak at metric and topological reasoning (Chen et al., 2024; Fu et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025). Navigation demands exactly these abilities. Beyond recognizing objects and matching them to linguistic landmarks, an agent must reason about free space, relative scale, doorway structure, and route connectivity. These policies therefore struggle with depth-sensitive decisions, such as judging whether a landmark is nearby, whether a passage is traversable, or whether to continue exploring rather than stop prematurely.

Existing methods compensate for this weakness with additional machinery at inference time. Geometry-enhanced methods give the policy explicit spatial support, running a frozen 3D encoder alongside the backbone (Zeng et al., 2026; Fan et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or lifting RGB-D observations into geometry-aware BEV maps (Yang et al., 2026). As shown in Figure 1(b), these components remain active at deployment, with depth sensors adding hardware requirements and 3D encoders increasing GPU memory usage and inference latency. Other methods restructure the system, adopting dual-system designs in which a slow reasoning module guides a fast controller (Wei et al., 2026; Intern Robotics, 2025; Xue et al., 2026) or zero-shot pipelines of LLM planners, perception, and path-planning components (Zhou et al., 2024; Long et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). Such designs require coordination among multiple modules, complicating system integration and deployment.

By contrast, humans act with rich spatial awareness from visual experience alone, without explicit depth sensing at every step. For navigation, such spatial awareness should help the agent judge distances, identify traversable regions, and recognize passages that connect spaces. We therefore ask whether geometric supervision can equip an end-to-end VLA navigator with these abilities during training, while requiring only RGB observations and language instructions at deployment.

To this end, we propose GeoScaffold, a training-only geometric enhancement framework for streaming VLN. GeoScaffold supervises the policy with three geometric targets. Depth captures metric scale, while connectivity and traversability mark route-relevant passages and free space, respectively. The supervision enters through a small set of learnable geometry query tokens (Carion et al., 2020; Li et al., 2023; Mu et al., 2023; Lai et al., 2024), inserted before each action block, one dedicated group per target. Each group learns to reconstruct its own target from its hidden states. Training proceeds in two stages. Stage I learns a compact depth tokenizer offline. Stage II then fine-tunes the policy with the navigation objective unchanged plus the auxiliary reconstruction losses. This pressure compresses scene geometry into the query hidden states, which act as compact geometric latents for action decoding. After training, all auxiliary modules are discarded. The deployed policy runs on RGB and text alone, with only the learned geometry tokens remaining in the prompt.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce GeoScaffold, a lightweight, removable geometric enhancement framework for efficient end-to-end streaming VLN that requires no depth sensors, 3D encoders, or reconstruction modules at inference time and deploys on edge hardware.

We design a query-token reconstruction objective whose dedicated depth, connectivity, and traversability groups shape their hidden states into compact geometric latents.

We present an empirical study of training-only geometric supervision for VLN, showing consistent success-rate gains across different backbones and in real-world deployment, with only the learned geometry tokens retained at inference.

1. We introduce GeoScaffold, a lightweight, removable geometric enhancement framework for efficient end-to-end streaming VLN that requires no depth sensors, 3D encoders, or reconstruction modules at inference time and deploys on edge hardware.

2. We design a query-token reconstruction objective whose dedicated depth, connectivity, and traversability groups shape their hidden states into compact geometric latents.

3. We present an empirical study of training-only geometric supervision for VLN, showing consistent success-rate gains across different backbones and in real-world deployment, with only the learned geometry tokens retained at inference.

title: Who Went Where When on the Lunar Surface: Forensic Trajectory Analysis to Identify Byzantine Rovers
authors: Lachlan Holden,Feras Dayoub,Melissa de Zwart,David Harvey,Tat-Jun Chin
abstract: Future planetary surface missions are likely to involve multiple independently operated rovers sharing the same deployment region, raising the need to verify compliance with operational constraints such as Lunar Safety Zones. Because continuous in-situ observability is rarely available, such verification requires post-hoc reconstruction of rover trajectories from sparse telemetry, including odometry, pose priors, and relative inter-rover detections. We introduce the problem of forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers in the presence of Byzantine agents: rovers that provide miscalibrated or deliberately falsified measurements to support an incorrect trajectory. We show that standard outlier-robust pose graph optimisation methods are vulnerable in this setting, because Byzantine rovers can generate measurements that are internally consistent and numerous enough to make truthful incriminating measurements appear as outliers. To address this, we propose an attribution-aware trajectory estimation method that reasons over rover credibility rather than individual measurement validity. The method evaluates candidate credible rover subsets by comparing the statistical consistency of their internal and boundary relative detections against provided priors, and then estimates trajectories using only measurements attributed to credible agents. Across synthetic simulations and real planetary-analogue trajectory data, the proposed method identifies Byzantine rovers and produces significantly more accurate trajectory estimates than existing robust pose graph optimisation baselines.
introduction:
One of the key characteristics of the New Space era of the 21st century is the rise of space missions driven by private companies [1]. With lunar landings no longer solely the domain of individual nation-states, current and future missions involve the rovers and landers of multiple companies and countries working together in close proximity. This is exemplified by missions like IM-2, which involved multiple US and Japan-based companies [12]. For successful co-located operation of this kind, efforts like the Artemis Accords [21] and the Chinese-led International Lunar Research Station [23] are attempting to establish norms. One relevant provision of the Artemis Accords is that of Lunar Safety Zones, where stakeholders can establish areas where only certain parties may enter.

To be able to determine the compliance of different rovers with protocols like Lunar Safety Zones under the situational awareness constraints typical of planetary missions, a method for post-hoc determining the trajectories that rovers have taken based on relatively low-fidelity downlinked data is essential. This data includes metrics like odometry, map localisation estimates, and relative detections from infrequent images. For the real-world application of these trajectories, it is crucial to design a method that is Byzantine-resilient, which is to say capable of handling agents that are providing poorly calibrated or deliberately misleading data. This work introduces this problem of “forensic trajectory analysis”: post-hoc determination of multi-rover trajectories in the presence of adversarial measurements.

This paper makes three contributions:

We formulate forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers as a post-hoc state-estimation problem with Byzantine measurement sources;

We propose an attribution-aware credibility inference method that scores candidate rover subsets using internal consistency and boundary inconsistency of relative detections; and

We demonstrate, using synthetic and planetary-analogue trajectories, that conventional robust pose graph optimisation (PGO) methods can be systematically misled by Byzantine agents, while the proposed method identifies non-credible rovers and improves trajectory reconstruction.

1. We formulate forensic trajectory analysis for non-cooperative planetary rovers as a post-hoc state-estimation problem with Byzantine measurement sources;

2. We propose an attribution-aware credibility inference method that scores candidate rover subsets using internal consistency and boundary inconsistency of relative detections; and

3. We demonstrate, using synthetic and planetary-analogue trajectories, that conventional robust pose graph optimisation (PGO) methods can be systematically misled by Byzantine agents, while the proposed method identifies non-credible rovers and improves trajectory reconstruction.

title: DeltaWorld: Physically Consistent Interactive World Simulators via Action-Conditioned Latent Increment Learning
authors: Boyuan Hou,Xiaoge Cao,Chaofan Zhang,Shuo Wang,Shaowei Cui
abstract: Interactive world simulators can provide scalable environments for robot planning, policy training, and evaluation by predicting action consequences while reducing reliance on repeated physical rollouts. To serve these applications, they must generate future image sequences that respond faithfully to robot actions and preserve the dynamics of robot-object interactions over long horizons. However, existing world models typically predict the entire next latent state and often fail to capture subtle changes induced by robot actions. Such omissions can produce physically implausible outcomes, including object interpenetration and excessive deformation. To address this limitation, we propose DeltaWorld, a physically consistent interactive world simulator for robotic manipulation. Our method introduces the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-induced latent feature changes and adds them to the current latent state to obtain the next state, rather than predicting the next latent state directly. To mitigate object interpenetration and excessive deformation in predicted future frames, Interaction-aware Latent Alignment is introduced to construct counterfactual interaction regions and supervise interaction-related latent changes. DeltaWorld is evaluated on the IWS manipulation benchmark and a self-collected cross-robot dataset covering multiple robot embodiments and manipulation tasks. On the cross-robot dataset, DeltaWorld reduces FVD by 46.6% and LPIPS by 31.1% relative to the IWS baseline. These results highlight the potential of DeltaWorld for long-horizon action-conditioned video prediction in robotic manipulation.
introduction:
With the increasing adoption of data-driven approaches in robotic manipulation, real-world robot interaction data have become a fundamental resource for learning complex manipulation behaviors [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. However, policy training, action exploration, and performance evaluation often require repeated physical robot rollouts. These rollouts consume time and hardware resources, limiting the scale and reproducibility of experiments [1, 6]. World models offer a promising way to reduce reliance on physical rollouts by learning action-conditioned environment dynamics from existing robot interaction data. Such models can simulate the outcomes of robot actions, thereby supporting planning [7, 8], policy learning, and evaluation [9, 6, 10]. Unlike conventional image prediction models that primarily focus on visual appearance changes, world models for robotic manipulation place greater emphasis on action-conditioned environment evolution, including object motion, robot–object interactions, and long-horizon action consequences [11].

To realize action-conditioned prediction, recent work has explored different representations of future robot observations. JEPA-style models forecast learned visual features without directly reconstructing pixels [12, 13]. The Interactive World Simulator (IWS) learns action-conditioned dynamics in a compact image latent space and decodes predicted states into video [6]. In parallel, video-generative world models support interactive evaluation by conditioning future frames on policy-derived latent actions [14] or on frame-level controls with pose-conditioned memory [10]. More recently, dWorldEval has modeled observations and actions jointly as discrete tokens, with sparse keyframes to support long-horizon prediction [15].

Despite these advances, predicting robot manipulation videos remains difficult when an action changes only a small part of the scene. Most of the image may stay the same between adjacent frames, while a robot action can move an object or alter its shape. Models that directly predict future frames or their latent representations may capture the largely unchanged scene while missing small changes to manipulated objects. The resulting errors can grow during autoregressive rollout and cause object drift or implausible deformation. Therefore, the key challenge is to predict the changes caused by robot actions, especially in regions where the robot interacts with objects.

To address this challenge, we propose DeltaWorld, a physically consistent interactive world simulator that predicts action-induced latent changes instead of the entire next latent state. Our method introduces the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which estimates these changes and adds them to the current latent state to obtain the next state. Interaction-aware Latent Alignment uses counterfactual interaction regions to emphasize changes around robot–object interactions during training. Experiments on the IWS benchmark and a self-collected cross-robot dataset show improved action-conditioned video prediction quality and long-horizon consistency across multiple manipulation tasks and robot embodiments. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose DeltaWorld, an interactive world simulator built on the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-conditioned latent increments to update the current state, promoting stable long-horizon prediction and physically plausible interaction dynamics.

We propose DeltaWorld, an interactive world simulator built on the Delta Latent Transition Model (Delta-LTM), which predicts action-conditioned latent increments to update the current state, promoting stable long-horizon prediction and physically plausible interaction dynamics.

We introduce Interaction-aware Latent Alignment, which provides structured supervision over task-relevant regions and encourages the simulator to capture the physical regularities underlying object changes rather than appearance-dominated latent transitions.

We conduct systematic evaluations on the IWS manipulation benchmark and a self-collected dataset covering multiple robot embodiments. Experimental results show that DeltaWorld outperforms existing world model baselines across image- and video-level metrics for action-conditioned video prediction, while ablation studies further verify the complementary roles of Delta-LTM and Interaction-aware Latent Alignment.

title: A Passive AI System for Verifying Physical State on Automated Liquid Handlers
authors: Junqiong Joanne Qiu,Zeckria Kamrany,Ananya Anand,Emma Vidal,Yunjia Johanna Bai,Nathan S Chen,Sean Son,Varada Abhyankar,Taryn Jakub,Eleazar Eskin
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Laboratories are increasingly automating routine workflows. In a 2025 survey, 49% of respondents reported using robotics or automation in their company’s laboratories [1]. Automated liquid handlers are a key tool in laboratory automation, supporting molecular biology workflows such as sequencing library preparation, PCR setup, and high-throughput processing [2]. They enable workflows to be run reproducibly with minimal manual labor. These systems are offered by manufacturers such as Opentrons, Tecan, and Hamilton. Quality-control studies of laboratory automation show that liquid handlers require routine checks to stay accurate and reliable, since components can fail over time [3, 4]. Setup errors, however, can occur even earlier: a plate placed in the wrong slot, the wrong tip rack loaded, a reservoir missing, or labware shifted or occluded on the deck. These errors can cause collisions, damage the robot, or lead to incorrect liquid transfers that compromise the experiment. This physical starting state requires manual assembly: labware, reagents, plates, and tip racks must be placed on the deck in the correct locations before the protocol begins. Correct deck setup relies on user confirmation, and there is no system in place to confirm that the setup matches the robot’s expectations, making the initial manual deck setup step prone to errors. Therefore, a monitoring layer is needed to answer three questions: what experiment the operator is running, whether the deck is prepared correctly for it, and whether the robot is executing the protocol correctly.

To implement a monitoring layer, a visual system is required. Currently, camera-based deck checking is available on the Opentrons Flex, which carries a built-in 2 MP camera that records images and video [5]. The camera sends images to an operator or to storage, but does not report whether the observed labware is correct for a given protocol. Tecan Fluent workstations run DeckCheck, which photographs the worktable after loading and compares the live layout against a stored reference [6]. However, DeckCheck only compares pixels and not labware identity, leading to the manual listing differences it cannot flag: different tip types, missing tubes on partially loaded runners, plates rotated by 180 degrees, and well shape [6]. Research systems have used computer vision to monitor laboratory processes and detect anomalies during automated liquid transfer [7, 8], and have supported colorimetric titration [9], but these remain isolated capabilities rather than a general check against a protocol’s requirements.

Existing options do not provide a modular and accessible verification layer that a laboratory can add to the liquid handler it already owns. DeckCheck is integrated into a high-end workstation and is unavailable for lower-cost platforms. Accessible self-driving laboratories close the loop between planning, execution, measurement, and decision-making [10, 11, 12], but also require tightly integrated instruments, data infrastructure, and expertise that academic life-science laboratories often lack [13]. As a result, a laboratory running an affordable liquid handler has no straightforward way to check its deck against the intended protocol.

Such a system must meet four constraints: it must be inexpensive, leave robot hardware and firmware untouched, run on an available computer, and add no work to the operator’s routine. Computer vision makes this checking system practical: a camera is an inexpensive non-contact sensor, and deep learning now localizes, segments, and classifies objects reliably in visually cluttered scenes [14, 15]. Applied to a deck image, these methods can find each slot, separate labware from its background, identify the labware type, and map it to the robot’s canonical deck coordinates, turning a photograph into a structured deck state that can be compared with a protocol.

We present the Labware Setup Checker, a passive vision system for the Opentrons Flex that utilizes a low-cost camera and lightweight models to confirm an observed deck setup against an intended protocol within seconds. A consumer webcam outside the robot observes the deck. The checker segments the image into slots, classifies masked and cropped labware images, corrects the assignments against canonical slot geometry, and compares the result with a reference protocol library, marking each slot as correct, wrong, misplaced, or unexpected. The checker operates passively and noninvasively, requiring only a simple session setup and checking the deck automatically without interrupting robot operation or adding manual steps to the established procedure. This work contributes an external verification architecture for the Opentrons Flex that requires no hardware or firmware modification, protocol-aware deck perception at seconds-scale latency in a deployed setting, and an evaluation system compatible with routine laboratory workflows.

title: Real-time Event-camera Stereo Visual Odometry via Keytime Gaussian Process Regression
authors: Nikan Nobari,Jonathan D. Gammell
comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027, . The corresponding video can be found atthis https URL
abstract: Event cameras have microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range which make them more resilient to motion blur and poor illumination than standard frame-based cameras. Event-camera visual odometry (VO) pipelines maximize these benefits when they process the asynchronous event stream at the native temporal resolution. Continuous-time Gaussian process (GP) regression and a white-noise-on-acceleration (WNOA) prior can handle asynchronous measurements but result in a prohibitively large estimation state when applied naively.
introduction:
Frame-based cameras capture visual information as discrete images. Visual odometry (VO) and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) pipelines built on these cameras have achieved remarkable success [1, 2, 3] but they struggle in the presence of motion blur or poor image contrast which degrade feature tracking and cause inaccurate estimates. This often occurs with highly dynamic camera motions and in environments with poor illumination.

Event cameras use a fundamentally different sensing paradigm that can avoid these problems. They report pixel intensity changes with microsecond-level temporal resolution and possess a higher dynamic range than traditional frame-based sensors. This combination reduces the limitations of standard cameras and promises VO pipelines that are more resilient to motion blur and poor lighting [4].

Event-camera VO pipelines must account for the asynchronous nature of event data to achieve the full potential of event cameras. Some discrete event-camera VO pipelines maintain the asynchronous measurement times by using motion-compensated event frames [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10] or extracting event-based features [11, 7] in their front end but then group events during state estimation and reduce temporal resolution. Continuous-time estimation methods alternatively provide tools to handle the asynchronous measurement times during estimation [12]. Some Gaussian process (GP) continuous-time VO pipelines (e.g., GPCT [13]) use a white-noise-on-acceleration (WNOA) motion prior [14] to maintain the individual measurement times but naive application of the estimator requires a state for each event feature and does not run in real time.

This paper presents a real-time continuous-time event-camera VO pipeline that uses keytime interpolation [15, 14, 16, 17] to reduce the size of the estimation state. The pipeline considers event features at individual timestamps to reject outliers with motion-compensated RANSAC (MC-RANSAC) [18]. It then defines a smaller estimation state at a selected set of sparse keytimes but still evaluates each measurement at its individual measurement time by interpolating between the keytimes with a WNOA prior (Fig. 1).
This ensures that the pipeline runs in real-time while maintaining the temporal resolution of the event camera.

The presented pipeline is evaluated on the multi-vehicle stereo event camera (MVSEC) [19] and driving scenarios for event cameras (DSEC) [20] datasets. The experimental results show that the keytime approach maintains similar estimation accuracy as the not-real-time GPCT pipeline [13] while significantly reducing state size in all tested sequences (Sec. IV-C). It also achieves better estimation accuracy than event stereo parallel tracking and mapping (ES-PTAM) [21], a state-of-the-art discrete stereo pipeline, in all but one of the tested sequences (Sec. IV-D). It does this with an estimation frequency of 22 Hz on MVSEC and 6 Hz on DSEC by using keytimes and a producer-consumer architecture analogous to keyframing [5].

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section II provides a brief review of event-camera VO pipelines. Section III details the real-time continuous-time pipeline. Section IV presents experimental results of the pipeline across two datasets and comparisons against GPCT and ES-PTAM on the MVSEC and DSEC datasets. Finally, Section V summarizes our findings and concludes the paper.

title: CriticHack: Evaluating Visual Rewards Under Robot Policy Optimization
authors: Jiaxuan Luo,Xingguo Xu,Shanshan Wang,Yuhan Zhou,Zhen Zhang
abstract:
Learned visual reward models are increasingly used to optimize robot policies,
yet a reward model can score an execution that acts on the wrong object as
highly as one that completes the task. We show that optimizing such a reward
can amplify these wrong-object failures while reward and task success both
rise, so the signals a practitioner would normally monitor look healthy.
We fine-tune every denoiser parameter of a diffusion policy against Robometer
on a drawer task. Starting from a supervised policy with no prior reward
exposure, five training runs raise task success by 10.2 percentage points and
wrong-object failures by 10.9 points on 512 evaluation seeds, whereas five runs
trained on the simulator’s task-completion signal raise success without
amplifying wrong-object failures (difference 9.2 points, 95% CI 5.6 to 13.0).
The amplification recurs from a policy previously optimized against learned
rewards, under the policy’s native diffusion sampler, at matched distance from
the initial policy, and across constrained-policy experiments with two critics
and two optimizers. A tilt model explains when it occurs: under KL-regularized
optimization, an outcome becomes more frequent whenever its expected reward
under the initial policy exceeds the population average. Robometer separates
successes from failures well overall (AUROC .81) but scores wrong-object
failures slightly above successes (AUROC .37), so optimization raises both.
The same model predicts the outcome shifts across 26 constrained settings
(Spearman .89), including those in which task success falls, and Robometer’s
own published success-termination recipe inherits the error. A frozen outcome
verifier redirects the same optimization toward the requested task.
introduction:
Learned visual reward models provide feedback for robot policy optimization
from camera observations and a task description, replacing hand-designed task
rewards (Lee et al., 2026; Liang et al., 2026). A reward model does not
need to fail broadly to steer a policy wrong. It can score most failures
correctly and still reward one coherent semantic mistake, and optimization is
built to find exactly such mistakes.

Consider a robot instructed to open the middle drawer
(Figure 1). Opening the upper drawer instead looks like
manipulation progress but fails the requested task. A stacking policy can
likewise build a stable stack with the wrong cube. We call these outcomes
wrong-object failures: executions that manipulate a distractor in a
task-consistent way while the requested task fails. Liang et al. (2026)
showed that RoboReward assigns high scores to such executions and that these
false positives reinforce incorrect behavior during online learning. What is
less understood is how such errors interact with genuine task learning. If
optimization simply degraded task success, standard evaluation would catch it.
We show that it does not have to: optimizing a visual reward can raise task
success and wrong-object failures at the same time. The two checks a
practitioner relies on, the reward model’s aggregate success–failure
discrimination and the policy’s task success after optimization, can both
look healthy while a specific semantic failure grows.

We study this with CriticHack, a closed-loop evaluation of visual rewards under
robot policy optimization in which simulator state measures task success and
wrong-object failures independently of the reward. Our main experiments
fine-tune every denoiser parameter of a diffusion policy against Robometer on
a drawer task. From a supervised policy that has never been exposed to a
learned reward, five training runs raise task success by 10.2​[6.9,13.6]10.2\,[6.9,13.6]
percentage points and wrong-object failures by 10.9​[7.3,14.4]10.9\,[7.3,14.4] points on
512 evaluation seeds. Five runs trained on the simulator’s task-completion
signal raise success at least as much without amplifying wrong-object
failures, so the amplification is specific to the learned reward
(Table 1). The same pattern holds from a warm-start
policy previously optimized against learned rewards, where paired executions
show that the new successes and the new wrong-object failures both come from
converting former failures. It persists when the fine-tuned policies are
decoded with their native 100-step diffusion sampler, at matched KL distance
from the initial policy, and across distractor-motion thresholds from 5 to
40 mm. Constrained experiments that optimize a selector over a fixed bank of
diffusion-noise sequences reproduce reward gain with wrong-object
amplification across two task–reward pairings, Robometer and Language-Image
Value learning (LIV) (Ma et al., 2023a), and two optimizers, proximal policy
optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO).

Why does a reward with strong aggregate discrimination produce this? A
trajectory-level audit shows that Robometer separates successes from all
failures well (AUROC .813) but scores wrong-object failures slightly above
successes (AUROC .372); good discrimination against the far more common other
failures hides the inversion. A simple model turns this observation into a
prediction. Under KL-regularized optimization the optimal policy tilts the
initial policy toward high reward, and an outcome becomes more frequent exactly
when its average tilted reward exceeds the population average. A reward that
scores wrong-object failures about as highly as successes therefore raises
both, and stronger optimization is decided by the upper tail of the score
distribution. Fitted with a single strength parameter, the model reproduces
the outcome changes across 26 constrained settings (Spearman .89 for
wrong-object failures and .79 for success), including the drawer settings in
which task success falls, and it places the full-denoiser and constrained
results on one continuum of optimization strength. Robometer’s own published
recipe, dense progress with success-triggered termination, does not escape the
error: its success detector fires on 89% of wrong-object executions and on
73% of successes.

Finally, we use a frozen success verifier trained on outcome labels as a
diagnostic intervention. Reweighting the critic reward by the verifier raises
task success by 7.1 points and lowers wrong-object failures by 4.4 points
relative to critic-only training, and verifier-only rewards match it, which
identifies outcome supervision as the source of the recovery.

(i) We show, with independent training runs and simulator-measured outcomes,
that optimizing a visual reward can amplify wrong-object failures while task
success rises, and that a ground-truth completion reward under the same
optimizer does not. (ii) We show that strong aggregate discrimination can hide
the semantic misranking that drives this amplification, and give a tilt model
that predicts the resulting outcome changes across settings and unifies
semantic amplification with classical success loss. (iii) We show that outcome
verification redirects the same optimization toward the intended task.

The simulated experiments cover occluded-drawer manipulation and
identity-sensitive stacking. Full-denoiser fine-tuning uses Robometer’s
terminal success probability on two drawer layouts; constrained experiments
add LIV and stacking. The verifier is task-specific and trained on simulator
labels. The real-robot study is a case study with one training run per
fine-tuned condition.

title: RUL-Aware RRT*: Degradation-Balanced Motion Planning for Robotic Manipulators
authors: Haibo Li,Zhiguo Zeng,Xu Li
abstract: Robotic manipulators operating over long durations often experience uneven joint degradation, which causes the weakest actuator to fail prematurely, leads to unplanned downtime, and results in significant operational losses. Traditional motion-planning algorithms do not account for joint health conditions and therefore tend to exacerbate this imbalance during extended operation. To address this challenge, this study introduces the RUL-aware RRT*, a motion-planning method that incorporates joint remaining useful life information into the planning process and adaptively adjusts joint usage in response to evolving health conditions. The method is evaluated across three representative scenarios, namely the Full Health Scenario (FHS), the Heterogeneous Degradation Scenario (HDS), and the Local Degradation Scenario (LDS). The results show that the RUL-aware RRT* effectively suppresses degradation imbalance, delays the emergence of bottleneck failures, and improves the long-term reliability of the robotic system during extended operation. These findings demonstrate that integrating health feedback into motion planning provides a practical and robust pathway for enhancing the durability and operational resilience of manipulators subject to continuous wear.
introduction:
In modern manufacturing, industrial robots have become essential equipment for achieving automated production and flexible manufacturing(Rüßmann et al., 2015). As the most critical component of industrial robots, multi-degree-of-freedom robotic arms rely on multiple joint motors that must operate in close coordination to perform complex, continuous, and high-precision tasks (Fan et al., 2019). However, in practical operation, motion planning is typically optimized for geometric efficiency or energy performance (Noreen et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2024), while differences in joint health conditions and the resulting uneven motion usage across actuators are often overlooked. This leads to uneven motor utilization (Raviola et al., 2021), where certain joints may experience accelerated degradation due to high workloads or frequent movements, eventually becoming the weakest link of the system (Kot et al., 2021). Once such a motor fails, the entire robot must be shut down, resulting in unplanned downtime and seriously affecting production continuity and equipment reliability (Lei et al., 2025; Mahyari and Locker, 2018; Raviola et al., 2021). This issue, in which local degradation triggers overall system failure, has become one of the key challenges in the reliability management of industrial robots.

To address such issues, extensive research has been conducted in recent years in both academia and industry within the fields of condition monitoring and predictive maintenance (PdM) based on robotic arms (Lei et al., 2025; Moore and Sawyer, 2024; Uhlmann et al., 2020). By leveraging remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and digital twin technologies, researchers are able to monitor equipment health in real time, predict the degradation trends of critical components, and make informed maintenance decisions accordingly (Mourtzis et al., 2023; Borgi et al., 2017). These approaches have significantly enhanced the intelligence of maintenance management, shifting it from a reactive mode to a proactive strategy (Molęda et al., 2023). However, most existing studies remain at the monitoring and scheduling layers, where the focus lies in sensing system health and determining maintenance timing (Kumar et al., 2023). Their outputs, such as health indicators, degradation trajectories, or maintenance schedules, are seldom integrated into the motion-planning layer, preventing health information from directly influencing path generation or motion decisions (Schacht-Rodríguez et al., 2018). In other words, although health information is effectively perceived, it is rarely incorporated into the robot’s path generation and motion decision-making processes, thereby limiting the realization of a closed-loop predictive maintenance framework.

On the other hand, sampling-based motion planning algorithms, such as RRT, RRT*, and PRM, provide a flexible framework for incorporating multidimensional constraints into the planning process (Kingston et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2023). In recent years, various studies have introduced factors such as energy and consumption (Alam et al., 2023), collision risk (Liu et al., 2023), safety distance (Mainprice et al., 2011), battery endurance (Chitre and Sinha, 2023) into the cost functions of these algorithms, thereby achieving a comprehensive optimization of efficiency, safety, and reliability. These works demonstrate that path planning can be applied not only for geometric feasibility analysis but also holds great potential for integrating health-related factors. However, existing research has not yet systematically incorporated the uneven degradation conditions across multiple motors and their imbalanced RUL distribution into planning models, leaving robotic systems lacking health awareness at the path-planning level.

Based on the above analysis, three major research gaps can be identified. First, traditional path-planning algorithms often lead to uneven motor degradation, as they optimize only geometric or efficiency-related objectives without considering motor health conditions. Second, predictive maintenance techniques largely remain at the monitoring and scheduling levels, without direct integration into the motion-planning process. Third, existing path-planning studies mainly focus on energy efficiency or collision avoidance, while overlooking the uneven degradation conditions across multiple motors and the resulting lifetime bottleneck.

To address these challenges, this study proposes an RUL-aware RRT* motion-planning algorithm that aims to redistribute joint-level motion usage, enhance health awareness, and mitigate lifetime bottlenecks. The proposed algorithm is developed on the basis of the traditional RRT* framework (Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011), whose original cost function considers only the path length, while RUL-aware RRT* extends it by introducing an RUL-aware cost function that incorporates joint health information into the path-cost formulation, thereby enabling deep integration of health awareness into the motion-planning process. In addition, two key mechanisms are designed within the framework: (1) an Online RUL Update Mechanism,which dynamically updates the current remaining useful life (RUL) of each joint before each motion-planning process; and (2) an RUL-driven Adaptive Joint Weighting Mechanism, which adaptively balances motor loads under different degradation conditions to achieve health-aware motion planning.

In multi-scenario experiments conducted on a UR5 six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, including the Full Health Scenario, the Heterogeneous Degradation Scenario, and the Local Degradation Scenario, the results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves balanced degradation, enhances health-awareness, and extends the first-replacement time of critical motors, thereby realizing planable predictive maintenance. This study provides a new perspective for achieving health awareness and lifetime balancing at the task-execution level of industrial robots, and lays the foundation for future research on reliability-aware motion planning.

The implementation and experimental data are available at https://github.com/HelpLee/MotionPlanning_RULRRTstar.

title: OpenRUA: Robot-Use Agents Are Zero-Shot Visuomotor Policies
authors: Zhaoyang Chu,Earl T. Barr,Claire Le Goues,Peter O'Hearn,Mark Harman,Federica Sarro,He Ye
abstract:
Coding agents are extending their reach into the physical world by writing and executing robot control programs.
One might expect the agents to use the existing mature software stack that engineers have developed over decades to access sensors and control motion.
Yet prior work primarily engineers complex custom harnesses to orchestrate agents for robot use, particularly by prescribing specialized workflows and providing bespoke interfaces.
This raises the question: “Is such additional harness engineering necessary?”
We introduce OpenRUA, a zero-abstraction harness that bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by providing off-the-shelf coding agents with only terminal access to the robot’s native software interface ROS 2.
OpenRUA employs a minimalist workspace-as-harness design, only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools while leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without orchestrating any agentic workflow.
Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding.
With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, demonstrating that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native interface, without bespoke primitives or task-specific training.
Under this minimalist design, further analysis reveals striking emergent behaviors of coding agents:
1 For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs (e.g., reconstructing point clouds from depth) and derive metric measurements (e.g., computing coordinates for Cartesian motion targets) in 96.80% of episodes.
2 For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds motion-control clients (e.g., gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs (e.g., adjusting motion based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes.
Our code is available at https://github.com/terminalworld/OpenRUA.
introduction:
Robot control has long been engineered by writing explicit programs that translate task specifications into physical motion (Fikes and Nilsson, 1971; Li et al., 1994; Siciliano et al., 2009).
These programs execute on a multi-layered software stack, through which human engineers coordinate drivers, messaging, planning, and actuation to implement the required behavior (Macenski et al., 2022; García et al., 2020).
However, this process requires substantial effort and human expertise, with further engineering often needed for new tasks or environments.

One path is to learn end-to-end visuomotor policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (Team, 2025; Kim et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2026; Bjorck et al., 2025) and World Action Models (WAMs) (Agarwal et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), that map visual observations and language instructions directly to low-level actions.
However, they require large-scale demonstration data, and their generalization remains limited beyond the training distribution (Zhou et al., 2025; Fei et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026).
For example, LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025) reports that OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) and π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024), despite average success rates above 90% on standard LIBERO, achieve 0.0% success under position and task perturbations.

Another path is to revisit explicit programming for robot control (Fu et al., 2026), while replacing the human engineer with modern coding agents such as Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025) or Codex (OpenAI, 2025).
Such an approach is known as Code as Policies (CaP) (Liang et al., 2023), where the policy itself can be inspected, edited, and debugged by the coding agent without retraining (Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026).
As a result, the coding agent acts as a Robot-Use Agent (RUA) (Isola, 2026), operating the robot the way it operates a computer (Team, 2025; Fu et al., 2026; Robocurve, 2026; Berman et al., 2026).

Despite this progress, existing RUA systems devote significant effort to engineering custom harnesses for robot use, especially designing the tool interfaces and primitive libraries through which agents compose policies to operate robots in prescribed workflows.
These systems either wrap learned visuomotor policies as callable tools (Zhang et al., 2026b; Galanti et al., 2026; Ding et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a) or hand-craft custom libraries of perception and control primitives based on human expertise (Fu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a).
However, it remains unclear whether such additional harness engineering is necessary for coding agents to operate robots effectively, given that robots have a mature ecosystem of software interfaces developed over decades for human engineers to access sensors and control motion (Macenski et al., 2022; García et al., 2020).
This raises the question: “Can an off-the-shelf coding agent serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native software interface, without relying on bespoke primitives or learned policies?”

In this work, we introduce OpenRUA, a zero-abstraction harness for robot-use agents that builds on the robot’s native interface, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) (Macenski et al., 2022), the de facto standard of the robotics community.
OpenRUA bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by offering off-the-shelf coding agents only terminal access to ROS 2, allowing them to operate the robot as a human engineer would.

As illustrated in Figure 1, OpenRUA frames robot use as a live, interactive software project and employs a minimalist workspace-as-harness design.
This design rests on the observation that frontier coding agents already operate autonomously on unfamiliar repositories to complete tasks (OpenAI, 2024; Merrill et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026).
We hypothesize that the orchestration with bespoke interfaces in existing RUA systems compensates for limited agent capability rather than reflecting a requirement of robot control, and that a capable coding agent needs only a workspace directory.
Specifically, the workspace serves as the harness by only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools, leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without a prescribed agentic workflow.
Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding: task-specific perception and control strategies emerge as the agent acquires observations, interprets images, computes metric measurements, and writes control programs.
As a result, the coding agent itself serves as a zero-shot visuomotor policy: it goes from raw observations to motor commands, reasoning explicitly about geometry and iteratively refining its actions from execution feedback.

We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate OpenRUA on three widely used benchmarks, i.e., CaP-Bench (Fu et al., 2026), LIBERO-PRO (Zhou et al., 2025), and RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2026), in a zero-shot setting without access to privileged simulator state and the benchmark’s success predicates.
With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, exceeding leading systems such as ASPIRE (Lu et al., 2026) and Harness VLA (Zhang et al., 2026b) by 18.0 and 4.6 percentage points, respectively.
On unseen composite tasks in RoboCasa365, OpenRUA achieves 28.1% success, exceeding Harness VLA by 13.1 percentage points.
The results show that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native software interface, without bespoke primitives or learned policies.

Further analysis reveals several findings about emergent agent capabilities:
1 For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs (e.g., cropping images, adding grids, and reconstructing point clouds from depth) and derive metric measurements (e.g., computing coordinates for Cartesian motion targets) in 96.80% of episodes.
2 For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds its own motion-control clients (e.g., trajectory execution and gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs (e.g., adjusting motion or stopping based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes.
3 On RoboCasa365, OpenRUA maintains comparable success rates on seen and unseen composite tasks (26.3% and 28.1%, respectively), whereas RLDX-1 drops to 5.0% and Harness VLA, which orchestrates RLDX-1, drops to 13.8% on unseen tasks.
This contrast highlights the generalization potential of OpenRUA without reliance on a learned robot policy.
4 Increasing test-time computation through more interaction or greater reasoning effort improves task success without additional robot training or bespoke primitives, while performance eventually saturates at levels that vary across models.

title: Autonomous mobile robot operations logistics: a dataset of jobs, dispatch events and robot states
authors: Jan-Felix Klein,Yongkuk Jeong
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) increasingly perform material transport in production logistics, where their operation is governed by job generation, dispatching and robot control. We present MoRoOp, a dataset of AMR operations recorded in a laboratory kit preparation and supply scenario over nine eight-hour shifts. During each shift, an AMR executed stochastically generated kit supply, empty-box refill and charging jobs. The dataset links job specifications, the operations constituting each job, dispatch events documenting operation state transitions and outcomes, and robot-state observations comprising position, orientation, velocity, per-wheel state of charge and diagnostics. It contains 1,382 jobs, 4,815 operations, 19,352 dispatch events and 140,386 robot-state observations together with the kit specifications used during job generation. The dataset was recorded in an operating laboratory environment, and technically valid observations of delays, obstructed navigation and unsuccessful operations were retained. Both raw and cleaned robot-state tables are provided. Documented reuse directions include the evaluation of AI agents on operational decision records, disturbance detection, operation prediction, data-driven simulation and event-log analysis.

title: Keep the Effect, Drop the Actor: Programmable Effect-to-Execution World-Action Models
authors: Junyi Hu,Zhewen He,Zhenhua Li,Yi Fang
abstract:
A robot demonstration records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one
particular arm made it happen. We condition on the first. A demonstration is compiled into an effect
program: the 3D keypoint trajectories of the objects that moved, two points marking where each was held,
and the configuration the scene ends in, with the demonstrator removed. PEWAM, a 71.5M-parameter
world-action model, generates effect, robot execution, action and terminal state as four streams with
independent flow-matching times, so clamping a program and sampling the execution turns inference into
programming, re-solved closed loop from the live scene. On held-out LIBERO-Goal tasks, one demonstration’s
program completes 40 of 90 episodes, where the same backbone given a goal image or language, and published
demonstration-conditioned methods, complete at most 19; on three of Meta-World’s held-out classes it exceeds
the best published results, though not on the five-class mean. Because a program is a set of coordinates, a person can edit it: the placement
follows a shifted terminal state and the grasp turns with rotated contact points. The same program runs on
four robot arms without retraining, and after a push, re-solving completes 23 of 60 episodes where replaying
the demonstration completes 6. On a Franka arm, fine-tuned on real demonstrations of other tasks, programs compiled from single human videos complete 36 of 40 trials, against 22 for the same backbone conditioned on the video’s last frame as a goal image.
introduction:
Showing a robot what to do is often easier than describing it, and a single demonstration is a direct way to
specify a new manipulation task (Vosylius and Johns, 2025; Di Palo and Johns, 2024; Goswami et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025). A demonstration, however,
records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one particular arm made it
happen. Watch someone put a bowl on a stove and you learn where the bowl should end up, roughly how it
travels and where it can be held; you do not learn to bend your elbow the way they bent theirs. Most systems
that learn from demonstrations keep the two together. Policies that transfer the demonstrator’s motion keep
the body and treat the world as context (Park et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2024; Haldar and Pinto, 2025), and video-action models
prompted with a demonstration predict both at once, as one pixel-level future (Li et al., 2026b; Zhou et al., 2026). The
task is then entangled with one body’s motion: no variable states it on its own, so it can be neither edited nor given to another robot.

This viewpoint exposes a limitation of both dominant formulations. Conditioning on the demonstrator’s
trajectory or video (Zhu et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2024; Vosylius and Johns, 2025) ties the task to one execution, which is valid only for the
arm, the grasp and the layout that produced it. Methods built on object motion do separate the object from
the actor (Xu et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024; Dharmarajan et al., 2026), but they generate that motion from language
or video and execute it with a planner, a controller or a per-task policy. What is missing is a task interface
that leaves the actor out, that one multi-task model accepts with no parameter update, and that a person can edit.

As illustrated in Figure 1, our key observation is that the change in the world is the task,
and the demonstrator’s motion is one of many ways to produce it. We therefore compile a demonstration into an
effect program: keypoints of each relevant object tracked over time, two contact points recording where
the object was held, and the configuration the objects end in. Nothing in the program refers to the robot.
Based on this view we propose PEWAM, a world-action model that describes effect, end-effector execution,
native action and terminal state as four streams with separate flow-matching times
(Bao et al., 2023; Lipman et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2025), so that every conditional is a query of the same weights. Clamping the program and sampling the execution poses the question of how to make the effect happen, which turns inference into programming. At deployment the unfinished part of the program is re-solved from the live scene every few
control steps. Because a push moves an object just as a grasp does, progress through the program is counted
only for effects the robot has caused, and a disturbance becomes a new observation.

We evaluate PEWAM on LIBERO, Meta-World and RLBench, on four arms, under pushes, from pixels and on a real
Franka arm programmed by human videos. Where the demonstrator’s motion stays valid, copying it is stronger; the
program pays off where copying breaks: after a push, on another arm, and from a person’s hand.

We summarize our contributions as follows: (i) we formulate the task carried by a demonstration as an
actor-free effect program of object keypoints, contact points and a terminal state, and propose PEWAM, a world-action model whose independently noised streams let one set of weights both execute and predict; (ii) we show that the
program is an interface a person can edit and hand to another body: its terminal state moves the placement, its contact points turn the grasp, and one program runs on four simulated arms and, from a human video, on a real arm; (iii) we treat progress as an effect the robot causes and gate the program on engagement, so that
re-solving absorbs pushes that defeat replay; and (iv) we show that editability needs contact written as points,
not weights, and training data with several executions of one effect.
