title: Rethinking World-Action Model for Compositional and In-Context Robotic Manipulation
authors: Shukai Gong,Xuanran Zhai,Yintianrun Zhang,Ruopeng Cui,Ye Huang,Yiyang Fu,Dexuan Lyu,Chaojie Li,Xinyi Song,Peiwen Lin,Chuang Wang,Mingyuan Jia,Yufan Deng,Jiaxin Fang,Bo Liang,Jiaxin Li,Yuxiang Gao,Hao Liu,Daquan Zhou
abstract:
Long-horizon compositional manipulation has become increasingly important for real-world robot deployment, where a single task involves multiple coordinated subtasks. Existing world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict short-horizon visual futures and actions, but typically lack explicit subtask-level reasoning. We propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR), a hierarchical framework that factorizes manipulation into
a visual subgoal planner and a subgoal executor.
Given the current observation and global instruction, the subgoal planner predicts a visual subgoal for the next subtask. The subgoal executor then jointly generates future visual trajectories and actions conditioned on the predicted subgoal. Both components share a pretrained world-model representation, enabling task-level planning and action generation to benefit from common physical knowledge. Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: using a global goal image as context can induce different subtask decompositions and behaviors without parameter updates.
On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark, ViGAR achieves 82.00% and 67.02% success rates under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate.
Real-world robot experiments on five compositional and two in-context learning tasks further confirm the effectiveness of ViGAR.
introduction:
Robots in production and service settings increasingly face compositional manipulation tasks that involve multiple coordinated subtasks. Such tasks require policies to maintain progress across subtask transitions while generalizing to unseen scenes, objects, and spatial layouts, rather than replaying a fixed sequence from training.
Policies for real-world deployment therefore need both embodied generalization and mechanisms for organizing behavior over extended task horizons.
World-Action Models (WAMs) offer an appealing paradigm for this goal. By jointly predicting future visual states and actions, WAMs learn physically grounded action dynamics from dense video supervision and have demonstrated strong generalization across tasks, environments, embodiments, and visual distribution shifts [9, 19, 34, 1].

Despite these strengths, existing WAMs are not explicitly designed for long-horizon compositional manipulation. WAM formulations typically provide a useful local control signal by modeling what is likely to happen next, but do not explicitly organize behavior across a sequence of subtasks or expose a task-level interface through which the desired progression can be specified.
Recent studies [4, 40, 16] reveal that long-horizon task progression requires more than supervision on short-term evolution of the physical world, and further demonstrate the value of predicting semantic subtasks for open-world long-horizon manipulation and generalization. The core challenge is therefore to endow WAMs with explicit task-level decision making while preserving their strong world-centric prediction and physical generalization.

One line of work externalizes this decision making to a language planner that exploits VLMs to decompose a task into linguistic subtasks for a policy to execute.
However, language subtask descriptions often underspecify precise spatial outcome without ambiguity, whereas visual subgoals impose stronger constraints on the desired scene configuration [17]. Our key insight is that compositional manipulation can be factorized into long-term future selection and short-term future realization. World-action modeling for long-horizon tasks should first make explicit the target state robot intends to realize, and then generate the actions that will bring it about.

To this end, we propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR), which treats subgoal images as explicit decision variable linking task-level reasoning to physical action generation.
Given the current observation and the global task instruction, ViGAR first performs visual goal reasoning to predict the desired subtask goal image.
Then, conditioned on the current observation, global task instruction and predicted subgoal image, it jointly predicts future visual trajectories and corresponding robot actions leading to the subgoal.
Both task-level decision and physical realization are learned in one shared generative world-model representation, so that the model can leverage the same physical knowledge for both stages.

Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: with the scene and instruction held fixed, changing only the global goal induces a different composition of behaviors, forcing the policy to reorganize its action sequence rather than default to the most likely training trajectory. We term this in-context robotic manipulation: the global goal image serves as context for inferring a subtask decomposition, so an out-of-distribution global goal elicits a task composition unseen in training, with no parameter update.

Experiments on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional tasks validate the effectiveness of ViGAR. On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark [11], ViGAR achieves success rates of 82.00% and 67.02% under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline [32] by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate.
In real-robot experiments, ViGAR outperforms strong VLA and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy baselines on five compositional tasks, and exhibits in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our method.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We factorize compositional manipulation into long-term future selection and short-term future realization, and propose ViGAR, a hierarchical framework that predicts the next subgoal as an explicit decision variable and conditions joint video-action generation on it.

We identify in-context robotic manipulation as a capability that emerges from explicit goal conditioning. With the scene and instruction held fixed, a new global goal image elicits a different subtask decomposition and a correspondingly reorganized action sequence, specifying out-of-distribution task compositions at deployment without any parameter update.

ViGAR outperforms strong baselines on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional manipulation tasks, and exhibits strong in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our approach.

1. We factorize compositional manipulation into long-term future selection and short-term future realization, and propose ViGAR, a hierarchical framework that predicts the next subgoal as an explicit decision variable and conditions joint video-action generation on it.

2. We identify in-context robotic manipulation as a capability that emerges from explicit goal conditioning. With the scene and instruction held fixed, a new global goal image elicits a different subtask decomposition and a correspondingly reorganized action sequence, specifying out-of-distribution task compositions at deployment without any parameter update.

3. ViGAR outperforms strong baselines on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional manipulation tasks, and exhibits strong in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our approach.

title: SocialVLA: A Social Perception Gateway for Human-Reaction-Based Failure Detection and Recovery in VLA Manipulation
authors: Sofya Konstantinova,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Artem Lykov,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies enable diverse robotic manipulation but remain susceptible to execution failures that may not be recognized by the policy itself. An observing human provides complementary information: unexpected robot behavior can elicit rapid vocal, facial, or explicit verbal reactions before an undesirable manipulation outcome is completed. We introduce SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts spontaneous human reactions into runtime intervention signals for VLA manipulation. SocialVLA combines causal paralinguistic audio detection, visual reaction recognition, explicit stop phrases, and robot-relevance estimation. An asynchronous first-event fusion mechanism allows the earliest sufficiently confident signal to request a VLA hold without waiting for complete multimodal agreement. After intervention, a separate speech channel records the participant’s verbal correction and associates it with the interrupted VLA action, enabling participant-directed continuation, restart, or instruction revision. We evaluate SocialVLA during physical Unitree G1 manipulation using recordings from 15 participants, comprising 238 annotated intervention-worthy reaction episodes and 1.038 h of annotated non-intervention behavior. Frozen offline replay of the multimodal cascade achieves 54.6% event recall and 69.5% precision, while unfiltered first-event audio–video fusion reaches 64.3% recall. The relevance module reduces false-stop episodes from 100 to 57 and increases precision from 60.5% to 69.8%. In a prospective deployment on a 16th unseen participant, the frozen system achieves 59.5% recall and 91.7% precision. Median detector-to-fusion delivery is 47.9 ms, median VLA-gate-to-physical-hold latency is 336 ms, and matched reaction-onset-to-physical-hold latency is 1.021 s. These results demonstrate a complete local pathway from spontaneous social reaction to physical VLA interruption and a participant-directed recovery interface.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, enabling policies to generalize across objects, tasks, and semantic commands [1, 2]. Their generality, however, does not eliminate execution failures. During pick-and-place manipulation, a policy can select the wrong object, generate an unsuitable approach, fail to establish a grasp, drop an object, or place it at an incorrect location. These failures may occur even when individual actions appear locally plausible.

Recent methods detect failures from robot observations, trajectories, uncertainty estimates, or internal VLA representations. SAFE learns a failure score from VLA features and successful and failed rollouts [3]. FAIL-Detect frames runtime monitoring as sequential out-of-distribution detection [4]. AHA uses a vision-language model to identify and explain manipulation failures [5]. These approaches provide direct task evidence, but they may require access to policy internals, compatible observations, representative training data, or an explicit model of task progress.

An observing person provides a different source of information. Humans can discriminate complex visual scenes within a fraction of a second [6], while nonverbal vocalizations can communicate recognizable affect within several hundred milliseconds [7]. When a robot acts unexpectedly, a person may use an explicit stop phrase, alter vocal prosody, display a negative facial reaction, shake their head, or redirect attention. These responses reflect the person’s appraisal of the interaction [8] and may reveal discrepancies that were not enumerated during policy training. Moreover, an observer need not wait until a failure is physically complete. From the evolving scene, motion direction, and task context, a person may recognize that a grasp or placement is developing incorrectly and react before the object is dropped, displaced, or released at the wrong location. Recent HRI benchmarks explicitly distinguish such anticipatory responses from reactions observed after failure completion [9].

Prior human-robot interaction (HRI) studies have established that human reactions correlate with robot errors [10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. However, retrospective reaction classification is not equivalent to an operational gate for a continuously executing VLA. In manipulation, detection time is part of the task: a correct decision made after an object has already been dropped or incorrectly placed cannot prevent the consequence. A runtime system must therefore process the earliest reliable signal with low delay, handle missing or uncertain modalities, and avoid waiting for unnecessary multimodal agreement. It should run locally without dependence on an Internet service, remain independent of the internal VLA architecture, and connect as an external layer to any policy that exposes a pause, hold, or stop interface. Repeated evidence must reinforce an intervention rather than reverse an already issued stop. The key challenge is therefore to convert spontaneous social behavior into a sufficiently fast and reliable runtime intervention signal for a continuously executing VLA, while avoiding unnecessary stops caused by unrelated human behavior.

We address this challenge with SocialVLA, a modular social perception gateway between a human observer and an executing VLA. Rather than attempting to infer physical failure solely from the robot state, SocialVLA detects human-perceived discrepancies from continuous audio-visual behavior and converts them into structured runtime intervention events. The framework is local and does not require access to VLA activations, action probabilities, or internal uncertainty estimates. In this work, failure detection refers to detecting human-perceived intervention need during robot execution rather than exhaustively identifying all physical robot failures.

The main contributions are:

SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts
spontaneous human audio-visual reactions and explicit stop commands into
runtime interventions during VLA-controlled humanoid manipulation;

SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts
spontaneous human audio-visual reactions and explicit stop commands into
runtime interventions during VLA-controlled humanoid manipulation;

a causal multimodal intervention architecture that combines fast and
extended-context paralinguistic detection, visual reaction recognition,
explicit stop phrases, separately estimated robot relevance, and
asynchronous first-event fusion, allowing the earliest sufficiently
confident signal to request a hold without waiting for complete multimodal
agreement; and

a real-robot evaluation on the Unitree G1 using a 15-participant annotated
corpus and a prospective frozen-system deployment on a 16th, previously
unseen participant, measuring reaction detection, false interventions,
timely recall, and end-to-end physical stopping latency.

Together, these contributions establish spontaneous social behavior as an operational input to VLA execution rather than only an offline observation signal. SocialVLA complements robot-internal failure monitors by contributing the observer’s task-level assessment while remaining independent of the internal architecture of the underlying VLA.

title: Filter-Aware Fine-Tuning for Safe Humanoid Whole-Body Tracking
authors: Pranit Mohnot,Christian Helten,Daniele Gammelli,Marco Pavone
abstract: Safe whole-body motion is essential for deploying humanoid robots in unstructured environments. Modern humanoid control commonly separates reference specification from execution, with a planner, teleoperator, or motion generator providing a reference that a reinforcement-learning policy tracks through dynamically feasible whole-body control. Runtime safety filters, such as control barrier functions (CBFs), offer a promising approach for enforcing newly introduced constraints via interventions on the tracker’s outputs. We show, however, that treating the tracking policy and safety filter independently induces fundamental mismatches, as filtering alters both the executed actions and the induced state distribution. We study this policy–filter interface through case studies that isolate dynamics, objective, and information mismatches, highlight their root causes, and use these insights to develop CoFiT (Constrained Filter-aware Tuning), a filter-aware fine-tuning method for pretrained trackers. Across diverse constraint scenes, CoFiT reduces violation time relative to filter-only training by 91% on TWIST2 and 21% on SONIC, while requiring smaller safety filter corrections. On Unitree G1 hardware, CoFiT reduces violation time by 83% for TWIST2 and completes every trial without operator intervention, whereas 50% of baseline trials require an operator stop. Together, these results provide actionable insights into policy–filter interactions and establish design principles for integrating learned trackers with runtime safety filters.
introduction:
Humanoid robots are rapidly moving toward deployment in homes, warehouses, hospitals, and other human-centered environments, where safe operation requires coordinating the full body under task- and environment-dependent constraints.
Whole-body control increasingly relies on learning-based motion tracking, in which a motion source, such as a teleoperator, recorded demonstration, or kinematic motion generator, provides a reference trajectory that a reinforcement-learning (RL) tracking policy translates into joint commands consistent with the robot’s dynamics [1, 2, 3].
While this control architecture enables expressive whole-body motion, ensuring its safety in real-world environments remains challenging.
A reference trajectory specifies the intended motion but does not, in general, encode every constraint of the environment in which that motion will be executed.
Obstacles, workspace limits, and other safety requirements may be absent from the motion source, emerge only at runtime, or change after the tracking policy has been trained.

Two broad strategies have emerged for enforcing safety in whole-body control.
The first internalizes safety within the learned tracking policy, for example by training with penalties on constraint violations or barrier-based rewards that encourage avoidance of unsafe states [4].
This approach tightly couples safety to training, as accommodating a new constraint generally requires retraining, and the resulting policy does not by itself provide a runtime guarantee.
The second strategy places a safety filter downstream of the tracking policy to correct its actions at runtime [5, 6].
This modular approach leaves the nominal policy unchanged and can enforce constraints that were not present during training.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) are widely used to construct such safety filters.
A CBF expresses a constraint as a condition on the control input, and the filter modifies the tracker’s proposed command only as much as needed to satisfy that condition [5].
Whole-body formulations can additionally account for contact constraints and task priorities when selecting the correction [7].
This modularity is appealing, as the tracker can be treated as a fixed nominal controller, while the filter supplies policy-agnostic corrections, seemingly allowing the two components to be designed independently.

In this work, we show that treating the tracking policy and safety filter independently induces fundamental mismatches in closed-loop execution (Fig.  1).
The safety filter changes the tracker’s outputs even though the tracker was trained under an unfiltered closed loop.
As a result, both the actions executed by the robot and the states induced by those actions differ from those encountered during training.
Through systematic case studies, we identify three key sources of incompatibility at the policy–filter interface: dynamics mismatch, objective mismatch, and information mismatch.
Guided by these findings and their underlying causes, we develop CoFiT (Constrained Filter-aware Tuning), a method that adapts a pretrained tracker to an existing CBF filter.
CoFiT fine-tunes the tracker with filters active and supplies it with compact constraint information, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware penalties.
This allows the tracker to anticipate filter interventions and respond with coordinated, constraint-compatible motion while retaining its original tracking objective where possible.

Our contributions are as follows:

We provide a systematic analysis of the policy–filter interface, identifying dynamics, objective, and information mismatches between pretrained tracking policies and runtime CBF filters and relating them to specific training and interface design choices.

We introduce CoFiT, a filter-aware fine-tuning method that adapts pretrained whole-body tracking policies to an existing CBF filter using action-space constraint observations, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware rewards.

We validate CoFiT through extensive ablations and experiments across multiple base trackers in simulation and on hardware, demonstrating fewer constraint violations, smaller filter corrections, and smoother motion.

2. We introduce CoFiT, a filter-aware fine-tuning method that adapts pretrained whole-body tracking policies to an existing CBF filter using action-space constraint observations, temporal feedback, and constraint-aware rewards.

title: NEEDLEWORK: Offline Rewriting of Robot Data with Verified Local Stitches
authors: Juntao Ren,Yifan Hou,Shuran Song
comment: Submitted to ICLR 2027. Project page:this https URL
abstract: Robot demonstrations may contain useful behavior even when individual episodes are inefficient or unsuccessful. Trajectory stitching offers a way to compose these behaviors into improved training data, but identifying useful connections and verifying their feasibility is difficult in high-dimensional robot data, where many prior methods rely on low-dimensional state representations. We introduce Needle, an offline dataset-augmentation algorithm that addresses these challenges by adding short, verified action bridges between recorded observations in high-dimensional robot demonstrations. First, Needle identifies and creates connections that bypass suboptimal detours, broaden action coverage, and augment the original dataset with failed trajectories, using only RGB images, proprioception, and episode-level outcomes, without new environment interaction or privileged object state. Next, we present a sampling technique that incorporates accepted bridges into policy training without synthesizing intermediate images or discarding the original demonstrations, allowing policies to learn alternative actions while retaining the original dataset’s coverage. On real-robot tasks, Needle improves success rate over the strongest baseline on each task by an average of 21 percentage points. Videos and supplementary materials are on needle-work.github.io.
introduction:
The best robot behavior may not exist in any single trajectory of a dataset. Consider a bimanual laundry-folding task. One demonstration may fold the sleeves reliably but require several corrective grasps to complete the bottom fold; another may fold the sleeves poorly but fold the bottom cleanly. Neither demonstration alone completes the task well, but synthesizing a connection between the two good segments would produce a demonstration better than either individually.

This example illustrates one of three opportunities offered by trajectory stitching (Fig. 1). Within a trajectory, it can bypass inefficient detours within a demonstration, allowing a policy to learn shorter routes to success. Across successful trajectories, it can combine complementary behaviors and expose continuations that were never recorded together. From failure trajectories, it can recover useful behavior from failed episodes by connecting states along an unsuccessful execution to a successful continuation.

Despite this promise, realizing this in real-world robot manipulation is difficult. A stitch must be both useful, offering a better continuation, and feasible, with actions that physically reach its target. Most prior methods that stitch trajectories typically assume access to low-dimensional or privileged state (Yu et al., 2025; Lee and Choi, 2025; Hepburn and Montana, 2024; Li et al., 2024; Char et al., 2021), while methods designed to improve mixed-quality robot data typically filter or reweight recorded behavior without supplying the actions needed to connect desirable segments (Du et al., 2023; Hejna et al., 2025; Agia et al., 2025; Dass et al., 2026). We ask if we can get the best of both.

We introduce New Edges from Existing Demonstrations through Local Editing (Needle), which identifies valuable segments with no existing connection, and proposes verified action bridges to connect them. Our key insight is that rather than learning a globally accurate dynamics model or task-specific value function and asking either to reason over long horizons, we can reduce stitching in high-dimensional spaces to a series of locally supervised reachability problems.

Specifically, the feasibility and duration of a local connection can be learned directly from recorded action sequences. Across any episode, successful, suboptimal, or failed, each short segment is an example of which two observations can be connected, the specific action sequence that connects them, and the exact number of steps it takes. We use this insight to train two modules. Given source and target observations, a goal-conditioned diffusion Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) generates action sequences that attempt to reach from source to target. In parallel, we supervise an action-conditioned verifier that receives the same source and target observations and predicts whether, and after how many steps, the proposed actions reach the target.

To make these connections useful for policy learning, Needle turns accepted bridges into action sequences at recorded observations. Pairing each bridge with the originally-recorded actions leading up to its source exposes the synthesized actions from multiple preceding observations, without needing to generate intermediate images. Original training examples remain available, including those the bridge bypasses, so the policy receives new ways to make progress without losing supervision for the situations and behaviors covered by the original demonstrations.

Our contributions are threefold:

(1) An offline stitching method that finds useful connections and verifies bridges with an action-conditioned reachability model.

(2) A training formulation that adds bridge actions while preserving recorded supervision, without synthesizing observations or requiring a shared coordinate frame.

(3) Evaluations on a real robot and in simulation of success, completion efficiency, recovery, and key design decisions.

title: SoTa: Soft Tactile Skins for Dexterous Manipulation
authors: Jingyun Yang,Baiyu Shi,Timothy Yu,Haitian Liu,Alberta Longhini,Weichen Wang,Rika Antonova,Zhenan Bao,Jeannette Bohg
comment: The first three authors contributed equally. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
A growing body of work suggests that tactile sensing gives robot policies contact information that complements vision in dexterous manipulation. However, visuo-tactile robot data remains scarce: dexterous demonstrations require teleoperating robots, which limits dataset scale. Human demonstrations are far cheaper to collect and offer a path to scale this data, but only if human and robot hands carry tactile sensors with corresponding signals. This requires sensors that conform to different hand geometries, cover the full hand, and share a common layout across embodiments.
We present SoTa, a low-cost capacitive tactile skin that provides full-hand coverage on humans and robots while preserving a shared layout of 202 taxels across corresponding finger and palm regions. Our multilayer design with fabric electrodes enables in-house fabrication of thin, soft skins with customizable geometry for under $10 in materials per skin.
The sensor retains over 97% of its initial response span after 10,000 loading-unloading cycles with traces retaining continuity through 1,280 tight-fist folding cycles.
The shared taxel layout supports human-robot co-training with a common tactile encoder and no learned cross-sensor mapping.
Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, tactile observations improve in-distribution success over vision-only policies.
With a fixed robot demonstration budget, adding human demonstrations more than doubles mean success across eight evaluation conditions, from 22.8% to 45.9%, improving success in all five out-of-distribution conditions.
We plan to open-source the resources needed to fabricate and operate these skins.
Project website: https://sota-skin.github.io
introduction:
Many dexterous manipulation tasks, such as lifting a fragile cup, wiping dirt from a table, or inserting a charger into a power strip, require carefully controlled contact between objects and different parts of the hand.
Vision-based policies can perform a wide range of manipulation tasks [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], but they observe contact only indirectly, and a growing body of work suggests that tactile or force observations improve performance on contact-rich tasks [7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15].

Scaling visuo-tactile policy learning, however, is limited by data. Dexterous robot demonstrations require teleoperation [16, 17, 18], which is slow and depends on costly hardware. Human demonstrations are much cheaper to collect and could supplement robot data, but only if human hands carry tactile sensors whose signals correspond to the robot’s. Existing visuo-tactile systems rarely meet this requirement. Most sense contact only at the fingertips [7, 19, 9, 11], so they miss contacts on the phalanges and palm in tasks such as table wiping and plug insertion, and most are built for a single embodiment. A sensor that supports learning from both humans and robots must therefore cover the full hand, conform to different hand geometries, withstand repeated contact and flexing, and present the same tactile structure on both embodiments.

We present SoTa, a low-cost capacitive tactile skin that meets these requirements.
Our laser-patterned, multilayer fabric-electrode design
produces thin, soft skins whose geometry is fitted to each hand while preserving a shared layout of 202 taxels, with corresponding indices assigned to the same semantic hand regions. Each skin costs under $10 in materials, responds to forces from 20mN to 10N, retains over 97% of its initial response span after 10,000 loading–unloading cycles, and keeps trace continuity through 1,280 tight-fist folding cycles.
Because both embodiments share the same layout, human and robot observations use a common tactile encoder without a learned cross-sensor mapping. Human demonstrations contain no action labels (as robot demonstrations do), so we incorporate human demonstrations through an auxiliary objective that predicts task phases from human and robot visuo-tactile observations, while action supervision comes only from robot data.

We evaluate the system on three dexterous manipulation tasks involving contact with different parts of the hand: box reorientation, cup picking, and plug insertion. Tactile observations improve in-distribution success on all three tasks, although these benefits do not consistently extend to out-of-distribution conditions.
With a fixed robot-demonstration budget, adding human visuo-tactile demonstrations improves every evaluated condition relative to robot-only visuo-tactile training, raising average success from 22.8% to 45.9%.

Our contributions are:
(1) a soft, flexible, low-cost, and customizable capacitive tactile skin with coverage across the fingers and palm and a shared 202-taxel layout for human and robot hands; (2) characterization of the sensor’s response, cyclic stability, flexing durability, and motion-induced artifacts; and (3) a language-supervised training pipeline that incorporates human visuo-tactile demonstrations into robot policy learning, with real robot experiments demonstrating improvements over robot-only training.
We will release the resources needed to fabricate and operate these skins.

title: World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Jie He,Wei Li,Junwen Tong,Rui Shao,Wei-Shi Zheng,Liqiang Nie
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies generate action chunks by transporting samples from a task-agnostic isotropic Gaussian source. As this source is conditioned on neither recent execution nor predicted future evolution, (i) it discards the local continuity established by recently executed motion. (ii) Even when predictive world representations are introduced, they often only condition the transport dynamics rather than determine where generation starts, how far it may deviate, or along which action directions it may expand.
Building on this observation, we introduce ProAct, a world-calibrated proposal-to-action framework that makes the generative source itself predictable.
(i) To preserve motion continuity, a lightweight Proposal Expert converts recent actions into a scene-aware hypothesis via one motion-anchored endpoint flow-matching step, initializing generation near the demonstrated action manifold.
(ii) To jointly capture intended scene evolution and proposal–future compatibility, a prospective World Expert treats the hypothesis as a soft motion prior while predicting the task-consistent latent future.
(iii) From this compatibility, the model calibrates a proposal-centered anisotropic source, where a bounded per-step extent controls the allowed deviation and a trace-normalized low-rank geometry under a condition-number budget allocates refinement over coupled translation, rotation, and gripper directions.
Compared with π0.5\pi_{0.5}, ProAct improves performance across simulation and real-world tasks while reducing denoising steps by 50%, inference latency by up to 25.8%, and increasing throughput by up to 34.8%.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models Black et al. (2024); Bjorck et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026b); Luo et al. (2026); Shao et al. (2025) increasingly use diffusion Chi et al. (2025) or flow matching Lipman et al. (2022) to generate continuous robot actions, building on broader progress in fine-grained multimodal understanding and visual grounding Peng et al. (2026); Shao et al. (2024); Shao et al. (2023); Shao et al. (2019). However, these generative decoders typically initialize each action chunk from a generic source distribution Intelligence et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2026), forcing the policy to repeatedly transport uninformed samples toward executable trajectories, as illustrated in the upper panel of Fig. 1.
Such a generic source ignores readily available context that could inform where action generation should begin.
By making the source distribution itself contextually predictable, action generation can begin from a more informed region of the action space, yielding
a policy that is both more accurate and substantially cheaper to sample during closed-loop policy execution.

A generic isotropic source leaves two useful sources of information unexploited.
The first is recently executed motion. Although task-level behavior can be highly multimodal, physical motion often exhibits strong local regularity over short horizons, and recently executed, reliable actions are already available during closed-loop control Black et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026a).
A naive strategy is to extrapolate this motion and reuse it for the next action chunk Jia et al. (2026); Zhan et al. (2026). Yet such continuation becomes unreliable around contact, reorientation, gripper actuation, or task-phase transitions, where appropriate motion may deviate sharply from recent behavior Yang et al. (2026c). Local continuity therefore indicates what is plausible from the recent past, but not necessarily what remains appropriate for the current scene and task. Recent motion should thus be treated as a proposal to be evaluated against the intended future, rather than as the action itself.

The second is predicted future evolution, which provides prospective evidence for calibrating such a proposal.
Prospective world modeling Zhao et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025); Tian et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026f); Zhu et al. (2026a); Li et al. (2026c) has increasingly been incorporated into VLA policies, but typically as auxiliary supervision or additional conditioning.
In these formulations, prospective information helps predict what should happen next, but is not explicitly used to calibrate an existing action hypothesis according to whether it remains appropriate for the anticipated task evolution.
The missing element is therefore an explicit interface between a candidate motion, prospective world reasoning, and generative refinement.

We build this missing interface around a propose–calibrate–refine principle and instantiate it as ProAct, a World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow framework. ProAct first constructs a scene-aware motion hypothesis, then uses prospective world reasoning to estimate the correction required to realize the intended future, and finally converts this calibration into the source distribution for flow-based action generation, as illustrated in the lower panel of Fig. 1.

Specifically,
(i) a lightweight Proposal Expert first converts recently executed actions into a scene-aware motion hypothesis. It extrapolates short-horizon motion and uses it to initialize the motion-anchored flow module, which grounds the proposal in the current VLM context through a single endpoint flow step. Rather than producing an executable action, this stage places generation near a plausible region of the demonstrated action manifold and provides a soft motion prior for subsequent reasoning.
(ii) A prospective World Expert calibrates this proposal against the task-consistent future. The motion hypothesis is provided as contextual evidence for prospective reasoning, while the prediction target remains the demonstrated future encoded in the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder Assran et al. (2025).
Calibration readouts are further supervised by the residual between the demonstrated action and the proposal, forcing the shared world representation to encode both the task-consistent latent future and the proposal–future compatibility.
(iii) The resulting calibration is finally expressed as a proposal-centered anisotropic source for action generation. A bounded per-step extent limits how far generation may deviate from the proposal, while trace-normalized low-rank geometry determines along which coupled action directions that correction should occur.
An Action Expert then transports samples from this calibrated source into executable action chunks using the base VLA’s original flow parameterization. Thus, ProAct changes where and how action generation begins while preserving the flexibility to depart from the proposal when needed.

Our primary contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate generative action prediction from a propose–calibrate–refine perspective, where recent motion provides a soft local hypothesis calibrated by task-consistent prospective reasoning, providing an interface between local motion continuity and future-aware action generation.

We introduce an asymmetric proposal-aware World Expert that uses motion to assist future prediction while anchoring the desired future independently of proposal correctness, and jointly predicts proposal-specific refinement extent and geometry at every horizon step.

We replace the isotropic Gaussian of flow-based VLAs with a world-calibrated, proposal-centered source while leaving their transport parameterization unchanged.

We validate ProAct across extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines while reducing denoising steps by up to 50%, demonstrating both superior effectiveness and inference efficiency.

1. We formulate generative action prediction from a propose–calibrate–refine perspective, where recent motion provides a soft local hypothesis calibrated by task-consistent prospective reasoning, providing an interface between local motion continuity and future-aware action generation.

2. We introduce an asymmetric proposal-aware World Expert that uses motion to assist future prediction while anchoring the desired future independently of proposal correctness, and jointly predicts proposal-specific refinement extent and geometry at every horizon step.

3. We replace the isotropic Gaussian of flow-based VLAs with a world-calibrated, proposal-centered source while leaving their transport parameterization unchanged.

4. We validate ProAct across extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines while reducing denoising steps by up to 50%, demonstrating both superior effectiveness and inference efficiency.

title: Awomo-SimDataEngine: Agentic Simulation-ReadyWorld Generation
authors: Awomo-PhysicalRSI Team,Danjiao Ma,Enhui Ma,Haohan Liu,Heng Jia,Hui Shan,Jianhua Xu,Jiahuan Zhang,Jiangdi Xu,Kaiwen Guo,Kaicheng Yu,Linwei Zhang,Liyang Jin,Maochun Luo,Pengyao Niu,Shiwen Li,Shuangyu Feng,Tong Zhang,Tianheng Wang,Xin Wang,Xiangru Huang,Yongqiang Huang,Zhaozhi Wang,Zijian Ma
abstract:
Generating useful robot-training data requires more than visually plausible
scenes: objects must support interaction, placements must remain physically
valid, and tasks must admit repeatable execution. We present
Awomo-SimDataEngine, an agentic system that connects asset and scene
generation to robot demonstration synthesis. Shared asset services provide
rigid and articulated objects, including structure-grounded part and joint
generation with ISArt. Scene generation supports two complementary routes:
Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from images, while SimForge builds
single-room and multi-room environments from text. A graph-native harness
coordinates construction, validation, and
bounded repair, routing failures to the responsible module while retaining
unaffected scene state. PolicyForge binds validated worlds to tasks and robot
embodiments to produce replayable demonstrations. Evaluations cover asset
geometry, scene quality, and downstream policy learning. On MuJoCo-based
LIBERO-Plus, co-training with Isaac Sim demonstrations improves the overall
success rate of a World-Action Model (WAM) from 77.17%77.17\% to 89.43%89.43\%. Goal and spatial
success improve by 31.6631.66 and 6.256.25 percentage points, respectively.
These results support the utility of the generated data for cross-simulator
policy training, with more limited gains on long-horizon tasks.
introduction:
Robot learning depends on demonstrations that cover varied objects,
environments, and manipulation goals. Collecting such coverage in the real
world is costly, while manually preparing each simulated environment limits
the scale and diversity of synthetic data. Generative models offer a way to
expand this training distribution, but their outputs must support interaction:
a plausible image or textured mesh can still hide invalid collision geometry,
inaccessible interiors, incorrect joints, unstable placements, or an
unreplayable initial state. These defects affect both whether demonstrations
can be collected and what policies learn from them.

Recent progress spans image-conditioned 3D assets, agentic scene construction,
and automated demonstration synthesis
[Tencent Hunyuan3D Team, 2025a; SAM 3D Team et al., 2025; Pfaff et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026; Mandlekar et al., 2023; Ranawaka et al., 2026].
Connecting these capabilities requires agreement on object identities,
coordinate frames, physical representations, task requirements, and validation
results. An asset replacement changes the geometry available for registration;
a revised scene changes the reset and interaction conditions seen by a
controller. An integrated system must preserve these dependencies and return
failures to the stage that can resolve them.

We introduce Awomo-SimDataEngine, an agentic system for constructing
simulation-ready worlds and converting them into robot demonstrations.
The system connects asset generation, scene generation, and demonstration
synthesis through a Graph-Native Harness for execution and repair.
Scene generation supports both visual references and language descriptions:
Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from single-view images, whereas
SimForge builds single-room and multi-room environments from text.
Both routes use shared asset services and produce worlds that can be checked,
edited, and bound to robot tasks. Figure 1
illustrates the shared execution framework and the image-driven route.

Scene construction begins with assets that are usable beyond rendering.
The asset module combines retrieval and generation with common geometry,
collision, and physical checks (Section 4). Articulated objects
add a structural requirement: their parts and joints must describe an
executable mechanism. ISArt addresses this through geometric–kinematic
planning, structure-conditioned part generation, and articulation binding.

The two scene-generation routes use these assets differently
(Section 5). Unravel progressively removes objects from a
reference image to expose occluded regions, then uses accumulated point-map
evidence to register and reassemble independently editable assets. SimForge
instead plans room geometry, object requirements, and spatial arrangements
from language, supporting both individual rooms and multi-room houses.
For both routes, plausible appearance
alone does not establish valid support, collision geometry, or articulation.

Construction failures need not be repaired where they are detected. A missing
asset calls for acquisition; an intersecting object calls for a placement
change; an incorrect joint may require revising the articulated asset.
The Graph-Native Harness (Section 6) makes these handoffs
explicit through shared state, validation evidence, bounded retries, and
checkpoints. It retains unaffected work and revalidates the dependencies of
each edit before construction proceeds.

PolicyForge then binds an accepted world to a task, robot embodiment,
and reset specification (Section 7). Scripted or
motion-planned teachers execute in Isaac Sim, producing synchronized images,
proprioception, and actions; successful validated episodes are retained for
training. Scene variants, object substitutions, and initial-state and language
augmentation diversify the resulting data. World validity, demonstration
success, and downstream policy performance remain distinct outcomes.

Module evaluations support the geometry and reconstruction methods: ISArt
achieves part-geometry CD 0.1630.163 versus 0.2680.268 for the combined
TRELLIS.2 + P3-SAM + X-Part baseline on 60 objects, while Unravel improves
blind human asset-fidelity scores from 4.94.9 to 8.68.6 on 160 objects.
These protocols are detailed in Sections 4.1 and 5.1.3.
Text-driven scene quality is evaluated separately on 179 room prompts and
31 multi-room prompts using the SceneEval and SceneSmith protocols
(Section 5.2). These evaluations test complementary
properties rather than a single pooled quality score.
On the MuJoCo-based LIBERO-Plus benchmark, SimData-Ultra co-training increases
World-Action Model success from 77.17%77.17\% to 89.43%89.43\% when comparing each configuration’s best
evaluated checkpoint up to and including 13K steps, selected by overall
success, with gains of 31.6631.66 and 6.256.25 percentage points in goal and
spatial generalization (Section 8). These results support the training utility of the
combined data-generation system across simulator boundaries; they do not
isolate each generator or augmentation’s contribution. The smaller
long-horizon gain motivates richer sequential task supervision.

This report makes four contributions:

Simulation-ready asset generation, including ISArt’s
structure-grounded articulated-object pipeline and shared candidate
validation, canonicalization, collision construction, and physical augmentation.

Complementary scene-generation routes: image-driven
reconstruction with Unravel and text-driven single-room and multi-room
construction with SimForge.

Integrated execution and demonstration synthesis: a
Graph-Native Harness coordinates attributed repair and acceptance, while
PolicyForge generates replayable demonstrations across scenes, tasks, and
robot embodiments.

Cross-simulator policy-learning evidence, showing a
12.2612.26-point overall gain on LIBERO-Plus at the best evaluated checkpoints
within a 13K-step budget,
with the largest improvement in goal generalization.

title: Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis
authors: Keerthi Kaashyap,Dennis Anthony,Akshay Krishnan,Nhi Ngoc Nguyen,Jeremy Collins,James Hays,Shreyas Kousik,Animesh Garg
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
This paper examines the role of Novel View Synthesis (NVS) in geometric representation learning.
In principle, NVS should reason about 3D scene structure, thereby enabling transferable multi-view geometric representations. Yet, existing encoder-based NVS methods yield poor representations. This is not because of a lack of supervisory signal, but rather due to inconspicuous architectural choices: spatially expressive decoders that dilute representational capabilities of the scene encoder, and low-level pixel-space targets that hinder feature learning.
We present SNAP, a self-supervised encoder-decoder transformer that addresses both through a pose-conditioned local decoder and a latent-space reconstruction objective.
SNAP is task agnostic, and we show that it is competitive with special-purpose geometry-supervised methods.
SNAP also performs competitively against self-supervised representations across five tasks: visual localization, pose estimation, point correspondence, depth estimation, and robot manipulation.
Remarkably, SNAP’s patch features exhibit emergent viewpoint invariance that approaches heavily supervised models despite lower compute and data budgets. Under camera shifts where standard 2D representations collapse, SNAP degrades more gracefully, revealing that restricting decoder expressivity actively prevents the suppression of transferable geometric structure. https://snap-nvs.github.io
introduction:
Geometric understanding from images is a foundation of computer vision.
Methods like DUSt3R [1], MASt3R [2], and VGGT [3] demonstrate that transformers can produce rich, transferable geometric representations, when trained on large-scale annotated 3D data.
This supervision requirement is a fundamental bottleneck since dense 3D ground truth is expensive to collect at scale.

Novel View Synthesis (NVS) offers a compelling alternative [4, 5, 6, 7].
These models must reason about 3D scene structure to predict unseen viewpoints, providing a rich geometric supervision signal only from posed images, which are abundantly available across videos, robotics platforms, and structure-from-motion pipelines.
However, representations produced from feed-forward NVS methods transfer poorly to downstream geometric tasks.
We argue this poor transfer is not a signal failure, but rather an architectural failure, driven by two identifiable and independently addressable choices that dilute signal.

First, spatially expressive decoders tend to absorb the representational load of the task.
When a decoder has sufficient capacity to reconstruct a target view from any encoder output, the encoder is not pressured to maintain structured, locally discriminative features.
While the reconstruction task is solved, the latent representations are not geometrically grounded.
Second, pixel-space reconstruction targets require modeling high-frequency aliasing statistics that are weakly related to 3D structure and semantics. Consequently, the reconstruction loss produces gradients that encourage the representation encoder to preserve fine-grained, image-specific statistics that are not directly informative about the underlying 3D structure or semantics.

We present SNAP, which addresses both failure axes with two targeted interventions. First, a pose-conditioned local decoder built on PRoPE [8] restricts the decoder’s receptive field via an explicit BlockNN mask applied to queried-view self-attention. This constraint forces the geometric structure to reside within the encoder’s scene representation rather than being an effect of the generative capacity of the decoder. Second, SNAP operates directly on frozen DINOv3 ViT-B patch features to provide a richer supervision signal than RGB reconstruction. This structured grounding is jointly aware of appearance, geometry, and semantics and produces higher quality representations.

Our main contributions are:

SNAP, a self-supervised multi-view spatial reasoning backbone that builds upon frozen 2D semantic latent spaces with an asymmetric NVS prediction objective, and latent feature targets to learn geometrically transferable representations without dense 3D supervision.

Mechanistic analyses isolating the independent impact of decoder expressivity and prediction space on geometric transfer, via receptive field sweeps and prediction space landscape experiments.

Empirical evaluation across five tasks matching or exceeding self-supervised baselines and competitive with geometry-supervised methods that require large-scale annotated 3D data.

title: UniIntervene++: An Adaptive Intervention Agent for Efficient Real-World Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yudong Lin,Haoyuan Deng,Zhuoxuan Yuan,Zaijia Yang,Yuanjiang Xue,Ziwei Wang
comment: Yudong Lin and Haoyuan Deng contributed equally. Ziwei Wang is the corresponding author. Code is available in our \href{this https URL}{GitHub repository}
abstract:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot policies to improve through physical interaction, but the assistance they require changes as their competence evolves. Existing intervention strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore become mismatched to the current policy. To address this, we propose UniIntervene++, an adaptive intervention agent that learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, UniIntervene++ first formulates the evolving RL policy, trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy as Options in a unified semi-Markov decision process and learns their relative values online. Building on this, competence-adaptive intervention periodically probes the RL policy through unassisted execution, keeping control allocation responsive to its evolving capability. Finally, coupled experience learning allows assisted behaviors to improve the RL policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions. In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene, and when to return control as the RL policy improves.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of 89.67%, outperforming all baselines by at least 6 percentage points, while reducing human intervention to 0.77%, a relative reduction of at least 94.6% from the best baseline. Code is available in our
GitHub repository.
introduction:
Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables robot manipulation policies to
improve through physical interaction and adapt to contact dynamics, perception
errors, and task variation [1, 2, 3]. However, real-world online RL remains costly:
rewards are often sparse, exploration can be unsafe or unproductive, and failed
rollouts consume robot time [4, 5, 6]. Human-in-the-loop RL (HiL-RL), such as HIL-SERL,
mitigates these issues through timely human corrections during online learning [7]. Yet current HiL-RL systems require a skilled operator to
continuously monitor training and repeatedly allocate control between autonomous
execution and assisted behavior, limiting real-world scalability [8, 9, 10].

Recent work has begun to automate this role. AutoSERL reuses a single
demonstration to guide exploration and recover from predefined failure regions
[11], while UniIntervene detects sustained value degradation
and invokes a goal-conditioned recovery policy learned offline
[12]. These methods provide useful automated assistance,
but the assistance required by the RL policy changes as its competence
evolves during online RL. Early in learning, intervention can prevent repetitive
failures and provide useful experience; later, excessive assistance can limit
the autonomous execution needed to further improve the RL policy [13, 14, 15]. Intervention
strategies based on offline estimates or fixed decision rules can therefore
become mismatched to the current policy.

What is missing is an intervention agent that learns to allocate control
between autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors as the task
policy improves online. This requires learning their relative values online
while keeping control allocation responsive to the policy’s evolving
competence. We therefore ask: Can an intervention agent learn a unified
control-allocation policy that adapts as the RL policy improves during
online RL?

To address this gap, we propose UniIntervene++, an adaptive intervention agent that
learns to allocate control between autonomous execution and heterogeneous
assisted behaviors during online RL. Specifically, to compare autonomous
execution and different forms of assistance within a unified decision process,
Unified Intervention Policy Learning places the evolving RL policy,
demonstration-guided trajectory correction, and a task-structured CodePolicy in
a shared decision space and learns their relative values online. To prevent
initially effective assistance from obscuring the RL policy’s evolving
competence, Competence-Adaptive Intervention, as illustrated in Fig. 1, periodically probes the RL
policy through unassisted execution, providing direct evidence of its current
competence and enabling control allocation to progressively shift from
assistance-heavy to autonomy-heavy execution. Finally, to ensure that
intervention also contributes to improving the RL policy,
Coupled Experience Learning uses assisted experience to train the task
policy, whose evolving outcomes in turn reshape future intervention decisions.
In this way, UniIntervene++ jointly determines when to intervene, how to intervene,
and when to return control as the RL policy improves, without requiring a
separate offline intervention-learning stage. Across five sparse-reward
real-world manipulation tasks, UniIntervene++ achieves an average success rate of
89.67%, exceeding the best baseline by 6 percentage points, while reducing
the human intervention rate to 0.77%. Its control allocation progressively
shifts toward the RL policy as autonomous competence improves.

The main contributions are:

We formulate online intervention as a unified control-allocation problem,
placing autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors in a shared
decision space and learning their relative values online.

We develop competence-adaptive intervention with coupled experience
learning, which keeps control allocation responsive to the RL policy’s
evolving competence while using assisted experience to improve the policy and
reshape subsequent intervention decisions.

Extensive real-world experiments across five manipulation tasks show that
UniIntervene++ achieves 89.67% average success, outperforming the best baseline by
6 percentage points, while reducing the human intervention rate to 0.77%.

1. We formulate online intervention as a unified control-allocation problem,
placing autonomous execution and heterogeneous assisted behaviors in a shared
decision space and learning their relative values online.

2. We develop competence-adaptive intervention with coupled experience
learning, which keeps control allocation responsive to the RL policy’s
evolving competence while using assisted experience to improve the policy and
reshape subsequent intervention decisions.

3. Extensive real-world experiments across five manipulation tasks show that
UniIntervene++ achieves 89.67% average success, outperforming the best baseline by
6 percentage points, while reducing the human intervention rate to 0.77%.

title: Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration Curriculum for Reinforcement Learning
authors: Juri Pfammatter,Kaixian Qu,Clemens Schwarke,Victor Klemm,Marco Hutter
abstract:
Long-horizon tasks with sparse rewards pose an exploration bottleneck for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning: a policy started from the initial state rarely reaches the goal and receives no learning signal. Reference motions, hand-designed curricula, and shaped rewards supply this signal but require demonstrations or task-specific engineering; automatic start-state and goal curricula avoid this but typically expand from one side only, so the full distance to the target must be covered from that side.
We propose the Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration curriculum for Reinforcement learning (BVER), which expands from both ends at once. Inspired by bidirectional RRT planning, BVER grows start states outward from the goal and goals outward from the initial state distribution, biases both toward unexplored task space, and steers them toward each other, training one goal-conditioned policy on both.
On point-mass mazes, quadrupedal box climbing, and robot-arm ring-on-peg transfer, BVER learns faster than all compared reference-free curricula. On box climbing, it reaches 95% success on a 0.4 m0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box in roughly 65% fewer iterations than the best of them, is the only one of them to learn to climb a 0.7 m0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, and yields a policy robust to start, goal, and yaw variation. Without a demonstration, it approaches the sample efficiency of reference-based curricula on the 0.4 m0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box and on ring-on-peg transfer. Ablations show that expanding from both ends outperforms either direction alone.
Project website, videos, and code: https://bver-rl.github.io/
introduction:
Many robotic tasks are naturally posed as reaching a goal: a quadruped that should climb onto a box is rewarded for standing on top of it, not for how it gets there. With such a sparse reward and a long horizon, a policy started from the initial state distribution rarely reaches the goal and thus receives no learning signal (Florensa et al., 2017): policy gradient methods such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) learn from the returns of the trajectories the policy currently generates, and a reward that none of them collects cannot guide it.

In robot control, the missing signal is typically supplied by terrain curricula with dense rewards (Rudin et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2020), reference motions (Fuchioka et al., 2023), hand-designed curricula (Atanassov et al., 2025), or curiosity rewards (Schwarke et al., 2023). These have enabled highly capable controllers but require a demonstration, task-specific engineering, or reward terms beyond the task objective.

Automatic curriculum learning replaces this design effort with intermediate tasks generated during training (Narvekar et al., 2020; Portelas et al., 2020b). Start-state curricula begin closer to the goal, with start states taken from a reference trajectory (Peng et al., 2018; Resnick et al., 2018) or from random walks outward from the goal (Florensa et al., 2017), and goal curricula keep the start fixed and propose intermediate goals (Florensa et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019; Cho et al., 2023). Both expand from one end only: the frontier must cover the entire distance to the fixed end, and the policy trains on the target task from that side only.

Two mechanisms from sampling-based motion planning address this limitation. Rapidly-exploring random trees (LaValle & Kuffner, 2001, RRT;) extend the vertex nearest to a uniform sample of the space, so growth is biased toward large unexplored regions (the Voronoi bias), and RRT-Connect (Kuffner & LaValle, 2000) grows one tree from the start and one from the goal and extends each toward the other until they meet. BVER (Bidirectional Voronoi-biased Exploration curriculum for Reinforcement learning) transfers both to curriculum generation. It grows start states outward from the goal by random walks (the backwards expansion) and goals outward from the initial state distribution in the same way (the forwards expansion), connects the two sets, and trains a single goal-conditioned policy on both. Like reverse curriculum generation (Florensa et al., 2017, RC;), BVER keeps only tasks of intermediate difficulty for the current policy, while its expansion covers the task space (Figure 2).

Our contributions are:

A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

An expansion mechanism that carries the Voronoi bias of RRT and the connect step of RRT-Connect over to curriculum generation to propose feasible states as tasks.

Experiments showing that BVER learns fastest among the reference-free curricula on all six compared tasks, is the only one of them to learn to climb the 0.7 m0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, transfers to scanned terrains with the same hyperparameters, and outperforms either expansion direction alone.

1. A bidirectional start–goal curriculum for sparse-reward, long-horizon goal-conditioned RL that generates both intermediate starts and goals, without reference motions, shaped rewards, or a hand-designed curriculum.

2. An expansion mechanism that carries the Voronoi bias of RRT and the connect step of RRT-Connect over to curriculum generation to propose feasible states as tasks.

3. Experiments showing that BVER learns fastest among the reference-free curricula on all six compared tasks, is the only one of them to learn to climb the 0.7 m0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} box, transfers to scanned terrains with the same hyperparameters, and outperforms either expansion direction alone.

title: Native Action-Prior Learning from Videos for World Action Models
authors: Zhaochong An,Fei Zhang,Menglin Jia,Duncan Frost,Zijian Zhou,Yikai Wang,Xudong Wang,Aditya Patel,Belinda Zeng,Tao Xiang,Serge Belongie,Amir Bar,Sen He
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
World action models integrate future visual dynamics with robot action prediction, but their scalability remains limited by the need for action-annotated robot trajectories.
Observation-only videos contain rich evidence about interaction dynamics, but existing approaches typically use them either to pretrain visual representations that must later be adapted for control, or to infer latent actions that are subsequently grounded to robot commands.
We present NAVA-WAM, which introduces native action-prior learning by directly pretraining the action policy from observation-only videos, avoiding indirect representation-to-control transfer or a separate latent-action model.
Our training consists of two stages.
First, we pretrain on observation-only videos, where future-video flow-matching supervision over visual transitions is propagated through transition-structured joint attention to optimize the Action-DiT and learn action-relevant priors.
Second, we use action-labeled demonstrations to post-train the Action-DiT for robot control through joint video–action flow matching, while asymmetric attention decouples the visual branch from iterative action denoising and enables efficient action-only inference.
Extensive experiments show that NAVA-WAM consistently outperforms prior approaches under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, while demonstrating strong action-label efficiency and effective real-robot generalization.
These results establish native action-prior learning as an effective approach to directly pretrain action policies from observation-only videos, providing a scalable path beyond action-labeled robot data.
introduction:
World action models (WAMs) (Zhu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026a; Bi et al., 2026a) incorporate future visual dynamics into action learning, with strong potential to improve policy generalization.
However, scaling WAMs remains challenging because they rely on action-annotated robot trajectories that are costly to collect and hard to standardize across embodiments.
In contrast, large-scale observation-only videos provide abundant information about physical interactions and state transitions without action labels.
The key challenge is therefore how to leverage such videos to learn priors that effectively improve action policy learning.

Existing approaches largely follow two paradigms for exploiting observation-only videos.
Vision representation learning first learns visual or predictive representations from videos and then trains an action policy on top of them using action-labeled robot demonstrations (Nair et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2025; Assran et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026).
Because the learned video prior remains encoded in a vision-centric representation, its connection to executable actions is established only during downstream robot training, introducing an indirect representation-to-control transfer.
Latent-action learning instead infers action-like variables from visual transitions and uses them as intermediate supervision for subsequent policy learning (Schmidt and Jiang, 2024; Ye et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025b; Bu et al., 2025b; Bi et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026b).
While more action-oriented, this paradigm requires an additional latent-action modeling stage and relies on complex architectural or optimization constraints (Yang et al., 2026b; Wang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d) to avoid shortcut solutions in which the latent action simply copies information from the target observation.
These constraints increase modeling complexity and can restrict the expressiveness of the latent-action space, thereby limiting the supervision provided to the policy and impairing its control learning.

These limitations motivate a simple question:
Can observation-only videos directly optimize an action policy without relying on an intermediate interface?
We answer this question with NAVA-WAM, which introduces native action-prior learning for world action models.
As illustrated in Fig. 1, instead of first learning a separate visual representation or latent-action space and then using it in policy training, NAVA-WAM uses future-video prediction to directly pretrain the action policy.
This creates a direct learning path from scalable observation-only videos to the action policy, avoiding intermediate representation constraints and enabling more effective policy learning.

Specifically, NAVA-WAM adopts a joint Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture (Liang et al., 2024), comprising a Video-DiT and an Action-DiT that interact through joint attention while retaining modality-specific parameters.
During action-free pre-training, the Video-DiT is frozen and the Action-DiT is optimized solely through future-video flow-matching supervision.
Our transition-structured joint attention allows the Action-DiT to model visual transitions while participating in future-state prediction, enabling the video objective to directly optimize the action policy.
In this way, the Action-DiT learns action-relevant priors directly from visual transitions without requiring an intermediate interface.
During downstream post-training, we jointly optimize the video and action streams on action-labeled robot demonstrations through video–action flow matching, adapting the pretrained Action-DiT to embodiment-specific control.
We make cross-stream attention asymmetric to decouple the visual stream from the evolving action sample, allowing its representations to be cached and enabling efficient action-only inference without explicitly generating future videos.

We evaluate NAVA-WAM on the simulation benchmarks LIBERO/LIBERO-Plus (Liu et al., 2023; Fei et al., 2025) and RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025a) under both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings, demonstrating superior performance across both regimes.
We further deploy NAVA-WAM on a physical Franka FR3, achieving 93.3%93.3\% success across tabletop manipulation tasks, compared with 66.7%66.7\% for DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026c) and 53.3%53.3\% for π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Physical Intelligence et al., 2025).
Controlled experiments show that native action-prior learning consistently outperforms representation-based and latent-action-based approaches across action-label budgets, with larger gains in low-budget regimes.
Together, these results demonstrate that native action-prior learning can effectively leverage observation-only videos to learn action priors, improving generalization and action-label efficiency.

title: Self-Repairing Recurrent Ensembles for Real-Time Recovery from Distribution Shift
authors: Julian Lemmel,Pedro D. Wendel Garcia,Taisuke Kobayashi,Radu Grosu
subjects: Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract: Deploying a pretrained controller exposes it to conditions that are absent from its training data. Sensor drift, outright sensor failure and accumulating measurement noise all induce a distribution shift that can collapse an otherwise competent policy – typically at a point in time where no expert is available to supply corrective labels. We present a method that lets a policy recover from such shifts online and without supervision. Our controller is an ensemble of recurrent networks, each of which observes a randomly masked subset of the observation vector, and whose Gaussian outputs are combined through sequential Kalman fusion so that confident members dominate the consensus action. At deployment, we treat this consensus as a self-supervised label and fine-tune each member towards it, scaling each member’s contribution proportional to the complement of its squared Kalman gain. Gradients are computed using RFLO, an efficient and biologically plausible approximation of Real-Time Recurrent Learning, so that a parameter update follows every environment step and the policy reacts to a shift as it unfolds. On a range of simulated continuous control tasks, our approach recovers close to the original performance after a sensor shift, while ensembles that see the full observation are unable to recover. The same framework subsumes fully online interactive imitation learning: when an expert is present, the consensus label is replaced by the expert action and the identical update rule refines the policy during teleoperation.
