title: EmbPASS: Towards Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation
authors: Pujun Guo,Yuanfan Zheng,Fei Teng,Mengfei Duan,Guoqiang Zhao,Yuheng Zhang,Kai Luo,Kailun Yang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Panoramic images provide a complete 360∘360^{\circ} field of view, enabling comprehensive scene understanding for embodied perception. However, heterogeneous embodied platforms exhibit substantial differences in observation viewpoints and spatial layouts, giving rise to cross-embodiment observation shifts that pose additional challenges to consistent and reliable panoramic perception, while systematic studies of this problem remain limited. To bridge this gap, we introduce a new task, termed Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation. Meanwhile, we establish EmbPASS, a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark spanning Vehicle, Drone, Wearable, and Quadruped platforms under a unified semantic taxonomy, providing a testbed for systematically studying cross-embodiment panoramic perception. We further propose EPONet, an open-vocabulary panoramic semantic segmentation network that integrates Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA) and Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST) to enhance spatial modeling and semantic transfer under heterogeneous embodied observations. Extensive experiments show that EPONet achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS with 35.82%35.82\% mIoU, outperforming the strongest baseline by 1.10%1.10\%, while remaining competitive on existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks. The source code and EmbPASS benchmark will be made publicly available at https://github.com/guopj1/EmbPASS.
introduction:
Environmental perception is fundamental to autonomous robots operating in complex and unconstrained real-world environments, where reliable scene understanding supports navigation, planning, and decision-making [1, 2]. In recent years, panoramic vision has attracted increasing attention in robotic scene understanding due to its complete 360∘360^{\circ} Field of View (FoV) and more comprehensive environmental observations [3, 4]. Despite the inherent projection distortions of panoramic imagery, panoramic scene understanding has continued to advance and has progressively expanded toward more open perception settings [5, 6, 7, 8].

However, systematic studies of panoramic semantic segmentation across heterogeneous embodied platforms remain relatively limited [5, 6, 8, 9].
In practical robotic deployments, differences in embodied platform configurations and sensor mounting conditions often result in distinct observation heights and viewpoints [10, 11], leading to substantial differences in panoramic appearance and spatial layout. Such differences give rise to cross-embodiment observation shifts, posing additional challenges to consistent and reliable panoramic perception. Meanwhile, acquiring dense panoramic annotations for each embodied platform is costly and becomes increasingly impractical as the diversity of embodied platforms continues to grow.

To enable panoramic scene understanding across diverse embodied platforms and address the above challenges, we introduce a new task, termed Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation. Accordingly, the model is trained only on pinhole images from a label-rich source domain and directly performs open-vocabulary semantic segmentation on panoramic images captured by unseen embodied platforms, without requiring target-platform annotations. As illustrated in Fig. (b), OPS [9] extends the FoV to 360∘360^{\circ} panoramic observations, while our task further considers heterogeneous embodied platforms to unlock platform diversity.

To systematically study this task, we construct EmbPASS, a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for heterogeneous embodied platforms, as shown in Fig. (a). EmbPASS covers multiple representative platforms under a unified semantic taxonomy, providing a common testbed for evaluating cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation. Compared with existing panoramic benchmarks [12, 13, 14, 15], EmbPASS explicitly incorporates platform diversity, enabling systematic analysis of platform-dependent observation variations. EmbPASS further reveals clear platform-dependent differences in the spherical spatial organization of scene semantics. Since ERP projection distortion is inherently latitude-dependent, such semantic layout variations introduce additional geometric challenges for cross-embodiment panoramic perception.

Accordingly, we propose EPONet, an open-vocabulary panoramic semantic segmentation network for heterogeneous embodied platforms. To accommodate the diverse local distortion conditions encountered in heterogeneous embodied observations, we introduce Relation-Aware Metric Adapter (RAMA), which predicts metric parameters from content representations and directional neighborhood relations and uses them to constrain the sampling support, enabling structured spatial aggregation under diverse local geometric distortions. Meanwhile, to better exploit transferable pretrained semantics under varying observation conditions, we propose Content-Adaptive Semantic Transfer (CAST), which adaptively reorganizes and transfers intermediate CLIP [16] representations according to the current observation.

Extensive experiments on the established EmbPASS benchmark and existing panoramic segmentation benchmarks verify the effectiveness of EPONet. EPONet achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS, reaching 35.82%35.82\% mIoU and outperforming the strongest competing method by 1.10%1.10\%. It also remains competitive on the public Stanford2D3D [12] and DensePASS [15] benchmarks.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation and further establish EmbPASS, a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for systematically studying this task.

We propose EPONet, a cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation network that integrates RAMA and CAST for effective panoramic perception across heterogeneous embodied platforms.

Extensive experiments on EmbPASS and existing panoramic benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EPONet, which achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS while remaining competitive on public panoramic benchmarks.

1. We introduce Cross-Embodiment Open Panoramic Segmentation and further establish EmbPASS, a multi-platform panoramic semantic segmentation benchmark for systematically studying this task.

2. We propose EPONet, a cross-embodiment open panoramic segmentation network that integrates RAMA and CAST for effective panoramic perception across heterogeneous embodied platforms.

3. Extensive experiments on EmbPASS and existing panoramic benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of EPONet, which achieves the best platform-balanced performance on EmbPASS while remaining competitive on public panoramic benchmarks.

title: CrowdOcc: Monocular Semantic Scene Completion for Quadruped Robots in Crowded Indoor Environments
authors: Feiyang Chen,Jincheng Hu,Yiduo Chen,Jihao Li,Yue Liang,Bingzhao Gao,Yanjun Huang,Yuanjian Zhang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
abstract: Monocular semantic scene completion (SSC) for quadruped robots remains underexplored in real crowded indoor environments, where human-scene occlusion disrupts static geometry and human occupancy predictions are often incomplete or spatially misplaced. We present CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset and monocular SSC framework for this setting. CrowdOcc contains 25.1K frames from 11 indoor scenes, with semantic occupancy annotations constructed through static-dynamic decoupling. Our framework combines: (i) Normal-Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) to complement depth-aware lifting with surface-normal cues for occlusion-robust geometry; and (ii) Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) to selectively model human-human and local human-scene relations in 3D. Our method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance on CrowdOcc’s scene-disjoint test set, reaching 15.80 IoU, 11.40 mIoU, and 46.23 Human IoU, demonstrating generalization to unseen indoor scenes.
introduction:
Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) predicts dense 3D occupancy and semantics from partial observations [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Monocular SSC further reduces the sensing requirement to a single RGB image, making it attractive for onboard perception on quadruped robots [8]. However, most existing SSC datasets are built around static indoor scenes or autonomous-driving settings, where the sensing viewpoint, scene dynamics, and occupancy distribution differ substantially from those encountered by quadruped robots in crowded indoor environments [9, 10, 11, 12]. In particular, existing datasets provide limited coverage of low-viewpoint observations with dense human presence and dynamic human occupancy. As summarized in Table I, this leaves real crowded indoor SSC for quadruped robots largely underexplored.

Crowded indoor scenes introduce two difficulties that are not well addressed by conventional monocular SSC pipelines. First, humans frequently occlude large portions of walls, floors, doors, and other static structures. The resulting incomplete observations weaken depth-based feature lifting and make the recovery of scene geometry less reliable [13, 14]. Second, human occupancy remains difficult to recover reliably in crowded scenes. Partial observations and foreground-background ambiguity frequently lead to incomplete human geometry and erroneous spatial placement. These issues become more pronounced when the test environment differs from the training scenes, where scene-specific geometric priors no longer transfer reliably.

To address this difficulties, we introduce CrowdOcc, an RGB-D dataset for monocular SSC in real crowded indoor environments, together with a model tailored to scene geometry and human occupancy. CrowdOcc contains 25.1K frames collected from 11 independent indoor scenes using a quadruped robot. As illustrated in Fig. 1, synchronized RGB-D, LiDAR, and IMU measurements are used for offline occupancy construction, while inference takes only a single RGB image. For scene geometry, we propose Normal-Guided Scene Geometry Fusion (NGSGF) module, which complements depth-based lifting with surface-normal cues and improves the representation of partially observed static structures. For human occupancy, we introduce Human-Centric Sparse Interaction (HCSI) module, which selects human-related voxel candidates and explicitly models human-human and local human-scene interactions in 3D. We evaluate cross-scene generalization on test scenes excluded from both training and validation. Our method achieves state-of-the-art SSC performance under this protocol.

title: OmniAct3D: Leveraging Foundation Geometry and Evidence-Grounded Reasoning for Panoramic 3D Detection
authors: Runtong Wu,Fei Teng,Di Wen,Guoqiang Zhao,Kunyu Peng,Kailun Yang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Accurate 3D detection is essential for mobile embodied agents, while Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) offer transferable visual and geometric priors. Yet existing VFM-based 3D detectors rely on narrow-view monocular images or discrete perspective views, limiting coherent surround perception; equirectangular projection (ERP) instead encodes a continuous 360∘360^{\circ} scene in a single image. Direct transfer remains difficult because ERP organizes geometry and visual information differently, making object-relevant cues hard to model, localize, and preserve. We propose OmniAct3D, a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP while preserving transferable VFM priors. To resolve geometric mismatch, the ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter (ERGA-Ray) models spherical viewing rays and periodic spatial structure. To localize evidence in scene-wide context, the Visual-Action Reasoning Chain (VARC) grounds each hypothesis in relevant panoramic evidence and converts it into a structured geometric action. To recover local cues lost under fixed token budgets, the Appearance-Guided Heading Expert (AGHE) re-encodes object regions at higher resolution for heading estimation. Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves over the previous best 3D detector by 2.962.96 NDS points on Spheriverse and over the unadapted VFM baseline by 24.8724.87 mAP points on PanoMMOcc. With target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 9595–98%98\% of the same-configuration mAP, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/FeiT-FeiTeng/OmniAct3D.
introduction:
Accurate and robust 3D detection is essential for mobile embodied agents to understand and interact with the physical world.
From autonomous vehicles to mobile robots, agents must estimate the 3D locations, dimensions, and orientations of surrounding objects to support navigation, motion planning, and embodied decision-making [1, 2].

Recent VFM-based 3D detectors [5, 6] leverage transferable visual and geometric priors for object-level 3D perception. Despite this progress, existing methods primarily follow two perspective-image paradigms. As shown in Fig. 1,
monocular methods [3, 7] infer 3D boxes from a single perspective image but observe only a limited field of view;
Multi-view methods [8, 9] extend the surrounding coverage using discrete perspective observations.
In contrast, equirectangular projection (ERP) encodes the surrounding spherical field of view within a single image, providing a unified and spatially continuous representation for coherent 360∘360^{\circ} perception [10, 11].

However, directly transferring perspective-trained VFM-based 3D detectors to ERP observations remains challenging because ERP organizes geometry and visual information differently from perspective imagery. This representation mismatch makes object-relevant cues difficult to model, localize, and preserve, giving rise to three challenges. First, the geometric priors of VFMs are learned predominantly from locally planar and non-periodic perspective imagery, whereas ERP exhibits spherical viewing directions, latitude-dependent distortion, and horizontal periodicity. Reusing these priors without adaptation therefore produces geometric representations misaligned with ERP structure, particularly at high latitudes and across the horizontal boundary. Second, although a single ERP image captures scene-wide context, the evidence relevant to each object occupies only a small portion of the panorama. Directly decoding 3D hypotheses from global features makes it difficult to localize and associate the supporting evidence for each object, especially when objects are small or occluded. Third, encoding an ultra-wide panorama under a fixed token budget compresses individual objects and discards fine-grained local appearance cues. The loss of features such as front–rear asymmetry impairs directed heading estimation.

To address these challenges, we propose OmniAct3D, a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors. To resolve the geometric mismatch, we introduce the ERP-Ray Geometry Adapter (ERGA-Ray), which models spherical viewing rays and ERP-aware spatial interactions to align pretrained foundation geometry with ERP-specific spherical and periodic structure. To localize object-relevant evidence in scene-wide context, we introduce the Visual-Action Reasoning Chain (VARC), which grounds each 3D hypothesis in relevant panoramic evidence and converts that evidence into a structured geometric action for object-level 3D reasoning. To recover local cues lost under a fixed token budget, we introduce the AGHE, which re-encodes object regions at higher resolution for directed heading estimation.

We evaluate OmniAct3D on Spheriverse [12] and PanoMMOcc [13]. On Spheriverse, OmniAct3D achieves 0.1887/0.18250.1887/0.1825 mAP/NDS, improving the previous best NDS by 2.962.96 points. On PanoMMOcc, it achieves 0.5897/0.40320.5897/0.4032 mAP/NDS and improves the unadapted VFM baseline by 24.8724.87 mAP points. Moreover, with target-specific geometry adaptation via ERGA-Ray, VARC retains 95%95\% and 98%98\% of same-configuration mAP on Spheriverse and PanoMMOcc, respectively, indicating reusable object-level 3D reasoning across sensing configurations.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose OmniAct3D, a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors.

We introduce ERGA-Ray to align foundation geometry with ERP spherical and periodic structure.

We introduce VARC to ground 3D hypotheses in relevant panoramic evidence and convert that evidence into a structured geometric action, and AGHE to recover fine-grained local cues for directed heading estimation.

Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves NDS by 2.962.96 points over the previous best detector on Spheriverse and mAP by 24.8724.87 points over the unadapted VFM baseline on PanoMMOcc; with target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 9595–98%98\% of same-configuration mAP across sensing configurations.

1. We propose OmniAct3D, a framework that adapts perspective-trained VFM detectors to ERP observations while preserving transferable VFM priors.

2. We introduce ERGA-Ray to align foundation geometry with ERP spherical and periodic structure.

3. We introduce VARC to ground 3D hypotheses in relevant panoramic evidence and convert that evidence into a structured geometric action, and AGHE to recover fine-grained local cues for directed heading estimation.

4. Experiments show that OmniAct3D improves NDS by 2.962.96 points over the previous best detector on Spheriverse and mAP by 24.8724.87 points over the unadapted VFM baseline on PanoMMOcc; with target-specific geometry adaptation, VARC retains 9595–98%98\% of same-configuration mAP across sensing configurations.

title: RYOPO: Bringing End-to-End Category-Level Object Pose Estimation into Real Time
authors: Hakjin Lee,Junghoon Seo,Jaehoon Sim
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Category-level object pose estimation predicts the rotation, translation, and metric size
of unseen instances within known categories.
Many accurate RGB-D methods rely on external instance segmentation and crop-based pose
estimation, introducing separate stages and object-dependent processing costs that hinder
real-time inference.
To bring accurate pose estimation into real time, we present RYOPO, an end-to-end trainable
query-based RGB-D set predictor. It jointly detects and segments objects and estimates their
9-DoF poses without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or a separately trained instance segmentor.
Shared image and scene encoding avoids repeated per-object crop encoding.
A query-conditioned geometry pathway associates observed 3D points and RGB features with
object queries and incorporates shared scene context.
Object-centric refinement uses the resulting point descriptors to update an explicit pose state
through pose-conditioned cross-attention and recurrent residual corrections.
On NOCS, RYOPO substantially improves on published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation results.
It achieves competitive performance compared with two-stage methods
under all-object evaluation on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, while enabling
real-time full-frame pose estimation at 31.831.8 FPS on an RTX A6000.
Project page: https://yopo-series.github.io/RYOPO-project-page/.
introduction:
Category-level object pose estimation predicts poses and metric sizes for unseen instances
within known categories, without test-instance CAD models [1].
Common RGB-D pipelines use a separately trained instance segmentor to obtain object masks
and extract each object’s RGB crop and depth-derived point cloud for a per-object pose
network [2, 3].
This design adds an external segmentation stage and repeats crop encoding and pose
estimation for each detected instance, increasing inference cost with object count.
The resulting inference latency can limit closed-loop visual-servoing
performance [4].
It can also reduce manipulation throughput by extending task cycles when perception
cannot be overlapped with robot motion [5].

Joint methods already combine localization and pose prediction. CenterSnap [6]
and ShAPO [7] use learned CAD-derived shape representations for RGB-D inference,
whereas YOPO [8] extends a detection transformer with parallel pose heads on
image-derived queries. We aim to extend the set-prediction formulation used by YOPO
to end-to-end RGB-D object pose estimation while achieving real-time inference.
The challenge is to gain accuracy from measured 3D geometry while keeping full-frame
computation within a real-time budget. This favors shared image and scene encoding over
independently encoding a crop for every object.

A straightforward RGB-D extension is to fuse encoded depth and RGB features before query decoding.
Early fusion makes depth available through shared features, but does not by itself specify
how each object’s measured 3D geometry should guide pose corrections.
In reference-box-based detection transformers such as DINO [9], queries combine
content features with positional embeddings derived from 2D boxes. These spatial references
support image localization but do not explicitly represent 3D rotation, translation, or metric size.
We therefore investigate object-specific pose corrections guided by measured geometry and
the current pose estimate.

We present RYOPO (Real-Time YOPO), a query-based RGB-D set-prediction framework for joint
detection, segmentation, and category-level object pose estimation. To the best of our
knowledge, RYOPO is the first end-to-end trainable query-based RGB-D set predictor for
category-level object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors.
Built on the DETR-style EdgeCrafter architecture [10], RYOPO
learns localization and pose estimation jointly, without a separately trained instance
segmentor or per-object crop encoder.

The key design couples object-associated geometry with an explicit pose state.
A query-conditioned geometry pathway associates measured 3D observations with object queries
and combines them with RGB appearance and shared scene context to update query content
and positional representations. Unlike YOPO’s parallel pose heads, object-centric refinement
combines object queries with current pose encodings for cross-attention to object
observations. Queries predict residual pose corrections; updated poses condition
further refinement without test-time optimization.

On NOCS, RYOPO substantially improves on published RGB-D joint detection and pose estimation
results. On REAL275 and HouseCat6D, performance is competitive with two-stage methods
under all-object evaluation. Our deployment achieves 31.831.8 FPS for full-frame pose estimation
on an RTX A6000 (Fig. 1).

Our main contributions are:

An end-to-end trainable RGB-D set predictor for joint detection, segmentation,
and object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or an external
instance segmentor.

An object-level depth integration method that associates observed 3D geometry with
DETR-style object queries, and a pose refinement method that combines query features
with the current pose state to attend to object observations and predict residual pose corrections.

Substantial gains over RGB-D joint methods on NOCS and competitive all-object
pose performance on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, with real-time pose inference.

1. An end-to-end trainable RGB-D set predictor for joint detection, segmentation,
and object pose estimation without explicit CAD-derived shape priors or an external
instance segmentor.

2. An object-level depth integration method that associates observed 3D geometry with
DETR-style object queries, and a pose refinement method that combines query features
with the current pose state to attend to object observations and predict residual pose corrections.

3. Substantial gains over RGB-D joint methods on NOCS and competitive all-object
pose performance on REAL275 and HouseCat6D, with real-time pose inference.

title: VIGOR: Zero-Shot Visual Generalization via Latent-Space Consistency in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Mingyu Park,Samyeul Noh,Hyun Myung,Donghwan Lee
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) achieves strong sample efficiency by planning within learned latent dynamics, yet its performance degrades substantially under unseen visual distractions such as background variations, lighting changes, or camera shifts. Unlike model-free RL, where encoder perturbations affect only single-step predictions, MBRL suffers from a two-level vulnerability: visual distractions first push encoder outputs out of distribution, and these errors then compound through recursive latent rollouts over the planning horizon. We propose VIsual Generalization via latent-space cOnsistency in model-based RL (VIGOR), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization to unseen visual distractions while retaining the sample efficiency of its MBRL backbone. VIGOR integrates three interdependent components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation, which pairs weak-only and weak-to-strong latent views within a single batch; (ii) dynamics-level consistency, which enforces augmentation-invariant transition predictions through direct latent regression; and (iii) encoder-level stabilization, which prevents encoder drift under the cross-augmentation supervision imposed by dynamics-level consistency. Evaluations on the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) and Robosuite show that VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art model-free and model-based baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4%3.4\% on DMC and 43.6%43.6\% on Robosuite. Ablations further show that VIGOR’s robustness is augmentation-agnostic: replacing the default augmentation with alternatives from distinct perturbation families preserves strong generalization, confirming that latent-space consistency, not the augmentation choice, drives robustness.
introduction:
Visual reinforcement learning (visual RL) trains control policies directly from pixels, eliminating task-specific state estimation [26, 25, 45, 44]. Despite success in locomotion and manipulation [8, 23, 17], visual RL remains sensitive to unseen visual distractions: even minor shifts in backgrounds, lighting, or camera position can cause substantial policy degradation.

In model-free RL (MFRL), visual generalization has been addressed through data augmentation [16, 20], robust representation learning [18, 4, 48], and stabilized value-function training [29, 19]. Model-based RL (MBRL) offers superior sample efficiency by planning in learned latent dynamics [17, 12], but achieving visual generalization in MBRL is structurally more challenging. In MFRL, encoder perturbations affect only a single-step prediction. In MBRL, the problem is two-level: visual distractions first push encoder outputs out of the training distribution, and these out-of-distribution (OOD) latents are then recursively propagated by the dynamics model over a planning horizon HH, causing errors to compound across steps (Figure 1). This two-level vulnerability, which does not arise in MFRL, means that techniques effective for single-step robustness are insufficient when the encoder simultaneously serves a recursive dynamics model, Q-value networks, and a planner.

We propose VIsual Generalization via latent-space cOnsistency in model-based RL (VIGOR), a framework that enables zero-shot generalization while retaining the sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone. VIGOR addresses the two-level vulnerability through three interdependent components: (i) asymmetric weak-to-strong augmentation (AW), an asymmetric batch-splitting strategy that produces paired weak-only and weak-to-strong latents; (ii) dynamics-level consistency (DC), which enforces augmentation-invariant transition predictions by anchoring dynamics outputs to stable targets; and (iii) encoder-level stabilization (ES), which prevents the shared encoder from drifting under the cross-augmentation pressure imposed by DC.

We evaluate VIGOR on the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) [40] and Robosuite [54] under the RL-ViGen zero-shot protocol [49], covering seven visual distraction types—a substantially broader evaluation than the two types (background-color, background-video) typically considered in prior work [18, 20, 4, 7] (Appendix D.3). VIGOR outperforms state-of-the-art MFRL and MBRL baselines, improving zero-shot generalization over the second-best baseline by 3.4%3.4\% on DMC and 43.6%43.6\% on Robosuite while retaining the sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone.
Ablation studies further reveal that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL: applying strong augmentation uniformly across the batch, without the asymmetric splitting of AW, achieves only 48%48\% of VIGOR’s performance on DMC (Section 4.3). Furthermore, VIGOR’s robustness is augmentation-agnostic: latent-space consistency, rather than any specific augmentation choice, drives generalization (Section 4.4; Appendix E.5).

Our contributions are:

Problem identification and analysis. We identify a two-level failure mode in MBRL: visual distractions first produce OOD encoder outputs, which then compound through recursive rollouts—a failure mode unique to recursive latent dynamics (Figure 1; Section 4.5).

Integrated framework for MBRL robustness. We propose VIGOR, which addresses this failure mode through three interdependent components (AW, DC, and ES) designed for the recursive world-model setting. We show that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL, that VIGOR’s integration is necessary, and that the resulting robustness is augmentation-agnostic (Sections 4.3–4.5; Appendix E.5).

State-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. VIGOR outperforms MFRL and MBRL baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4%3.4\% on DMC and 43.6%43.6\% on Robosuite while preserving the strong sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone.

1. Problem identification and analysis. We identify a two-level failure mode in MBRL: visual distractions first produce OOD encoder outputs, which then compound through recursive rollouts—a failure mode unique to recursive latent dynamics (Figure 1; Section 4.5).

2. Integrated framework for MBRL robustness. We propose VIGOR, which addresses this failure mode through three interdependent components (AW, DC, and ES) designed for the recursive world-model setting. We show that naive transfer of MFRL strategies fails in MBRL, that VIGOR’s integration is necessary, and that the resulting robustness is augmentation-agnostic (Sections 4.3–4.5; Appendix E.5).

3. State-of-the-art zero-shot generalization. VIGOR outperforms MFRL and MBRL baselines, surpassing the second-best baseline by 3.4%3.4\% on DMC and 43.6%43.6\% on Robosuite while preserving the strong sample efficiency of its TD-MPC2 backbone.

title: FUSEye: Training-Light Fisheye Detection with Overlapping Views and Zero-Initialized Adapters
authors: Wenya Su,Kai Luo,Di Wen,Ruiping Liu,Yufan Chen,Junwei Zheng,Kunyu Peng,Kailun Yang
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)
comment: Source code will be available atthis https URL
abstract: Fisheye cameras give mobile robots a single-sensor, low-cost view of their surroundings, yet the COCO-pretrained detectors that practitioners routinely reuse fail on them: strong radial distortion warps local image structure, while boundary compression shrinks objects to near-invisible sizes. Full fine-tuning closes much of the gap but requires abundant fisheye labels and compute. We present FUSEye, a training-light framework that turns a frozen-backbone COCO-pretrained extra-large YOLO26 detector (YOLO26-x) into a fisheye detector. FUSEye adds roughly 227​k227k new parameters while updating the inserted modules and the pretrained detection head. It addresses the transfer gap at three causally linked levels. At the input level, overlapping grid view generation and box remapping (GridViews) enlarge compressed boundary regions. At the feature level, zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) correct distortion-induced feature misalignment. At the decision level, learned cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) promotes low-confidence detections only when they are supported by consistent evidence across multiple views. On the WoodScape surround-view fisheye benchmark, FUSEye raises YOLO26-x from 0.1480.148 to 0.2660.266 mAP50 and retains 84.3%84.3\% fully fine-tuned accuracy. Moreover, randomly using only 25%25\% of the labeled training images, FUSEye achieves 0.2597±0.00340.2597{\pm}0.0034 mAP50, retaining 97.6%97.6\% of its full-label performance. FUSEye also consistently improves YOLOv8-11 detectors, showing that the recipe is architecture-agnostic. Source code will be available at https://github.com/Su-wenya/FUSEye.
introduction:
Fisheye cameras offer mobile robots a cost-effective wide-angle sensing solution: a single sensor captures a broad field of view, making fisheye cameras attractive for robot navigation and obstacle avoidance [1, 2].
Object detection is a fundamental perception task in these applications [3].
Annotating fisheye datasets is labor-intensive, and prior work has adopted COCO-pretrained YOLO-family detectors as a starting point for adaptation [4].
However, strong radial distortion causes spatially varying changes in object appearance and compresses objects near the image boundary, making features learned from perspective images less transferable to fisheye views [5, 6].
This limitation is particularly critical for mobile robots: pedestrians and obstacles entering the field of view may initially appear as small, strongly compressed boundary objects. Missing these early observations reduces the time available for braking or replanning.

This projection-induced domain shift poses a key challenge when adapting pretrained object detectors to fisheye imagery.
As illustrated in Figure , directly applying the COCO-pretrained extra-large YOLO26 model (YOLO26-x) to the mirror-view right (MVR) validation split of WoodScape [1] yields only 0.14800.1480 mAP50\mathrm{mAP}_{50} for car, person, and bus, while the complete cross-view fine-tuning reaches 0.31560.3156.
Beyond boundary compression, training-light transfer involves two additional challenges.
Distorted object appearances can misalign the backbone features learned from perspective images, while overlapping crops used to recover peripheral objects can introduce duplicate and conflicting detection hypotheses.

Existing distortion-aware approaches involve different adaptation costs. Projection-aware kernel adaptation can require camera calibration [7]; rectification networks introduce an additional preprocessing model [8]; and deformable convolution methods modify the feature extractor and typically require full-model retraining [9].
Generic parameter-efficient adapters reduce the number of updated parameters, but are not designed for the spatially non-uniform distortion of fisheye images [10].
Slicing and multi-view inference enlarge small boundary objects, but conventional suppression or fusion treats redundant detections without explicitly considering whether they are supported across multiple projections [11, 12, 13].
Although these methods provide useful building blocks, their integration within a frozen-backbone fisheye adaptation framework remains less explored.
This observation motivates the central question of this work: can a COCO-pretrained detector be adapted to fisheye imagery without full-model fine-tuning, while jointly addressing input-level boundary compression, feature-level misalignment, and decision-level cross-view conflicts under a limited labeling and training budget?

We answer this question with FUSEye, a training-light framework, which views the transfer gap as a chain of three causally linked problems rather than a single capacity deficit.
At the input level, boundary objects are too compressed for the network input scale, so overlapping grid view generation and box remapping (GridViews) generate the full frame plus four overlapping patches and remap all boxes back to the original coordinates, requiring no calibration or dewarping.
At the feature level, radial distortion misaligns the features extracted by the shared backbone, so zero-initialized residual adapters (Z-Adapters) are inserted at three high-level backbone stages; the zero-initialized output projection keeps the pretrained model unchanged at the first step and then learns a residual correction for the fisheye domain with only 222,480222{,}480 parameters on YOLO26-x.
At the decision level, multi-view inference produces duplicate and conflicting detections, so cross-projection agreement fusion (AgreeFusion) clusters per-view detections by class and intersection over union (IoU), re-scores multi-view clusters with a learned scorer of about 4,4004{,}400 parameters, applies confidence-weighted box fusion, and preserves the baseline precision policy for single-view detections. GridViews supplies candidates for AgreeFusion, while Z-Adapters preserve initial per-view predictions. Each component can be ablated independently with the backbone frozen.

On the WoodScape MVR validation split, FUSEye improves YOLO26-x from 0.14800.1480 to 0.26610.2661 mAP50, retains 84.3%84.3\% of fully fine-tuned accuracy while training far fewer parameters, and preserves 97.6%97.6\% of its full-label performance when trained with only 25%25\% of the labels.
It also generalizes across YOLO families, improving mAP50 by 0.05800.0580–0.08290.0829 on the extra-large variants of YOLOv8, YOLOv10, and YOLO11 (YOLOv8-x, YOLOv10-x, and YOLO11-x) and the extended YOLOv9 variant (YOLOv9-e).
Because FUSEye requires no camera calibration or dewarping and updates no backbone weights, it fits the label- and training-compute-constrained settings in which robots adapt their detectors; its only deployment overhead is running the same frozen-backbone detector over the five overlapping views.
In summary, our contributions are listed as follows:

We propose FUSEye, a lightweight modular framework for adapting COCO-pretrained YOLO detectors to fisheye imagery without full-model fine-tuning.

We propose FUSEye, a lightweight modular framework for adapting COCO-pretrained YOLO detectors to fisheye imagery without full-model fine-tuning.

FUSEye consists of three coordinated modules targeting different stages of detection.

It improves YOLO26-x from 0.14800.1480 to 0.26610.2661 mAP50\mathrm{mAP}_{50}, retains 84.3%84.3\% of full fine-tuning performance and 97.6%97.6\% of full-label performance using only 25%25\% of the labels, and consistently improves YOLOv8–11 detectors.

title: Mind the Refinement Gap: When Safe High-Level Robot Plans Produce Unsafe Executions
authors: Stabak Das,Priyesh Ranjan,Xiangfang Li,Lijun Qian
abstract: Language-enabled robot systems increasingly combine semantic-graph planning with temporal-logic safety monitors. We investigate a trace-completeness assumption in these systems: whether the high-level action sequence checked by a monitor represents the navigation and implicit action effects induced during execution. We audit this assumption in RoboGuard by comparing its verdict on a surface plan with its verdict on a graph-refined trace under the same Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specification. Our evaluation comprises 28 controlled cases spanning five action-abstraction families and 14 end-to-end cases in which SPINE [5] generates plans from natural-language instructions while RoboGuard generates scene-grounded safety specifications. In the controlled evaluation, all 12 targeted abstraction cases exhibit the predicted surface-versus-refined discrepancy while all 16 controls behave as expected, motivating graph-based trace refinement as a lightweight mitigation and a diagnostic tool for physical-AI safety monitors.
introduction:
Language-enabled robot planners increasingly use semantic graphs to connect natural-language instructions with objects, regions, and executable robot actions. Formal safety monitors can then evaluate the resulting plans against temporal-logic requirements. However, the guarantees provided by such a monitor are necessarily relative to the action trace that it observes. A semantic graph may contain enough information to identify an unsafe route, yet that information may never reach the monitor if navigation is represented only by its destination or is hidden inside a higher-level action.

For example, a surface plan may contain only goto(safe_lab_1), although graph search realizes the action as goto(construction_area_1) followed by goto(safe_lab_1). Similarly, an action such as inspect(sensor_1) may implicitly navigate to the object’s associated region without exposing that navigation as a monitored proposition. A prohibition against entering a construction area can therefore be satisfied by the surface trace while being violated by the graph-induced execution
trace. This is not a failure of temporal logic itself; it is a mismatch between the abstraction verified by the monitor and the behavior induced by the robot API.

RoboGuard [6] provides a suitable system for studying this boundary. It uses a protected language model to ground natural-language safety rules in a semantic graph, generates LTL specifications, and applies temporal-logic control synthesis to proposed robot API actions. Our central question is:

Let CC be a forbidden construction region. RoboGuard grounds the corresponding safety rule as the LTL invariant

We investigate this question at two levels. First, a controlled suite contains 28 fixed-plan cases with manually specified LTL constraints: 12 targeted abstraction cases and 16 safe or explicitly unsafe controls. The cases cover direct-action controls, hidden-waypoint position, route selection, action refinement, and multi-action plans. Second, a 14-case end-to-end suite provides natural-language tasks to SPINE and safety rules to RoboGuard over four paired semantic-graph scenarios. It covers goto, inspect, and map_region, including unique unsafe bridges, matched safe corridors, and graphs containing both safe and unsafe alternative routes.

Our contributions are:

A controlled methodology for distinguishing action-abstraction
failures from specification-generation failures by evaluating surface and
graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

A controlled methodology for distinguishing action-abstraction
failures from specification-generation failures by evaluating surface and
graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

A collection of paired negative cases and controls covering explicit
navigation, hidden intermediate regions, implicit navigation, route
choice, action refinement, and multi-action plans.

An end-to-end SPINE–RoboGuard evaluation that records planning,
contextual grounding, verification, graph-oracle, and interface failures
as separate outcomes rather than conflating them with safety verdicts.

An evaluation of graph-based trace refinement as a minimal mitigation
that exposes safety-relevant execution events already represented in the
semantic graph.

Our experiments operate over static semantic graphs and graph-derived execution traces. They do not model continuous robot dynamics, perception errors, collision avoidance, or physical execution. Accordingly, our claims concern the soundness of action-level monitoring relative to documented high-level execution semantics, rather than complete real-world robot safety.

1. A controlled methodology for distinguishing action-abstraction
failures from specification-generation failures by evaluating surface and
graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

2. A collection of paired negative cases and controls covering explicit
navigation, hidden intermediate regions, implicit navigation, route
choice, action refinement, and multi-action plans.

3. An end-to-end SPINE–RoboGuard evaluation that records planning,
contextual grounding, verification, graph-oracle, and interface failures
as separate outcomes rather than conflating them with safety verdicts.

4. An evaluation of graph-based trace refinement as a minimal mitigation
that exposes safety-relevant execution events already represented in the
semantic graph.

title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow
authors: Dongsu Lee,Haoran Xu,Amy Zhang
abstract: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent’s mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT), the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.
introduction:
Offline MARL is motivated by the need to learn coordinated multi-agent behaviors in safety-critical or cost-constrained domains where active data collection is infeasible or expensive, e.g., autonomous driving [1], logistics [2], and robotics [3]. In this setting, the learning objective is twofold. Agents must learn to coordinate their behavior from heterogeneous and suboptimal demonstrations, while avoiding the distributional shift that arises when the learned policy visits state-action regions unsupported by the data. Early offline MARL methods [4, 5, 6] rely on simple policy classes (i.e., Gaussian), which struggle to represent multi-modal and coordinated joint action distributions. When offline data contains a mixture of diverse coordination strategies, a unimodal policy often collapses onto a single mode and produces out-of-distribution joint actions that no agent in the data ever executed together.

To address this expressiveness gap, recent works adopt powerful generative models, including diffusion models [7, 8] and flow matching models [9, 10], as policy representations in offline MARL. Although these models improve the representational power of policy, their iterative sampling process incurs a high inference cost. MAC-Flow [10] and OM2P [9] mitigate this via one-step distillation and mean-flow generation, respectively. However, improved expressiveness and faster inference do not resolve a more fundamental limitation. Since the outcome policy is optimized against a learned Q-function, it inherently tends to collapse diverse coordination modes into a single or blurred one.

Methods that parameterize a policy and optimize it to maximize a learned Q-function must balance value improvement against staying close to the behavioral distribution. A fixed regularization coefficient controls this trade-off. If it is too large, the policy stays too close to suboptimal data; if it is too small, the policy exploits errors in the learned Q-function and produces OOD actions. Although this tension is well-known in single-agent offline RL [11, 12], the multi-agent setting introduces the following compounding difficulty. Training-time value maximization deforms each agent’s policy away from the behavioral prior, and the regularization coefficient bounds how far each marginal may drift, but cannot bound the compound effect on the joint. Even when every marginal remains within its individual support, the joint policy can place mass on action combinations that no trajectory in the data ever visited (i.e., regions where the learned Q-function is least reliable). In fact, the data may support multiple distinct joint modes of comparably high estimated value, but committing each marginal to a single greedy mode at training time discards the others before the agent has any way to tell them apart. Once new interaction data arrives, the policy can no longer use it to discriminate which mode is truly higher-value, because the alternatives have already been suppressed.

A natural alternative is to decouple two objectives, motivated by test-time training [13, 14, 15]. Instead of learning a policy that directly maximizes value, we keep the behavioral policy as a foundational prior and defer value-based refinement to test time. At deployment, we sample action candidates from this prior and then move them toward high-value regions using value gradients. The extent of this adjustment acts as adaptive control, replacing the need for a fixed regularization coefficient.

In this work, we ask a question not yet studied by prior works:

We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget.

We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap.

Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments.

1. We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget.

2. We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap.

3. Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments.

title: World Action Modeling with Progressive Visual Planning
authors: Fei Zhang,Zhaochong An,Duncan Frost,Yikai Wang,Pengfei Liu,Ya Zhang,Michal Drozdzal,Amir Bar
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual dynamics and actions from an initial observation and instruction. However, existing WAMs struggle with long-horizon prediction, as generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. Some recent WAMs address this by predicting a single future frame without generating the full video, but this approach neglects how to progress toward the goal. We present ProWAM, a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, providing explicit visual guidance to anchor action generation throughout task execution. This design scales naturally, as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, allowing the video backbone to offload complex visual planning from the action policy. For efficient action generation, ProWAM executes a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation and requiring only lightweight action denoising during replanning. Across extensive evaluations, ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks, it sets new state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Plus (85.8%) and randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), outperforming the strongest baseline with relative gains of up to +35.9%. On RoboCasa365, ProWAM achieves a 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, ranking 4th overall. Crucially, in zero-shot real-world experiments, ProWAM achieves 70.0% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes. These results demonstrate the value of progress-indexed visual foresight for closed-loop control.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models primarily inherit semantic knowledge from vision-language pretraining but remain data-hungry due to their reliance on large, costly collections of robot demonstrations (Kim et al., 2024; Black et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025). In contrast, world action models (WAMs) introduce a complementary source of transferable knowledge: visual-dynamics priors learned by video generation models from large-scale video datasets (Blattmann et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025). Recent WAMs have shown that incorporating such predictive visual knowledge can improve data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization in robotic control (Pai et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026c; Yuan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026).

Existing WAMs differ in how they utilize future visual prediction to guide action generation. Full-imagination WAMs (Pai et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026c; Li et al., 2026) leverage dense future rollouts that provide detailed near-term guidance but are inefficient as they require multiple denoising passes through a large video backbone. Alternatively, zero-imagination WAMs (Yuan et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026a) generate actions without predicting future visual states. Between these extremes, ImageWAM (Zhang et al., 2026b) conditions control on an action-horizon endpoint frame without explicitly representing intermediate visual states. These designs reveal a fundamental trade-off: dense visual rollouts provide short-horizon dynamics at high computational cost, whereas other efficient alternatives lack explicit intermediate-progress guidance over the full task.

To reconcile this trade-off, we introduce ProWAM, a progressive world action model that extends a single fixed-state prediction into an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals. Each sub-goal is indexed by normalized progress relative to the current state, where r=0r=0 denotes the current observation and r=1r=1 denotes the trajectory endpoint. This relative parameterization dynamically re-anchors sub-goals to the current observation, enabling consistent guidance across arbitrary task stages and varying trajectory lengths. Consequently, these sparse targets efficiently guide action generation without requiring dense video rollouts or separate high-level planning modules.

Specifically, ProWAM adopts a vision-action mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture consisting of a video generation expert and a lightweight diffusion-based action expert for policy generation. Each visual sub-goal is represented as a latent slot associated with a normalized progress value. The video expert jointly predicts near-term future transitions and progress-conditioned sub-goals, while the action expert attends to current observations and sub-goals to generate low-level action chunks. Asymmetric attention prevents action information from altering the visual prediction pathway. This design preserves the generative prior of the video expert, enabling video-only pretraining on large-scale action-free videos followed by joint fine-tuning on task-specific robot demonstrations to couple visual planning with action generation.
At inference, ProWAM reuses cached sub-goal features to eliminate repeated video-backbone computation, enabling efficient closed-loop control. Overall, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce progressive sub-goal imagination (Figure 1), a new visual planning paradigm for WAMs that represents long-horizon futures as an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals indexed by normalized task progress. This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

We introduce progressive sub-goal imagination (Figure 1), a new visual planning paradigm for WAMs that represents long-horizon futures as an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals indexed by normalized task progress. This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

We instantiate this paradigm in ProWAM, a WAM that natively integrates progress-conditioned visual sub-goal prediction with action generation for long-horizon control. By embedding sub-goal slots into the video pathway and coupling them via asymmetric attention, ProWAM enables scalable action-free video pretraining followed by joint vision-action fine-tuning. At inference, cached sub-goal features guide action denoising without repeated video-expert computation.

Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ProWAM achieves exceptional out-of-distribution robustness, setting a new state-of-the-art on LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) and randomized RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025) with an average absolute performance gain of +11.4 over prior WAMs. Furthermore, it ranks as the second overall on challenging long-horizon RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2024) benchmark, and outperforms DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026c) by +15.0 on zero-shot real-world tasks in novel scenes.

This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

By embedding sub-goal slots into the video pathway and coupling them via asymmetric attention, ProWAM enables scalable action-free video pretraining followed by joint vision-action fine-tuning. At inference, cached sub-goal features guide action denoising without repeated video-expert computation.

Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ProWAM achieves exceptional out-of-distribution robustness, setting a new state-of-the-art on LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025) and randomized RoboTwin (Chen et al., 2025) with an average absolute performance gain of +11.4 over prior WAMs. Furthermore, it ranks as the second overall on challenging long-horizon RoboCasa365 (Nasiriany et al., 2024) benchmark, and outperforms DreamZero (Ye et al., 2026c) by +15.0 on zero-shot real-world tasks in novel scenes.

title: Multi-Fidelity Policy Gradients Stabilize Data-Scarce Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xinjie Liu,Ruihan Zhao,Anirban Chaudhuri,Cyrus Neary,Ufuk Topcu,David Fridovich-Keil
abstract:
Policy gradient methods for on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) can become unstable when expensive, scarce target-domain data yield noisy gradient estimates. We address this challenge by complementing limited high-fidelity (HF)  target-domain data with abundant, cheap, but biased low-fidelity (LF)  data, e.g., from a simplified simulator.
Most existing methods directly optimize biased objectives based on LF data. In contrast,
the recently introduced multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework uses LF data solely to construct a control variate that reduces variance and improves HF data efficiency without biasing the policy gradient estimator.
However, published work on MFPG is limited to REINFORCE on small-scale simulation tasks.
We develop MFPG for modern actor-critic learning in GPU-parallel simulation and on a physical robot.
Our analysis and experiments show that naive extensions to proximal policy optimization (PPO) can lose cross-fidelity correlation or inflate variance.
Our MFPG-PPO addresses these failures by redesigning the sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation, and by monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation.
We also introduce a budget-aware MFPG-PPO to divide a fixed sampling budget among high- and low-fidelity data sources. Across simulated robot locomotion tasks of varying LF-to-HF transfer difficulty and HF data budgets, MFPG-PPO improves upon PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings, and consistently matches the performance of PPO trained with 16×16\times more HF data on the hardest task at the smallest HF budgets. In contrast, most baselines that use LF data perform well only where direct LF-to-HF transfer succeeds. MFPG-PPO enables stable learning on a physical Franka arm using only 4 real-robot episodes per update and no human demonstrations.
introduction:
On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) with policy gradient methods underpins advances in areas ranging from language-model post-training (Ouyang et al., 2022) to fine-tuning vision-language-action models (Lu et al., 2025) for robot control. Yet in many real-world settings, target-domain data are expensive
to collect and therefore scarce, e.g., a physical robot may collect only a handful of rollouts per policy update. In such data-scarce regimes, standard on-policy methods can break down because their policy gradient estimates become too noisy to support stable learning.

We study how to enable stable on-policy RL in data-scarce regimes, ultimately using as few as 4 real-robot episodes per update, or target-domain data batches up to 512×512\times smaller than in standard GPU-simulation RL pipelines (Rudin et al., 2022). The key is access to multi-fidelity data: we assume that the target environment (a physical system or high-accuracy simulator)
provides limited, expensive high-fidelity (HF) samples, whereas a simplified simulator provides abundant, inexpensive, but biased low-fidelity (LF) samples. Exploiting LF data requires care, however, and can easily bias policy updates and degrade performance in the target HF environment.

Existing approaches use LF data in different ways. Off-dynamics RL methods (Eysenbach et al., 2021; Lyu et al., 2024) learn to correct LF rewards for the dynamics mismatch, and sim-and-real co-training (Wei et al., 2025) mixes LF and HF data. However, reliability is a major challenge. Most of these methods still directly optimize biased objectives based on LF data, so their performance in the target HF environment is largely tied to how well policies learned from LF data transfer.

The recent multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework (Liu et al., 2026) offers a principled alternative. Here, LF samples are used to construct a control variate (Nelson, 1987)—a correlated auxiliary random variable with a known mean—for the HF policy gradient estimator. The MFPG estimator remains unbiased with respect to the HF objective, and the policy gradient surrogate variance shrinks as the cross-fidelity data correlation grows. MFPG is therefore robust to LF data biases.

However, the MFPG construction of Liu et al. (2026) is limited to the classic REINFORCE algorithm (Williams, 1992) and small-scale, single-environment simulation tasks. How MFPG interacts with modern actor-critic learning and GPU-parallel simulation (Mittal et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2024), and how it translates to real-robot learning, remain unresolved.
An earlier preprint (Liu et al., 2025)
directly substituted proximal policy optimization (PPO) for REINFORCE. The resulting
method did not consistently improve over the REINFORCE
instantiation and sometimes even underperformed single-fidelity
PPO. Hence, an effective extension requires more than algorithm substitution.

We address this gap with two contributions: (i) MFPG-PPO, a multi-fidelity PPO algorithm. Through analysis and experiments, we show how naive PPO instantiations of MFPG can lose cross-fidelity correlation or inflate variance by orders of magnitude. We address these failures by redesigning the sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation, and by monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation. Preserving correlation comes at the price of potential bias, a tradeoff we characterize analytically. (ii) A budget-aware MFPG-PPO. When HF and LF samples incur different costs, we allocate a fixed per-iteration sampling budget across fidelities, guided by the variance-minimizing allocation framework of Peherstorfer et al. (2016).

We test MFPG-PPO in GPU-parallel simulation (Mittal et al., 2025; Tao et al., 2024) and on a physical robot arm. Across simulation tasks and HF data budgets, we compare with 5 baselines that use LF data in different ways and with PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC) (Haarnoja et al., 2018) trained on HF data alone. MFPG-PPO is the only method in our comparison that improves over PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings, is never distinguishably worse, and scales monotonically with more HF data. Most baselines that use LF data perform well only where direct LF-to-HF transfer succeeds. On the hardest task at the smallest HF budgets, MFPG-PPO consistently matches the mean return of PPO trained with 16×16\times more HF data, cf. . Finally, MFPG-PPO enables stable RL on a Franka arm with only 4 episodes per policy update and no human demonstrations.

title: Network-in-the-Loop at Scale: GPU-Batched 5G Simulation for Massively Parallel Robot Learning
authors: Zifan Zhang,Mingzhe Han,Kannan Athreya,Yuchen Liu
subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: It is open source atthis https URL
abstract:
Massively parallel GPU simulators train multi-robot policies in thousands of environments, and many fleets use private Fifth-Generation (5G) networks, where each robot’s delay depends on its teammates’ traffic.
Network-in-the-loop training places a simulated 5G network inside this loop.
However, GPU robot simulators reduce the network to an independent delay per message, while packet-level simulators run one scenario per CPU process and cannot keep pace with thousands of parallel environments.
To bridge this gap, we present Isaac-Net, a GPU-batched 5G New Radio (NR) module that advances the uplink of thousands of environments in lockstep with Isaac Lab physics.
Isaac-Net simulates every slot, the 0.5 ms interval in which the base station decides which robots transmit, for all environments at once.
Extensive experiments confirm that its NR engine reproduces the median delay of ns-3 5G-LENA across loads, with a median delay 5–10% low on an unseen carrier and 9% high at 32 robots per environment in closed loop.
The engine also reproduces the Age of Information (AoI), the age of each robot’s newest delivered report, while an independent delay per message leaves the AoI tail about three times too light.
In a configuration validated against 5G-LENA, Isaac-Net keeps the network in the loop for about one million robots on one GPU at 83% of the Isaac Lab rate without the network, measured under a random policy.
Isaac-Net is open source at https://github.com/ZzZTripleZzZ/isaac-net.
introduction:
Robot learning has moved onto the GPU, where simulators such as Isaac Gym [1], Isaac Lab [2], ManiSkill3 [3], and MuJoCo Playground [4] step thousands of environments in parallel and feed the resulting experience directly into reinforcement learning.
This throughput has made it practical to train policies for whole teams of robots, such as warehouse fleets, drone swarms, and multi-arm workstations, in which each environment holds tens to hundreds of agents [5, 6].
Many of these teams report sensor data to an edge server and receive commands from it over a wireless network.
Moreover, private Fifth-Generation (5G) networks are increasingly deployed for mobile robots in factories and campuses [7, 8].
A policy trained for such a team therefore acts on information that the network may have delayed or lost, so the network belongs inside the massively parallel training loop.
We call such training network-in-the-loop, by analogy with hardware-in-the-loop testing, although the network inside the loop is simulated, not a real one.

In a 5G cell, the base station, called the gNB, divides one pool of radio resources among the robots in every slot.
A slot is a fixed scheduling interval, 0.5 ms at the common 30 kHz subcarrier spacing, in which the gNB decides which robots transmit based on channel quality and on Buffer Status Reports (BSRs), the reports in which robots state how many bytes they hold.
A robot may transmit only after the gNB sends it a grant, that is, a permission to transmit on given resources, which the gNB issues after a scheduling request and then sizes from later buffer reports.
A failed transmission is retried several slots later through Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ), a fast retransmission scheme of the radio link, and unsent messages wait in per-robot queues.
Consequently, the delay that a robot experiences depends on its own position and on what its teammates in the cell transmit, meaning that network behavior and team behavior are coupled.
This coupling also closes a loop between the policy and the network.
For instance, a policy may send more reports when reports arrive late, which could congest its own uplink and delay every later report.
A learning environment that captures this loop could teach a fleet when to send, how much to send, and where to move so that critical reports arrive in time.
However, GPU-parallel robot simulators typically model the network, if at all, as a fixed delay or as a delay drawn independently for each message.
For instance, the delayed actuator model of Isaac Lab [2] applies each command a set number of physics steps late, so it cannot express contention among teammates.

Motivation and Challenges: 
Putting a faithful 5G network inside a GPU-parallel training loop raises three challenges.
We measure simulation speed in robot-steps per second, where a robot-step advances one robot by one control step, the 100 ms interval at which the policy acts.
First, delays from contention among robots for the same radio resources, from HARQ retransmissions, and from scheduling arise per slot and persist across a robot’s successive messages.
Thus, an independent delay per message misses part of what a controller observes under load.
Second, a packet-level simulator on a CPU advances one scenario at a time, whereas GPU physics steps thousands of environments at once, so the network would stall the training loop.
Figure 1 shows that a pool of 12 ns-3 5G-LENA [9] processes, which run the 5G module of the packet-level simulator ns-3, delivers a few thousand robot-steps per second on a shared CPU.
One ns-3 process that advances in lockstep with the controller at 10 Hz keeps pace for only 48 robots.
In contrast, Isaac Lab physics alone reaches about 1.6 million robot-steps per second with simple sphere-shaped robots on one GPU.
Lastly, the network must stay aligned with 20 ms physics substeps and with control steps while Isaac Lab resets any subset of environments at any step.
A simulator that pauses or restarts as a whole would therefore hold back every other environment.

Limitations and Opportunities: 
Mature mobile network simulators, such as ns-3 with its LTE and 5G-LENA [9] modules, Simu5G [10], the Vienna 5G simulators [11], and the MATLAB 5G Toolbox, model cellular networks accurately, and Veins [12] couples such simulators with road traffic.
Recent works have also coupled robot simulators with network simulators [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 8], yet each typically pairs one robot scene with one network instance through the Robot Operating System (ROS) or a real-time broker, so it runs at or below wall-clock speed.
GPU network simulators such as GeDES [18] accelerate one large wired network.
Sionna SYS [19] batches the 5G link model and scheduler, but it keeps no queue per robot, no HARQ timing, and no uplink access driven by buffer reports.
QNet [20] learns when an agent should send over a shared network, yet its training network has no per-slot scheduling or HARQ and is not coupled to robot physics.

GPU-parallel reinforcement learning created three requirements that none of these tools meets together: 1) a batch dimension, so that thousands of independent scenarios advance together on one GPU; 2) lockstep with a physics engine, in which the network advances exactly one control step whenever the physics does, returns per-robot observations as tensors, and resets single environments at arbitrary times; and 3) closed-loop traffic and mobility, in which the policy decides what each robot sends and the physics decides where it is, so nothing can be precomputed or replayed.
Training experiments also need every environment to stay reproducible, which calls for a separate random stream per environment so that its results do not change with the batch size.
The network model must also avoid host synchronization, that is, it must never make the GPU wait for the CPU.
These requirements appeared with GPU-parallel learning, and Isaac-Net is built around them from the ground up.

Contributions: 
To this end, we develop Isaac-Net11

In essence, three core techniques are developed:

First, Isaac-Net stores each robot’s channel, scheduler state, HARQ processes, access timers, and message queue in fixed-shape tensors indexed by environment and robot. The same tensor operations then advance the state of all robots in all environments at every slot. Per-environment clocks, partial resets, and random draws keyed by environment and step let Isaac Lab restart any subset of environments while every other environment continues bitwise unaffected.

Second, a configurable NR engine (level L2 in the code) models 5G scheduling, decoding errors, retransmissions, and uplink grants, while a simpler prototype engine (level L2-legacy in the code) remains as a cheaper option. Equivalence tests feed identical random draws to a fast backend and the reference and compare every output and state value at every step, thereby verifying each speed-up before it runs at the scale of millions of robots.

Third, a mixin class, that is, a reusable add-on class, inserts the network through four hooks into any direct-workflow Isaac Lab environment, in which one class computes observations and rewards. It returns each robot’s Age of Information (AoI) [21], that is, how old its newest delivered message is, together with its queue length, Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and delivery flag. An Isaac Lab event term, a function called at every reset, redraws the radio parameters, so the policy trains over many radio conditions, which is called domain randomization.

Isaac-Net is released as the pip-installable package isaac-net, with its test suite, co-simulation bridges to ns-3 5G-LENA and to the OpenAirInterface (OAI) 5G stack [22], an Isaac Lab fleet task, and documentation on the project page.

Extensive experiments show that, in the scale configuration, that is, the validated NR configuration without the buffer-report grant procedure, Isaac Lab runs 1,048,576 robots with the network in the loop at 1.24 control steps per second on one GPU under a random policy, against 1.50 without the network. With that procedure and no fitted parameter, the NR engine reproduces the per-run median delay of 5G-LENA within a median absolute error of 2.5–4.8% from light to saturated load. Under load in closed loop, it also reproduces the AoI that a hand-written controller, not a learned policy, observes over ns-3, while an independent delay per message, even one drawn from the engine’s own delays, leaves the AoI tail about three times too light.

To the best of our knowledge, Isaac-Net is the first 5G network model that runs batched on the GPU inside a massively parallel robot learning loop.
